23500: A pilot hatchery for the locally common serranid is currently under development in Redondo Beach, CA. A captive broodstock of 36 adult individuals began voluntary spawning on May 19, 2002. Adult spotted sand bass were captured via hook and line from San Diego Bay, San Diego, CA. Eggs were collected continuously throughout the Summer into Fall 2002 until spawning ended in early December. Water temperature ranged from 18.5-22.5°C during that same timeframe. Spawning, and corresponding behavior, was documented in the evening hours (1700- 2100 hrs). Eggs were hatched from random spawns based on tank availability. Hatching rates in excess of 90% were routinely achieved, with hatching occurring 18-26 hrs after spawning. Large hatches (>200 individuals) of larvae were successfully developed up to 24 days after hatch (dah) with oldest larvae reaching 35 dah. Settlement was found to initiate after 25 dah in limited observations.

23501: Green frogs (Rana clamitans) are a ubiquitous species in Kentucky, and previous investigations have shown their larvae to consume algae as the largest component of their diet. Other studies on conspecifics have documented that detritus, and not algae, is the major dietary food. Our study investigates the assimilation of nutrients based on a strict algal diet in R. clamitans tadpoles. Through a series of feeding experiments using algal foods in a tadpole jello presented to the larvae, we were able to measure various nutritional components of the diet. Food passage rates were also measured both at the beginning and end of the study using fluorescent dye markers in the jello. R. clamitans were found to be very efficient consumers of algae. They were able to metabolize 87% of the energy they consumed as well as 82% of the organic matter available in the algal food. The algal food contained a 37% crude protein content of which 92% was assimilated by the tadpoles. Although algal phosphorus concentrations were low, the tadpoles were able to assimilate 95% of what was available. An average of 90 calories was consumed per group of five tadpoles. Clearance rates were found to be 9.8 hours at both the beginning and the end of the study. From the nutrient assimilation data, we conclude that R. clamitans are highly capable of utilizing algae as a nutritional food source.

23502: The reproductive biology of Paralabrax maculatofasciatus has received close scrutiny. In contrast, the spawning behavior of this diandric protogynous hermaphrodite has received far less attention. During the development of a pilot hatchery for the species, observations were made of the courtship and spawning of the captive broodstock. Most observations were made twice weekly from June-August 2002 during the hours of 1600-2000 via digital videotape. Two tanks housed a cumulative total of thirty-six adults, ten and twenty-six fish, respectively. Each tank contained a minimum of three males, determined by secondary sex characteristics. The predominant gender in each tank was female, to maximize egg output for the hatchery effort. Each tank represented a spawning aggregation density hypothesized for a diandric protogynous reproductive strategy. A low density tank of ten fish showed spawning activity dominated by a single male, who actively courted and pair-spawned with females, while intimidating subordinate males. The high density tank of twenty-six fish showed no male dominance and three major spawning types; pair spawning, sneak spawning and group spawning. Significant color modification was found within each sex and sexual dichromatism during spawning events. Females took on a overall darker green punctuated with dark vertical bars while males showed dark vertical bars with very light, off-white, background. The males were able to modify their color based on interaction intensity and type. Aggressive behavior was more prevalently during spawning periods, both male to male and male to female. Courtship and subsequent spawning occurred almost daily during the period of observation.

23503: A new species of genus Hyphessobrycon (Characidae) is described for the Parana river basin in Corrientes Province, Argentina. The new species is distinguished from all others in the genus by having relatively low body depth 30.3-36.8% SL; eye large 36.6-43.1% HL; maxillary bearing one small tooth typically tricuspidate; premaxilla with an outer row of 3-5 tricuspidate teeth; high number of anal fin rays 26-31; two humeral spots and a conspicuous dark lateral stripe widening at the base of the caudal fin and extending onto the middle caudal fin rays. Some additional considerations about the distribution of the genus in Argentina are included.

23504: Female home range was studied for the gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) on Ft. Stewart Army Reserve in Georgia. Gopher tortoises are long lived organisms (80+ years) and a keystone species in long leaf pine / wiregrass ecosystems. Most estimations of home range are based on short term radiotracking studies (1 year or less). We tested the relationships of short term radiotracking studies (1 active season) to long term recapture data (8 years) to assess which method provided a more accurate estimation of true home range. Fifty-three gopher tortoises were fitted with radiotags and were tracked from May through November 2002. All burrows and above ground locations were recorded using a GPS unit. Long term recapture data from 1994 to 2002 was used for female tortoises with three or more captures at different locations. The locations were mapped using ArcView and the home range analysis was performed using extensions of ArcView that included spatial analyst, 3D analyst, and Movement 2.0. Results will be presented and compared with published home range sizes. Vegetation studies were also conducted long term at Ft. Stewart and were used to observe the effect of vegetation on female homerange and burrow selection. X-rays were used to determine if there was any correlation between reproductive success (egg counts) to homerange size, or the quantity of vegetation available to the tortoises.

23505: This research was developed within a project named “Fishes of the Leticia’s Region” sponsored by the National University of Colombia, Colombian Tropembos Foundation and supported by the University of Seville, The CYTED of Spain and The Research Superior Council of Spain. This work was carried out using the material collected in 1999 in a black water stream named “La Arenosa” located at the 11th kilometer of the Leticia-Tarapaca (Colombia) road where 137 species, which belong to 7 orders and 27 families, have been reported. In order to know part of the trophic dynamics of the fishes community, there were carried out several stomach content analysis of 15 species, collected during the first semester of the year. The chosen species were, from the Perciformes order, Cichlidae family: Apistograma ortmanii, Cichla monoculus and Satanoperca jurupari. From the order Characiformes, Characidae family: Acestrorhynchus microlepis, Hemigrammus analis, Hemigrammus schamardae, Moenkhausia comma and Moenkhausia sanctafilomenae; from the Curimatidae family: Curimatella alburna, Semaprochilodus amazonensis and Steindachnerina guentheri; from the Gasteropelecidae family: Carnegiella strigata; from the Lebiasinadae family: Nanostomus marginatus and Pyrrhulina laeta; from the family Serrasalmidae: Serrasalmus rhombeus. To assess the dietary quantification subjective methods were used in order to find out the relevance of the different food items on each species; then, those feeding habits were related with the digestive tract morphology. It was found that the main alimentary resource is of allochtoneus origin, and is eaten by the majority of the species in the community. In the same way it was found a very close relation between the shape and the size of the digestive tract, stomach and pyloric ceca with the kind of food ingested.

23506: The fish eye muscle obliquus superior originates from the lateral surface of the ethmoid and inserts on the anterodorsal or dorsal rim of the eye ball. In teleosts, the section of the nervus olfactoris (cranial nerve I, the olfactory nerve) exposed in the orbital cavity is either on the external side (e.g., in most lower teleosts) or the internal (or medial) side of the muscle obliquus superior. In most cases, this muscle has no lateral extension and is only placed next to the side of the nerve. However, in Neoscopelus and some perciforms (i.e., Centropomidae, Percichthyidae, Carangidae, Menidae, Leiognathidae, Sciaenidae, Polynemidae) the dorsal surface of a section of this nerve is surrounded by a lateral extension of the muscle obliquus superior. This muscle in Elop and some perciforms (Glaucosomatidae, Bramidae, Toxotidae, and Nandidae) completely surrounds a section of this nerve. Distributions of the character states of these characters (relative position of the muscle and the nerve and enclosure of the nerve by the muscle) are reported. Character polarity is discussed and these morphological variations are applied to discuss the teleostean relationships.

23507: This studies deal with the reproductive ecology of Mannoprhyne herminae (Anura: Dendrobatidae) in Mountain Coastal Range of Venezuela, through the study of 84 females and 234 males. The obtained data allowed to evaluate the reproductive phenology and the quantitative relationships between corporal characteristics of both sexes and the reproductive variables associated to them. The reproductive events in this species showed a seasonal pattern, concentrating on the months of rain, with absent or not very representative reproduction in the months of drought. The litter size for female varied from 5 to 22 eggs (11.24 ± 2.86, n = 84). A positive relationship was detected among the corporal size of the female with the litter size and the diameter average of the eggs for litter. Contrarily to that waited, a positive relationship was observed between the number and the diameter of the eggs, but no relation was observed between the number and the variability of the size of the eggs. The number of tadpoles that the males transported varied from 1 to 15 (9.88 ± 3.80, n = 150), and was correlated negatively with the corporal size of males. Any relationship was observed among the male's size with the number of tadpoles that transported, neither with the longitude average of the tadpoles, neither with the coefficient of variation of the longitude of the tadpoles. Any male was observed transporting a bigger number of tadpoles that the maximum number of ovum of the ovarian complement of the females, that which seems to indicate that the males of this species take care and they transport a brood at the same time. Some aspects are discussed on the type of mating, the energy allocation to the descendants, be already eggs or tadpoles, and their variations with regard to the corporal size.

23508: The viviparous dinematichthyine fishes live mostly in cavities in coral reefs and rarely obtain more than 10 cm. They occur in the Indo-Pacific and the West Atlantic. Until the introduction of scuba diving and the use of fish poison they were rarely caught, but with these methods the catches exploded so many museums now hold large numbers of these fishes. An ongoing revision of the American dinematichthyine fishes based on ca. 1500 specimens has enhanced the known diversity of the group with two new genera and 26 new species. The following taxa are now in press or in preparation: Dinematichthys (1 W. Atlantic species) - Gunterichthys (1 W. Atlantic and 2 new E. Pacific species) - Ogilbia with 8 (7 new)) W. Atlantic species and 12 (9 new) E. Pacific species) - Typhliasina (resurrected with 1 W. Atlantic cave species) - New genus A (with 7 new W. Atlantic species) - New genus B (with 1 W. Atlantic species). The main separating characters are male pseudoclaspers, head pores, otolith, gill rakers, morphometric proportions, and finray and vertebral counts. This presentation briefly outlines the characteristics and distribution of the American species.

23509: The present study was carried out in the Ferreira Penna Scientific Station (ECFP), administered by the Museu Paraense Emilio Goeldi (MPEG). Located approximately 400 km east of the city of Belem, State of Para, Brazil, this area is characterized as a river-lake transition (ria fluvial) area due to geologic events that occurred during the Holocene and differs from the others rias of the Central Amazon. These features are mainly related to the low variation of water level (less than 2 meters in a year), which prevents the formation of floodplain lakes or even riparian zones that are used by fish species as sites for feeding and shelter. This paper presents an estimate of fish species richness in the Ferreira Penna Scientific Station calculated by means of protocol techniques. One hundred and forty-two species were obtained, 39 of which could not be identified beyond the level of morphospecies. This is considered to be a representative sample of the local ichthyofauna due to the extensive collecting performed. The characterization of fish communities and identification of species distribution patterns in the habitats under study were also conducted. Results indicate species composition in communities follow a pattern of substitution and addition. The greatest diversity of species was observed by the river mouth. Increase in area and water volume in some riverine habitats allows for their exploitation by a larger number of individuals or by new species.

23510: Peacock Cichlids (Cichla) are the favorite sport fish in Venezuela, due to their large size, excellent taste, and the tremendous fight they put up when hooked. This situation has made the lower Ventuari River a must visit fishing site for both national and international sport fishers. To evaluate the sport fishery of this area, we followed the activity of sport fishers in February and March of 2002, recording lengths and weights as well catch per fishing effort. A total of 1900 hours of fishing produced data on 760 Peacock Cichlids pertaining to three species: C. temensis, C. orinocensis and C. intermedia, a harvest rate of about 40 Peacock Cichlids per day per fisher. Inexperienced fishers harvested fewer, about 15 per day. The largest fish observed were C. temensis with 783 mm standard length and 7.000 grams (average 400 mm SL and 1535 g live weight); C. orinocensis reached 480 mm SL and 2.500 g (average 301 mm and 661 g) and C. intermedia 510 mm SL and 1800 g (average 332 mm and 833g). A combination of sport and subsistence fishing pressure that concentrate on Peacock Cichlids has led to declines in both maximum size of trophy fish and the total number of fish harvested in the region. Recommendations to preserve the fisheries are present.

23511: During dry months February - March 2002, populations of Peacock Cichlids (Cichlidae Cichla spp) were studied on the Ventuari River, Amazonas, Venezuela. A general fish inventory, population structure evaluation, habitat use analysis, reproduction and diet evaluations based on specimens obtained from sport fishers provided data for this study. We also studied Peacock Cichlid harvest by subsistence and commercial fishers. Three species are present: Cichla temensis, C. orinocensis and C. intermedia . The first two were most abundant and distributed among most habitats evaluated (lagoons, principal river channel, sandy beaches), C. intermedia was restricted to the main channel. C. temensis was the largest in standard length and weight (averages of 400 mm and 1535 g), C. orinocensisaveraged 301 mm and 661 g, and C. intermedia 332 mm and 833 g. Four hundred stomachs were analyzed (mostly by stomach lavage) of which 105 (92 empty and 13 full) were from C. temensis, 278 (202 empty and 76 full) from C. orinocensis. and 17 (14 empty, 3 full) from C. intermedia. Fishes were the principal food item found in stomachs. Reproduction in Cichlaspp takes place throughout the year with a peak the beginning of the rainy season (April to May). Females and males in stages II, III, IV, V and VI were observed during this study. Estimates of fecundity for Ventuari Peacock Cichlids are 3,647 ovules for C. orinocensis and 4,866 for C. temensis. No mature females were found for C. intermedia. Peacock Cichlids are a primary resource during the dry season (late December to April) for subsistence and sport fishers. Commercial fisheries concentrate on catfish. Interviews with locals indicate that Cichla populations have declined in recent years because of local population growth and illegal gold mining colonies.

23512: The Ventuari River, a tributary of the Orinoco River in Amazonas state, Venezuela is the principal river of the region studied. As with most Guyana Shield rivers, it is poor in nutrients, and the water has high transparency and acid pH. To better understand the richness and composition of the fish fauna of the lower Ventuari and establish criteria for management purposes, fish inventories were carried out from 1989 to 2002 by different institutions, among them UNELLEZ- Guanare, INIA in Puerto Ayacucho, and the LaSalle Foundation in Caracas. Many different methods and types of gear were used to capture the fish, such as nets of different sizes and meshes, and hook and line with both artificial lures and live bait. In addition, fishery activities of all types were recorded. We found 354 species of fishes grouped in 36 families and 10 orders, the most important of which were> Characiformes (57%), Siluriformes (21%), Perciformes (12%) and Gymnotiformes (6%). The most common fisheries observed were 1) subsistence fishing, 2) sport fishing (21 species were caught, but Peacock Cichlids were favorites), ornamental fishing (concentrating on 20 species, the most sought after being certain sucker mouth catfishes, Orinoco Angelfish (Pterophyllum altum) and other cichlids. The fish fauna of the Ventuari is one of the richest in all the Orinoco Basin. The fishes are threatened by local gold mining and over-exploitation of certain species that goes unchecked by government officials. Local fish biodiversity, lower quality sport fishing and damage to local aquatic ecosystems are to be expected as a result.

23513: The copperhead, Agkistrodon contortrix, is a medium-sized viper that occurs from southwest Texas east to Florida and northeast to New England. As part of an ongoing mark-recapture and radio-telemetry project in northwest Arkansas, we have monitored a population of copperheads over the past 6 years. Data collected for all individuals included SVL, sex, habitat type, location, air temperature, and any reproductive activity or foraging behavior observed. In addition, 15 snake-years of radio telemetry data were used to evaluate temperature profiles, home range size and movement rates. One hundred twenty snakes were captured (62M : 58F), with 23 recaptures, with an average SVL of 61.1 cm and 43.4 cm for males and females respectively. We located snakes most often in association with rock outcrops and glade habitat. Radio telemetry data indicates capture sites are biased and not indicative of the actual habitat utilization of these snakes. Copperheads have small home ranges relative to other crotalines, but greater movement rates. Agkistrodon contortrix at our study site seem to be active at higher temperatures than reported elsewhere. Copperheads apparently mate in the spring and fall near the den entrance. Females give birth to neonates in mid September at an average length of 17.4 cm SVL, and have a smaller clutch mass when corrected for body size of the mother relative to other vipers. Males have a larger average home range size than females. Morphology and ecology of Agkistrodon contortrix indicates that the copperhead follows the syndrome hypothesis associated with being an active forager, when compared to other crotalines.

23514: The lanceheaded pitvipers of the genus Bothrops (Serpentes, Viperidae) comprise about 40 currently recognized species that are responsible for over 90% of snake bite envenomations in Brazil. Despite its medical importance the phylogenetic relationships within this group are still uncompletely known and its biogeographic history is poorly understood. In the scope of an international research project we investigate the phylogeography of some of the most common species in the Southern part of Brazil (B. jararaca, B. neuwiedi and B. alternatus). Methods include the analyis of distributional patterns, external morphology and several genetic markers (mtDNA and tRNA). One major problem of the project is how climatic and vegetational shifts during the past may have influenced phenotypic and genetic differentiation of populations in our study area, especially between the Araucaria highlands (Parana, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul) and the southern lowland regions (Rio Grande do Sul and Uruguay). The preliminary results of our study are discussed with reference to some theories of Neotropical biogeography.

23515: Although mtDNA markers have several properties that make them suitable for phylogeographic studies they are not free of difficulties, and phylogeographic inferences within and between closely related species can be mislead by introgression and retention of ancestral polymorphism. Here we combine different phylogenetic, phylogeographic, and population genetic methods to extract the maximum information from the Liolaemus darwinii complex. First, we estimate the phylogeographic structure of L. darwinii across most of its distributional range, and second, we estimate relationships between L. darwinii and the syntopic species L. laurenti and L. grosseorum. Our results suggest that range expansion of these lineages brought them into secondary contact in areas where they are presently in syntopy, and here we present the first evidence in lizards from temperate South America, for introgression (of L. darwinii mtDNA into L. laurenti and L. grosseorum), and for incomplete lineage sorting (between L. darwinii and L. Laurenti). We show that a combination of methods can provide additional support for inferences derived from any single method and thus provide more robust interpretations and narrow the range of plausible hypotheses about mechanisms and processes of divergence. Further studies are needed in this group of lizards, and in other co-distributed groups to determine if Pleistocene climatic changes could be a general factor influencing the evolutionary history of a regional biota.

23516: Cnemidophorus longicaudus is a teiid lizard restricted to the Monte region in western Argentina, with a latitudinal distribution of more than 2,000 km, reaching the Calchaquies valleys in the north and the Atlantic shores of Golfo Nuevo in the south. This latitudinal range of more than 17 degrees does not present any apparent geographic barrier. Although there is no clear evidence of morphological differentiation in populations along this range; some chromatic characteristics in the dorsal pattern are variable between northern and southern populations. Using a mitochondrial molecular marker (ND4), we evaluate the genetic structure of this species along all its geographical range. Phylogenetic and population genetic analyses results indicate deep genetic structure among populations of C. longicaudus.

23517: The characid subfamily Paragoniatinae, as presently defined, includes six genera (Prionobrama, Rachoviscus, Paragoniates, Phenagoniates, Leptagoniates, and Xenagoniates) characterized by a compressed and elongated body, and a long anal fin. The monophyly and relationships of this group has not been tested yet. However, it is possible to delimit a group within the Paragoniatinae, composed by Leptagoniates, Phenagoniates, and Xenagoniates, based on the possession of a short maxilla, not surpassing anterior eye margin, and an extremely reduced abdominal cavity, the length from snout to the end of abdominal cavity shorter than from that point to caudal-fin base. Within this group, Leptagoniates sp.n. is distinguished from Phenagoniates macrolepis by the presence of an adipose fin, and strongly upturned mouth (vs. terminal to slight upturned); and from Xenagoniates bondi by the absence of ectopterygoid teeth, posterior margin of infraorbital 3, 4, and 5 straight (vs. posterior margins concave), dentary teeth median cusp longer than lateral cusps (vs. approximately of the same size), and posterior mandible margin surpassing the anterior eye margin (vs. not reaching). Leptagoniates sp.n. is distinguished from Leptagoniates pi by the presence of more than 50 branched anal-fin rays (vs. less than 50), and dorsal-fin origin posterior to the tenth branched anal-fin rays (vs. anterior to the fifth branched ray); and from Leptagoniates steindachneri by the presence of 56 unbranched anal- fin rays (vs. 61-67 branched anal-fin rays), and tip of pelvic fin reaching the last unbranched anal- fin ray (vs. not reaching). Despite of only one specimen of the new species is available, we feel that its description is necessary for conservation purposes. Considering that the extensive hydroelectric damming planned for the Rio Tocantins and its tributaries associated with the little knowledge on the fish-fauna of that region can lead endemic species, as Leptagoniates sp.n., to extinction prior to their recognition.

23518: The South American genus Thayeria, known in the aquarium hobby as penguim tetras, comprises small characids restricted to cisandean northern South America rivers which shares unusual characters in the coloration, caudal fin morphology, and swimming behaviour. The last review of Thayeria was published in 1960 and from a total of four nominal species, three were then considered valid: Thayeria obliqua Eigenmann, Thayeria boehlkei Weitzman and Thayeria ifati Gèry. Since then, extensive material of the genus have been collected, adding much information about variability and distribution of the known species, but also revealing that our knowledge of the taxonomy of the genus was far from complete. The monophyly of the genus was provisionally supported by four putative synapomorphies: 1) lower lobe of the caudal fin longer than upper lobe; 2) short anal fin (with 12-16 branched rays) with last unbranched and the first branched ray substantially longer than the remaining rays, forming a falciform lobe; 3) a longitudinal black stripe extending from the lower lobe of the caudal fin to at least the caudal peduncle; 4) an upward oblique swimming behavior. Despite some of these characters being not unique to Thayeria, it is more parsimonious to interpret these similarities with other groups as homoplastic. After examination of material deposited in main zoological collections from South and North America, we recognized six species in the genus, recognizable mainly through color pattern: Thayeria obliqua, from middle Amazon and rio Madeira basin; Thayeria boehlkei, from the Rio Tocantins/Araguaia, Rio Xingu and Rio Tapajós basins; Thayeria ifati, from the Maroni and Approuague rivers in French Guyana; Thayeria sp.1, from the Rio Negro, upper Río Orinoco, and upper Amazon basin; Thayeria sp.2, from the lower Rio Tapajós in Brazil; and Thayeria sp.3, from the Rio Madeira, Rio Tefè, Rio Tapajós, Rio Uatumã, and Rio Trombetas systems.

23519: Phrynops hogei is a small freshwater turtle endemic to the Paraíba do Sul River Basin. The turtle has been listed as endangered in Brazil since 1989. I studied a population of P. hogei in a section of the Carangola River in Minas Gerais. Turtles were captured in unbaited fyke nets, measured, marked, and released in the area of capture. I captured 71 turtles, 36 (50.70%) males, 31(43.67%) females, and 4 (5.63%) juveniles. Males were smaller than females (mean 1.92 kg, SD 0.69) vs. (mean 2.17 kg, SD 0.84). Recaptures were found within 900 m of first capture. The capture rate was highly seasonal, with the sex ratio varying between seasons. The population studied had a small proportion of juveniles compared to adults, suggesting that the decline in population size could be due to recruitment. The most probable cause of lack of recruitment is predation of eggs and hatchlings, but also reduced fecundity due to senility or pollution must also be considered. Based on the observation that the majority of the turtles captured are near the maximum size observed for this species, it appears as though the population is composed primarily of adults near the point of senescence. However nothing is known about the longevity or fecundity of this species at advanced ages. The high incidence of captures during the dry season corresponded to movements associated with the nesting season, as more females were captured than males, and gravid female were captured only at this time of the year. I began this study under the premise that the lack of systematic collecting was at fault for not documenting the fact that populations of this species were more widely dispersed and in higher numbers than reported, this was not the case, Phrynops hogei is the most endangered species of turtle in Brazil.

23520: The objective of this study was to define the nesting period of Phrynops hogei and determine other aspects of the ecology of this species in order to make recommendations to aid in the conservation of this endangered species. All the females captured in fyke nets were x-rayed to determine the presence and number of shelled eggs. The variation in egg size and number was correlated to the size of the female. Juvenile habitat was noted. A total of 46 females were captured, four of which were gravid, two were collected in April 2001 and the others in March 2002. The number of eggs varied from 5-7. The gravid females weighed between 2000-2800 g and ranged from 29.5 to 31.3 cm in carapace length. The clutch size, weight, and volume of eggs were positively correlated with the carapace length of the female. Gravid females were found only during the dry season. We captured two hatchlings in the Carangola Drainage, one 720 m and the other 3.72 km from the main river channel. Both were found in small streams during the rainy season. In reality we still do not know enough about the ecology of this species to recommend any management procedures
23521: In the Amazon basin the close relationships of fishes and the flooded forests are well known. Fruits, seeds, insects and other items are important food sources for many fish species that forage inside the flooded forests. However, our knowledge about the rhythm of foraging of the different species in this kind of habitat is scarce. The objective of this study was to verify the rhythm of feeding activity of the fishes in the flooded forest of Janauacá Lake, a floodplain area in the Solimões River near Manaus. Fish were captured at 5:30 am, 11:30 am, 5:30 pm and 11:30 pm during two 24 hour cycles. Stomach repletion was utilized to verify the variation on feeding activity, both for species and trophic categories. Characiformes and Perciformes species predominated in the catches in daylight hours, while Siluriformes and Clupeiformes occurred mainly during the night. The majority of the species fed with higher intensity during the day. Regarding the trophic categories, only carnivores showed a significant variation on the degree of stomach repletion, feeding with higher intensity in the daylight periods (mainly during the morning). These results indicate that the fish fauna of the flooded forest is dominated by diurnal species that forage on different food items. The predominantly diurnal feeding activity of carnivorous fishes suggests that visual detection of the prey may be an important factor shaping the fish communities that forage inside the flooded forests.

23522: The Iguanodectinae is a small characid subfamily composed of two genera, Iguanodectes and Piabucus, and 10 species. Species of the subfamily occur in the rio Amazonas (including its main tributaries), Río Orinoco, rio Paraguai and rio Tocantins/Araguaia, as well as Atlantic coastal basins from golfo de Paria (Venezuela) to immediately south of the mouth of the rio Amazonas, including rio Capim. The monophyly of the subfamily is well established, however few studies dealt with relationships of the group with other characiforms and none with the relationships among its species. In order to provide a hypothesis on the phylogenetic relationships among the species of Iguanodectinae, 91 morphological characters from osteology and external morphology were compiled and analyzed by strict parsimony. The analysis included all valid species of the group (except Iguanodectes polylepis and Piabucus caudomaculatus), plus two undescribed species. Iguanodectes spilurus, considered a polymorphic species, was included in the analysis as six separate terminals, each one from a different river basin, in order to allow for resolution of its potentially complex phyletic nature. Eight families of Characiformes, as a total of 35 non- iguanodectine terminals, were included as outgroups. Two most parsimonious cladograms of 625 steps, CI. 0.2 and RI. 0.65, were obtained. The cladograms support the monophyly of the Iguanodectinae; the non-monophyly of Iguanodectes, with some of its species more closely related to Piabucus than to other species of Iguanodectes; the position of Iguanodectes geisleri as sister-group of the rest of the subfamily; and the presence of several lineages within Iguanodectes spilurus. Characters previously proposed for Iguanodectinae were reevaluated, and most of them shown to be sinapomorphies for subgroups of the subfamily.

23523: Anostomidae is a Neotropical fish group widely distributed in South America basins. The species Leporinus macrocephalus is an endemic species found in the Paraguay river basin. Stock characterization of populations from this region may hold practical implications for conservation biology. Microsatellite loci have recently been used for many biological applications, including conservation genetics. In this study we intended to develop microsatellite primers for genetic characterization of natural stocks, management and conservation of L. macrocephalus. Total genomic DNA was extracted from liver using phenol-chloroform protocol. DNA was digested with Dra I and Ssp I restriction enzymes, and 500-1000 bp fragments were recovered from agarose gel electrophoresis and purified by phenol extraction. These fragments were ligated in double stranded SNX linker. The selection of segments with AC repeats was performed with biotinilated oligonucleotides and magnetic bead covered with streptavidin. After this the selected fragments were amplified by PCR. PCR products were ligated into a pGEM®-T vector and inserted into competent E. coli cells. Positive colonies were screened by hybridization with AC oligonucleotides using ECL detection system. Thirty seven positive colonies were obtained which are been sequenced on an ABI prism 377 Sequencer using BigDye Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Ready Reaction (Applied Biosystems) kit. Until now nine sequences with microsatellites repeats were obtained. Primers are being drawing for checking the degree of polymorphism of these microsatellites.

23524: Freshwater turtles, especially species of the genus Podocnemis (Podocnemididae), are an important source of protein to human populations of the Amazon region. Predatory action inflicted by these local communities may cause decline in populations of podocnemidid turtles. The natural history of these animals is poorly known, even though this knowledge is of crucial importance to establish programs aiming conservation and management of these turtles. For the present work, two species of Podocnemis were investigated, each one from a different locality in the northwestern region of Pará state, Brazil: P. expansa was studied at Reserva Biológica do Rio Trombetas, Oriximiná, from October to December, 2001; P. erythrocephala at Comunidade do Alema, Terra Santa, from August to December, 2002. Biometrical measurements were obtained for 5 females of P. expansa and their respective eggs and hatchlings. For P. erythrocephala, no adult female was observed nesting, but eggs and hatchlings of 5 clutches were measured. Different parameters were investigated for each stage of development: width, length and weight for the eggs; weight, body height, carapace and plastron width and length, head width and tail length for hatchlings and adult females. These data provide information on intraspecific relation between clutch size and egg size, egg mass and hatching period, egg mass and hatchling mass, female size and clutch size.

23525: A defining feature of the Wilbur-Collins model was the hypothesized existence of a developmental threshold, a minimum size or condition that had to be exceeded before metamorphosis could occur. Despite the central role of this threshold in the model, it did not immediately attract the sustained attention of empiricists. Thresholds are important in empirical evaluations of plasticity because they are signposts in development, on either side of which expectations about developmental rate differ. Experiments that evaluate effects of larval environment, executed without regard to the threshold, will be unable to discern between the opposing effects of pre- and post-threshold development in the same environment. Moreover, experiments that fail to consider thresholds may suffer from increased error variance if treatments inadvertently straddle thresholds. We performed food manipulation experiments on isolated larvae to identify thresholds for metamorphosis in spadefoot toads (Scaphiopus, Spea). In contrast to earlier results, we found that all post-threshold larval stages respond to changes in growth opportunity. We also found interspecific variation in the threshold, which suggests that the threshold can evolve and hence can be an adaptation. Species like Bufo periglenes and Crinia georgiana represent threshold extremes, having large eggs and larvae that can transform without post-hatching growth; they thus are beyond the threshold at hatching. Such life histories raise the question: Why are there thresholds? They may carry a price, which is that larvae cannot transform unless they attain a given size. These life histories suggest that threshold evolution is constrained early in development by how parents allocate resources to numbers versus size of eggs and late in development by selection on size at metamorphosis. The threshold can be shifted all the way down to hatching, but only by sacrificing either fecundity or size at metamorphosis. If attaining some critical size at metamorphosis is an important component of fitness, then the threshold enforces that size, even if the parental allocation to eggs is very small.

23526: The Northwest Forest Plan is an ecosystem conservation plan on 24 million acres (10.8 million hectares) of federal land in western Washington, Oregon, and California, USA. Over 70% of the federal land in the plan area is protected in large reserves which are managed to protect and promote old-growth forests. Much of the remaining federal land is open for programmed timber harvest. Survey and Manage is a multi-species management provision of the Northwest Forest Plan intended to provide, in combination with other Northwest Forest Plan provisions, a reasonable assurance of persistence for species that may not be protected by the reserve system. Over 300 rare and little known species including fungi, bryophytes, lichens, mollusks, and a small number of vertebrates are covered. Five species of plethodontid salamanders (Plethodon, Hydromantes) have been on the Survey and Manage list. The primary threat to these salamanders is programmed timber harvest. Some, such as P. stormi, have small ranges that are not intersected by reserves, and all five species have subdivided populations with distinct genetic lineages. Will it be possible to maintain unique populations, and allow for other Northwest Forest Plan goals such as timber harvest? Surveys on a random grid showed that one species, Plethodon elongatus, was well-represented in the reserves. Its persistence seemed assured under the Northwest Forest Plan, so it was dropped from the Survey and Manage list in 2002. Some small unique populations, however, may be lost due to habitat destruction caused by timber harvesting. This outcome illustrates the tradeoffs that are likely to occur under large planning efforts where a portion of the landscape is set aside in reserves and other uses are allowed within the remainder.

23527: Intraspecific insular variations in ecological and behavioral traits have been reported in snakes. Most of these variations would stem from genetically based local adaptations or phenotypically plastic variations due to local environmental conditions. We have been conducting an ecological and behavioral study of a colubrid snake, Elaphe quadrivirgata, on the Izu Islands, which are comprised of more than 10 small islands. On one uninhabited islet, Tadanae-jima Island, snakes show a remarkable gigantism in adult body size, being more than three times larger in body mass and presumably more than ten years older than snakes of other adjacent islands. Although E. quadrivirgata is a rather aggressive snake, often attempting to bite people when being handled, specimens on Tadanae-jima Island, based on our experiences, seemed to be much docile, having less inclination to bite. Because there are few possible predators of E. quadrivirgata on Tadanae- jima Island, this "calm temperament" may reflect a local adaptation under the relaxed selection pressure or ontogenetically induced character through an experience without facing predators. To examine this, we first compared aggressiveness of adult snakes among several islands. The results supported our original impression that snakes on Tadanae-jima Island is less aggressive than those on the other islands. The results also showed the presence of other geographic differences in defensive responses among islands. We, then, examined the differences in aggressiveness of newborn snakes among islands. Contrary to adults, newborn snakes exhibited few geographic differences in aggressiveness. We will discuss the possible factors, such as the presence or absence of potential predators, and mechanisms that may cause the observed differences in aggressiveness of E. quadrivirgata among the islands.

23528: Following a decade of research on species distributions, phylogeography, phylogeny and morphological diversity, the Australian wet tropics now has one of the best known tropical rainforest herpetofaunas. This has revealed major effects of Quaternary fluctauations in rainforest area on patterns of both species and genetic diversity, and that spatial patterns of neutral-molecular and phenotypic diversity are quite uncoupled, the former occuring across major vicariant barriers and the latter across environmental gradients. These Quaternary fluctuations have contributed little to development of taxonomically recognised species, though there is evidence for hybrid breakdown on secondary contact between morphologically similar but long isolated lineages. The implications of these findings for conservation and the extent to which they can reasonably be extrapolated to other rainforest herpetofaunas will be discussed

23529: Very few studies had been carried out with the description of the diet of snakes, in situations of extreme environmental stress such as the filling of hydroelectric power plants reservoirs. Some authors would rather not correlate these data as a natural behavior, owing to the high availability of food source as the animals (potential prey items) move away from the flooding area. However, we do not believe that the prey preference would shift so much from the original pattern, and these data are important to be correlated to a priori and a posteriori study of the feeding behavior. This is a preliminary result of an ongoing study of the feeding behavior of reptiles in environmental stress situations in Central Brazil. The results are related to stomach contents of snakes that regurgitated during the rescue operation, and are to be confronted with stomach contents of preserved specimens from before, during, and after the flooding of the Cana Brava hydroelectric power plant reservoir in the state of Goiás, Brazil. In total we collected data from 19 species of snakes representing the families Boidae (N = 3; 15.8%), Colubridae (N = 15; 78.9%), and Viperidae (1; 5.3%). The family Boidae computed 15 prey items as 4 lizards (26.7%), 6 passerine birds (40.0%), 2 marsupials (13.3%), and 3 muridae rodents (20.0%). The family Colubridae computed 70 prey items as 47 amphibians (67.1%), 21 lizards (30.0%), and 2 snakes (2.9%). The family Viperidae computed 4 prey items as 2 lizards (50.0%), 1 marsupial (25.0%), and 1 muridae rodent (25.0%). These data suggest a wider range of prey items to several colubrids and that the differences are more related to the volume of stomach contents as the prey items were more abundant than to prey preference.

23530: Pelagic fish larvae were collected in a plankton net moored over a reef flat off Carrie Bow Cay, Belize. Larvae were transported into an adjacent laboratory where selected specimens were anesthetized and microscopically identified to morphological type if possible. One by one, the specimens were placed in a saltwater-filled glass tank and photographed. A glass plate supported by fishing line and weights was used to trap the specimen against the front of the tank. Very small specimens (< 10 mm) were placed in a depression slide, which was then covered with a flat microscope slide and trapped against the front of the tank. Photographs with a white background were taken using a Nikon D1X digital camera (5.3 megapixel) with a 105 mm f2.8D AF Micro- Nikkor lens, and synchronized dual Nikon SB-28X flash units mounted on tripods. The flash units helped to maximize the depth of field. Because the living larvae were transparent and most lacked strong color contrast, the photographs were purposely underexposed. The photographs were then adjusted using Adobe Photoshop to correct for the underexposure. 23531: The Gurjaú Reserve is located south the city of Recife, in the state of Pernambuco, Northeastern Brazil. It constitutes the largest Atlantic Forest Reserve in the Recife metropolitan area, including 1,077.10 ha of protected areas, of which 400 ha correspond to Atlantic Rainforest remnants. Between August of 2002 and February of 2003, we studied the amphibians of the Reserve through biweekly visits that lasted three days each. Through active search and the use of pitfalls, we registered the occurrence of 24 species of anurans in Gurjaú, pertaining to four families: Bufonidae (Bufo crucifer, Bufo granulosus, and Bufo jimi), Hylidae (Hyla albomarginata, Hyla atlantica, Hyla branneri, Hyla semilineata, Hyla raniceps, Hyla decipiens, Hyla aff. nana, Phyllodytes cf. luteolus, Phyllomedusa hypochondrialis, Scinax auratus, Scinax nebulosus, and Scinax x-signatus), Leptodactylidae (Adenomera sp., Eleutherodactylus sp., Leptodactylus labyrinthicus, Leptodactylus ocellatus, Leptodactylus natalensis, Leptodactylus troglodytes, Physalaemus cuvieri, Pseudopaludicola sp.), and Ranidae (Rana palmipes). 23532: Genus Eigenmannia belongs to the order Gymnotiformes (Pisces: Teleostei), a monophyletic group of electrogenic freshwater fishes. This genus is widely distributed in the Neotropical region, but species diversity is greater in the Amazon basin. The genus Eigenmannia is composed of small populations presenting low vagility. Previous cytogenetic studies carried out in specimens of Eigenmannia from the Upper Paraná basin, Brazil, resulted in the identification of five distinct cytotypes which exhibit remarkable differences in chromosome number and formula. Eigenmannia sp. 2 presents 2n=31/32 chromosomes and a multiple system of sex chromosomes. We herein report the isolation and characterization of five microsatellite loci in Eigenmannia sp. 2, which represents the first steps to study the population structure in species of this genus. For genomic library development, genomic DNA of Eigenmannia sp. 2 was isolated and fully digested with the restriction enzymes HaeIII, HincII and AluI. The products of digestion were separated on a 1.0% low-melting-point agarose gel and fragments ranging in size from 300 to 800 bp were isolated and cloned into dephosphorylated pUC18 digested with SmaI. The ligation products were used to transform DH5α competent cells. Colonies were lifted onto nylon membranes and hybridization was carried out using a (GT)15 oligonucleotide probe. Plasmid DNA from 200 positive clones was isolated and inserts were manually sequenced by the dideoxy chain termination method using M13 forward and reverse primers. Primer pairs were designed for eight microsatellite loci, five of which were successfully amplified. Five primer sets were used to screen 49 unrelated individuals of Eigenmannia sp. 2 to determine allelic diversity. The number of alleles per polymorphic loci ranged from 3 to 14. The primers were also tested for cross- amplification in 11 other species of Gymnotiformes. The isolation of microsatellite markers offers new opportunities for conservation and population genetics studies in species of Eigenmannia.

23533: Creation and restoration of habitats are often used as conservation and recovery measures, however to judge their efficacy, the response of the target organisms must be evaluated. We followed the survival of embryos and size of metamorphs of a polyploid member of the Ambystoma jeffersonianum complex and its sexual host the smallmouth salamander (A. texanum) in a created pond and a natural pond at Kickapoo State Park, Vermilion County, Illinois. For two of the three years of the study, the natural pond did not hold water and for one of those years the created pond dried prior to the metamorphosis of any salamander larvae. There was no difference in embryonic survival to hatching of polyploid embryos between ponds in 2002. Salamanders emigrated from the created pond earlier than from the natural pond. Polyploid metamorphs from the created pond were significantly larger than those from the natural pond. There was no difference in size of A. texanum metamorphs between ponds.

23534: Several aquatic vertebrates have been introduced to fresh water systems in California over the past 100 years. Some populations of the two-striped garter snake (Thamnophis hammondii) have lived in sympatry with these species since their introduction; other populations have never encountered them. To assess the possible adaptation to novel prey, we tested the predatory responses of T. hammondii from different populations to chemosensory cues from native and introduced prey species. We presented chemical extracts from potential prey types and two control odors to individual snakes on cotton swabs, and recorded the number of tongue flicks and attacks directed at each swab. Subject response was higher for prey odors than control substances, but response values did not differ as a function of subject gender. Odors from introduced centrarchid fish (Lepomis spp.) elicited higher response levels than other prey types, including native anuran larvae (Hyla regilla). The pattern of response was similar for both populations of snakes (experienced and naïve, with respect to the introduced prey). We suggest that the generalist nature of T. hammondii has allowed it to take advantage of increasing populations of introduced prey. Decisions on the management strategies for some of these introduced prey species should include consideration of how T. hammondii populations might respond in areas of sympatry.

23536: Comparisons of species richness estimates reveal interesting patterns regarding the ecological biogeography of flatfishes. Within all regions, flatfishes are most diverse where extensive continental shelves with complex habitats are located in shallow water. Generally, diversity of marine flatfishes increases along continental shelves from polar to equatorial waters, with maximum diversity of flatfish assemblages usually occurring on tropical and subtropical continental shelves within each ocean. Flatfish diversity is also high at continental shelf areas where components from different faunal provinces intermix. Lower than expected diversity is noted on continental shelf regions where cold-water currents and upwelling occur. In all oceans, but especially in the West Pacific, flatfish diversity is lower at insular compared with continental locations at the same latitude. Within each geographic region, continental islands (usually larger with heterogeneous soft-sediment habitats) generally support higher numbers of flatfish species than do oceanic islands (usually smaller with less habitat complexity) located in the same region. Among four tropical marine regions, the highest diversity of flatfishes occurs in the western Pacific (125 species compared with 45 in the western Atlantic, 43 in the eastern Pacific and only 38 species in the eastern Atlantic). Diversity of flatfishes in northern temperate and boreal regions is greater than that of corresponding areas in the southern hemisphere. Far fewer species are known from temperate and boreal areas in the Atlantic and eastern Pacific oceans compared with those from the western Pacific at comparable latitudes.

23537: We compared Geographical Information Systems (GIS) and survey estimates of the amount of gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) habitat and number of individuals on 44 conservation areas in Florida. Estimates of total amount of habitat on conservation areas >20 ha in size differed by about 11%, with survey estimates ("realized habitat") unexpectedly larger than GIS estimates ("potential habitat"). This difference resulted mostly from the subjective evaluation of habitat suitability employed in the GIS method. Estimates of total number of individuals on conservation areas >20 ha in size differed by as much as 46%. This difference resulted mostly from the different ways in which numbers of individuals are estimated in the GIS and survey methods and the different ways in which numbers of individuals are calculated from numbers of burrows. Despite the differences between GIS and survey estimates, the GIS method produced important information about potential high quality gopher tortoise habitat. This information helps to identify locations where innovative management techniques might allow the gopher tortoise to expand its distribution, and to inventory suitable, but currently vacant, habitat (because of population declines resulting from upper respiratory tract disease, for example) for future re-establishment efforts.

23538: We estimated the number of male boreal toads Bufo boreas in a metapopulation in Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado, USA, using standard capture recapture methods and the Jolly Seber model for open populations. These data show a decline in population. However, due to limitations inherent in the Jolly Seber model, we were unable to address certain issues such as individual heterogeneity in capture probability and temporary emigration (skipped breeding years by individual toads). Using the robust design allows us to account for temporary emigration. The robust design is particularly relevant to pond breeding amphibians that have an explosive breeding pattern where animals are temporally and spatially concentrated for a short period of time. This breeding pattern allows us to collect capture recapture data on multiple occasions within the year while more closely approximating demographic closure and allows the estimation of a number of parameters that cannot be assessed under simple models such as Jolly Seber and Cormack Jolly Seber. The robust design is seldom used in amphibian studies probably because long term data sets are still relatively scarce. Using the robust design we are able to estimate parameters of interest in less elapsed time (2 versus 3 years minimum), an important difference when dealing with declining species. This presentation reports estimates of survival and population size for both methods and the estimation of temporary emigration for a population of boreal toads; we compare the methods and outline the advantages of the robust design using field collected data.

23539: In the llanos ecoregion, cattle grazing is and has been the predominant mode of land use. However, in the llanos of Venezuela, the conversion of grazing pastures to cropland is ongoing and significant yet little is known about its effect on anuran assemblages. This study investigates the effects of land conversion by asking three questions: (a) Does anuran species composition change when land practices go from moderate cattle grazing to rice cultivation? (b) Does fitness vary between the two areas? (c) Does rice cultivation change the breeding phenology of anuran species? Field techniques for addressing these questions include breeding call surveys, visual encounter surveys, and larval surveys. This study was initiated in the rainy season of 2002 and will continue for the following two rainy seasons. Preliminary results indicate that there has been a shift in species composition. Of thirteen total species noted from the breeding call surveys, two (Physalaemus enesefae and Pleurodema brachyops) were not recorded in the rice-cultivated areas. Conversely, one (Leptodactylus macrosternum) was not recorded in the grazed areas. Similarly, results from the visual encounter surveys recorded five species in the rice-cultivated areas compared to six in the grazed areas. This research contributes to our understanding of shifts in species composition with land use change and also provides a foundation for future monitoring of the long-term effects of such changes.

23540: We studied the circadian rhythms in juveniles (< 6 mo.) of cave (troglomorphic), surface (eyed), and hybrids (F1 cave X surface) populations of the characid Astyanax fasciatus (Pisces: Characidae) raised under both, light and darkness conditions. Surface fish showed a marked circadian rhythms; cave fish were much more active than surface ones and although their circadian rhythms was less pronounced than for surface fish, it was still present. Hybrids showed a great deal of variability in their circadian activity. In general all fish were more active during daylight time. These results strongly suggest that circadian rhythms appear early on during development. They are also consistent with the close genetic affinity among these populations despite widely phenotypic differentiation.

23541: The Gerrhosauridae is a diverse group of scincomorph lizards endemic to southern Africa and Madagascar. Phylogenetic relations among Gerrhosauridae, Cordylidae, and Scincidae are not resolved definitively. While gerrhosaurids and cordylids are often treated as sister taxa, a previous morphological analysis suggested that gerrhosaurids are more closely related to scincids. Relations within Gerrhosauridae are unresolved, and a recent molecular analysis placed the purported basal gerrhosaurid, Angolosaurus skoogi, within the more derived genus Gerrhosaurus. To attain a clearer picture of relationships both within Gerrhosauridae, and among the other scincomorph lizard families, more data pertaining to purported basal taxa are required. I generated such data by studying the detailed cranial osteology of both articulated and disarticulated skeletal preparations of gerrhosaurids and cordylids, as well as digital images of A. skoogi scanned at The University of Texas High Resolution X-ray Computed Tomography Lab. This rare lizard is endemic to the Namib Desert, and spends over 20 hours a day buried beneath the sand dunes. Thus, skeletal preparations of this species are rare, and minimal knowledge of its osteology exists. With the new data obtained from CT scans, I rescored characters used in previous morphological analyses, and found new characters in complex regions of the braincase. These characters contributed to a systematic reevaluation of the gerrhosaurid clade, and tentatively support the basal position of A. skoogi within this family. These data also add insight toward relations between Gerrhosauridae, Cordylidae, and Scincidae.

23542: A taxonomic revision of Bufo granulosus complex was undertaken in order to determine their evolutionary units. 23543: Physalaemus as currently defined is a leptodactylinae frog genus widely distributed throughout southern Mexico to northern Argentina. It includes 41 species presenting a high degree of polimorphism. On basis of available data at 70’s, this species were partitioned into four groups sensu Lynch: P. biligonigerus group, P. cuvieri group, P. signifer group, and P. pustulosus group. After that, some species were described and associated to one of these groups, but other, like P. deimaticus and P. rupestris, could not be grouped. The P. pustulosus group was the only one clearly defined and included four species. For the other groups it has been pointed some problems, mainly on inclusion of species and definition of diagnostic characters. We present the redefinition of the species groups of the genus Physalaemus and the designation of the species associated to each one, based on morphometric characters, external morphology and some osteologicals features. It was analyzed male and female individuals of all species, except P. fischeri, as well as two species of Pleurodema and two species of Pseudopaludicola, both genera considered related to Physalaemus. To the 15 morphometric characters analyzed, it was performed a size-free discriminant analysis and UPGMA, with 1000 replications by the bootstrap method. These analysis demonstrated that the species of genus Physalaemus are associated into at least five clearly defined groups, from which one more close to Pleurodema and other to Pseudopaludicola; some suggested groups and species were not clearly associated. External morphological and some osteological characters were combined to the morphometric analysis to support the proposed groups. It was possible to define eigth groups: P. biligonigerus group (5 species), P. cuvieri group (9 species), P. henselii group (3 species), P. gracilis group (5 species), P. deimaticus group (2 species), P. olfersii group (4 species), P. signifer group (9 species), and P. pustulosus group (4 species).

23544: Tucurui reservoir is located in the central region of Para state. Its size is 2,430 km2. 23545: The Siskiyou/Klamath Region of northern California and southern Oregon, USA is known for its high biological diversity and numerous endemic species. 23547: The purpose of this investigation was to determine if bromelicolous frogs exhibit selection for territory sites, and, if so, which habitat traits are most important. In addition, we tested hypotheses about the relationship between a frog's physical condition and his territory quality. We focused on Scinax perpusillus, a treefrog that lives and breeds in bromeliads throughout the Atlantic Forest in Brazil. To estimate habitat quality, we measured morphometric and water quality traits in bromeliads, some with resident frogs and others selected at random. The traits measured included species, height off ground, size, leaf number, number of nearby plants, tank size, coverage, pH, and dissolved oxygen. Our approach to evaluate territory selection was hypothesis free; we used various statistical techniques to test which suite of habitat traits could best discriminate between bromeliads with and without resident males. We also captured resident males and conducted a variety of non-invasive performance tests to evaluate their physical condition. We found that the physical traits of the plant, including size and water storage volume, were generally less informative, and probably less important to the resident frogs, than ecological traits. Male S. perpusillus were more likely to be found in plants close to the ground that had high water pH and large tanks. Resident frogs were also more strongly associated with bromeliad clusters, and isolated clusters were even more likely to have resident males. Once territory selection was evaluated, we created an index of territory quality based on what seemed to be favored traits. There was a strong positive relationship between bromeliads with high index scores (i.e., favored plants), calling rate, and several physiological traits related to capacity for activity. This suggests there is a relationship between body condition, behavior and territory quality in Scinax perpusillus.

23548: This study determined the effect of landscape change and the intensity of land use on reproductive dynamics of Phyllomedusa tarsius (Anura-Hylidae), a species of tree frog in Central Amazonia. This study was conducted in five habitats: pasture, regrowth of Cecropia, regrowth of Vismia , forest fragments and continuous forest. I studied the hatching rate eggs, and quantities and dispersal of adults of P. tarsius in the five habitats. Phyllomedusa tarsius used all habitats, but the most successful reproductive was ponds in forest and ponds in Cecropia regrowth. Dispersal was studied only in males and it was principally between ponds in disturbed areas. This result suggests that subpopulations in disturbed areas are not dependent on the continuous forest subpopulations, and their maintenance is more related to local condition than individuals arriving from continuous forest subpopulations. 23549: We studied the diversity and distribution of amphibians, lizards and snakes of Jau National Park (JNP). We sampled the principal habitats (terra firme Forest, igapo Forest, regrowth areas, campina and campinarana Forests) during last seven years. Fieldwork to determine the distribution of animal species was carried out during 12 travels to JNP (total of 112 days). In each habitat, two people recorded all acoustic (frogs) and visual observations of these three groups. Also, we used pit fall traps and collect did by people that live in JNP. We found 43 amphibian species; with one new register to Brazilian Amazon (Aparasphenodon cf. Venesolanus), 26 lizard species and 43 snake species. The terra firme Forest was the major habitat, following by igapo Forest, campina and campinarana and regrowth areas. The comparison of the JNP species and other four Amazonian regions (Belem, Manaus, Santa Cecilia and Iquitos) show a high similarity in composition of snakes and lizards communities. Several important range extension were documented in JNP, specially for amphibians previously found in Belem or Manaus, such as Hyla wavrini, Osteocephalus oophagus and Hyla walfordi or in Iquitos or Santa Cecilia, such as Bufo nasicus, Chiasmocleis cf. anatipes, H. sarayacuensis. 23550: Tropical reef fishes display a striking array of body colorations and patterns, which may function to signal species identity. Wrasses (Perciformes: Labridae) are a speciose group characterized by diverse color patterns. The distribution of closely related labrid species spanning the Isthmus of Panama presents a unique opportunity for comparative study. The Caribbean is characterized by clear water and bright, visually heterogeneous coral reefs, while the Eastern Pacific is more turbid and characterized by dark, visually homogeneous rocky reefs. The purpose of this study was to identify environmental effects on visual signal evolution, and to track evolutionary trends in body color, pattern, and size in species diverging in sympatry and allopatry. A species-level phylogeny of New World labrids was constructed from 16S, 12S, and CO1 gene regions. Color, pattern, and size characteristics of terminal-phase individuals of each species were mapped onto the species tree. Independent contrast analysis was used to determine ancestral states at interior nodes, and the directionality of evolutionary change was tested. Environmental tuning of visual signal components is discussed in terms of eastern Pacific and Caribbean ambient visual environments. This type of comparative analysis may prove to be critical in understanding the evolution and function of color patterns in reef fishes.

23551: Bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas, are a cosmopolitan species occurring in warm-temperate and tropical coastal regions, including the Gulf of Mexico. A total of 180 specimens were collected from both fishery dependent and independent surveys from Louisiana, Alabama, and Florida. Samples ranged from 555 - 2190 mm FL. Vertebrae were removed from below the first dorsal fin and processed for ageing. Samples were cleaned and a 0.3 mm section was cut and stained using crystal violet. Samples were aged by two of the authors, first independently and then after consultation for samples for which an ageing disagreement had occurred. A final age was assigned to each specimen and a von Bertalanffy growth model with Fabens adjustment was fitted to the observed data. The preliminary VBGF, for combined sexes, predicted Linf: 2204 mm FL and K: 0.09, with given a size at birth of 700 mm. Growth models were also fit to the back- calculated age estimates. Preliminary results indicate differences in both parameter estimates to those previously published with our model predicting a lower Linf and a higher K value.

23552: The North American Amphibian Monitoring Program uses a categorical calling index (ranging from 0 - 3) to estimate anuran abundance. Monitoring the green frog (Rana clamitans), this study compared population estimates obtained using three other methods (calls per minute, a visual encounter survey, and mark recapture) to populations categorized under the various levels of the calling index. Analysis of variance showed that mean population size estimates obtained using all three techniques differed significantly among estimates assigned to the various levels of the calling index (p < 0.001). Additionally, calls per minute per male were negatively correlated with male population size. This suggests that territoriality occurs in these populations, with a higher proportion of noncalling satellite males at high population densities. Thus, noncalling satellite males could reduce the accuracy of population estimates based on calls. These data support the assumption that various levels of the calling index are correlated with actual green frog abundance, but also indicate accuracy may decline at high population densities.

23553: Fishes of the genus Centropomus, known as snooks, represent species of great economical relevance and are widely distributed throughout the American shore. For molecular analysis, three other wild populations of C. mexicanus were surveyed [Cabo Frio, RJ - population 1, Angra dos Reis, RJ - Population 3 and Guaratuba, PR - Population 4] as well as a captive population from LAPMAR, at Floriano’polis, SC (Population 2), all comprising 20 individuals per locality. DNA samples were obtained from liver and amplified via PCR using four RAPD primers from Amersham Pharmacia Kit. The allele frequencies were calculated by the software TFPGA 1.3 and PopGene 1.31. The cytogenetical results demonstrated a great karyotypical similarity among populations, all composed by 48 acrocentric chromosomes and presenting pericentromeric single NORs, without any populational chromosomal marker for the species C. mexicanus by far. The inter- and intrapopulational RAPD molecular analysis revealed that the genetic variability measured by the proportion of polymorphic loci, was 81%, 74%, 79% and 91% for populations 1, 2, 3 and 4, respectively, where the population composed by cultured fishes presented the lower variation. 23554: Tunas are the only teleost fishes known to elevate the temperature of their aerobic locomotor muscle, and some tuna species can also maintain elevated visceral temperatures (they are regional endotherms). Tunas are effective predators, swim continuously, undertake trans-oceanic migrations, and have high metabolic rates. Their diet consists primarily of fishes, crustaceans, and cephalopods, and thus they ingest large quantities of protein and lipids. In tunas, the largest visceral organ is the caecal mass, composed of many branched pyloric caeca, which are thought to increase the surface area for digestion and absorption. It has been hypothesized that the caecal mass of tunas provides a region to which partially digested food from the stomach can be moved for more complete digestion, leaving the stomach empty in the event that another opportunity to feed arises. This study is a comparison of digestive enzyme activities in tunas and their close relatives that are not endothermic, to test the hypothesis that enzyme activities are greater in the endothermic tunas. Three tuna species [skipjack tuna (Katsuwonus pelamis), a species that warms its muscle but not its viscera, Pacific northern bluefin tuna (Thunnus orientalis) and albacore tuna (Thunnus alalunga), species that warm both the muscle and viscera] were compared with the ectothermic chub mackerel (Scomber japonicus) and eastern Pacific bonito (Sarda chiliensis). The specific activities of three digestive enzymes (trypsin, lipase and pepsin) in the stomach, intestine and caecal mass were measured at 20°C and 25°C. Pepsin activity was detected in the stomach, and trypsin and lipase activities were detected in the caecal mass and intestine. No significant interspecific differences have been detected in any of the digestive enzyme activities measured at either 20°C or 25°C. [Supported by NIH grant #R25GM56820]

23555: The Anchariidae is a group of catfishes endemic to the island of Madagascar, off the southeast coast of Africa. This group consists of a single genus, Ancharius (Steindachner, 1880), whose diversity has been poorly studied due to their rarity in museum collections. They have previously been considered a sister group to either the marine catfish family Ariidae or the African catfish family Mochokidae. Based on materials from recent collections, this talk will outline the diversity of Ancharius, as well as test current hypotheses of phylogenetic relationships of the Anchariidae to other catfishes using both morphological and molecular data. 23556: The abundant diversity of colors and patterns in Anolis lizard dewlaps has long been noted, but few studies have examined the evolution of dewlap morphology. Three hypotheses have been proposed to explain the diversity of dewlaps, but these hypotheses were not preceeded by any characterization of the total amount of diversity observable in dewlap morphologies. In this study I undertook a survey of Caribbean Anolis dewlap morphology (focusing on pattern, as comparative studies including coloration are not entirely feasible currently) and found that unlike snowflakes, dewlaps are easily placed into one of approximately 11 patterns (although some patterns are much less frequent than others). A few species are highly variable in coloration and patterning, but most are uniform. Within the few species where females possess dewlaps, approximately half possess dewlap morphologies identical to their male counterparts, while the other half possess distinctly different dewlap morphologies from their male counterparts. Preliminary comparative analyses have been conducted (more will have been completed by meeting time) and find that there is no correlation between dewlap pattern and phylogeny, dewlap pattern and ecomorph classification, male and female dewlap pattern and ecomorph classification or phylogeny, or male/female dewlap patterns and other sexually dimorphic characters (e.g., size or coloration). 23557: From 1985 to 1992, CVG-TECMIN (Corporación Venezolana Guyana - Técnica Minera) carried out an ambitious project to inventory the natural resources of the Venezuelan Guayana. I participated in seven missions in the Orinoco Basin: one by helicopter to uplands of the Caura River (29 Mar-4 April 1989) and five river-based expeditions to drainages in the upper Orinoco -- the Guayapo-Sipapo system (12 May-7 June, 1989), the Ventuari River (17 Sept-16 Oct 1989), the Atabapo-Atacavi system (23 Oct-17 Nov 1989), the Ocamo-Matacuni system (16 Jan-16 Feb 1990), and the Mavaca River (18 Jan-20 Feb 1991). Additional fish collections were made during other TECMIN missions by the botanist Basil Stergios (various sites, 1986-90), Donald Taphorn (Caura-Nichare River, March 1989), Aniello Barbarino (Casiquiare-Siapa River, April 1991), and LGN (upper Cuyuni- Essequibo tributaries, 26 Nov-10 Dec 1992), among others. 23558: Brazilian economic and social development during the last decade has resulted in a growing need for energy. One outcome of this situation has been the presentation of a number of projects establishing new dams in rivers all around the country, including some at the Paraná river system in southeastern Brazil. Establishment of dams invariably results in negative impacts over the ichthyofauna as a whole, with the "new" system just created often consisting of less diverse assemblages than the original one. The present study was mainly developed around the Funil dam area, the most recent relevant barrier established in the rio Grande basin. Objectives of this contribution are centered on the production of data for implementing conservative efforts regarding the ichthyofauna occuring in that area. Collections of fishes were made bimonthly between November/2000 and October/2001, representing a total of six field trips, and also encompassing the Cervo, Capivari, Ingaí, Jacaré, Verde e das Mortes rivers at the rio Grande basin (between the Furnas reservoir and the Itutinga dam at the rio Grande basin). During that period, 60 species were recorded (54% Characiformes; 30% Siluriformes; 5% Perciformes and Gymnotiformes; 4% Cyprinodontiformes; and 2% Cypriniformes). Three species are exotic (namely, Oreochromis cf. niloticus, Poecilia reticulata and Aristichthys cf. nobilis) and a hybrid was also noticed (Pseudoplatystoma sp.). Most abundant species during the study were, respectively, Galeocharax knerii, Astyanax cf. fasciatus, Cyphocharax nagelii, Steindachnerina insculpta and Astyanax altiparanae. Concerning biomass, most representative values were observed for G. knerii, Salminus maxillosus, A. cf. fasciatus, Schizodon nasutus and C. nagelii. Given the complexity of the ecosystems and environments in the rio Grande basin, and the current status of taxonomic knowledge regarding the Neotropical ichthyofauna, we expect new records and corrections to be added to the present list in the future.
