23559: Dermatonotus muelleri is endemic to South America, with a wide distribution. In São Paulo State, this species is restricted to the northwestern region. The seasonal occurrence of D. muelleri was studied monthly between November/2001 and December/2002, in a permanent pond in Vitória Brasil (20°12′ S, 50°29′ W), SP. The populational abundance was determined by the ‘visual encounter survey’ method. The correlation analyses were conducted by the Pearson test (r). The rostro-cloacal length of amplexed males and of their unamplexed nearest neighbors was measured and compared by t test, and no statistical differences were found, although the amplexed males were smaller. There was a positive correlation between monthly rainfall and male abundance (r = 0.67, p < 0.001), rainfall and number of monthly reproductive events (r = 0.78, p < 0.001), and rainfall and days of reproductive activity (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). There was no correlation between daily rainfall and abundance of calling males (December/2001: r = 0.26, p > 0.05; January/2002: r = -0.47, p > 0.05; February/2002: r = 0.29, p > 0.05), in consequence of a time lag between the rainfall and the constitution of the reproductive aggregates. This time lag seems to be related to the termite phenology, which constitute reproductive swarms soon after rainfall. In this period, males and females of D. muelleri were observed eating termites, but not at the ponds. The reproductive pattern of D. muelleri was characterized by aggregates of short duration, from one to four nights, with high densities per event (1079 ± 816, n= 11), apparently without sexual selection by female, with occurrence dispersed throughout the rainy season.

23560: Dermatonotus muelleri is a fossorial species, endemic to the Cerrado-Caatinga-Chaco biogeographic region. Despite its wide distribution, its ecology and behavior are little known. The behavioral ecology of D. muelleri was studied at a permanent pond in Vitória-Brasil (20o12'S, 50o29'W), northwestern region of São Paulo State, during monthly visits carried out from November/2001 to December/2002. The climate is tropical, but the dry season receives only 15% of the annual precipitation (1100-1250 mm/year). The behavior of males and females was observed by the focal animal method. To determine the call site, the substrate type, depth and distance of calling males from the pond margin were registered. In order to observe the foraging and burrowing behavior, 22 specimens were kept in terrariums. The females came to the permanent pond almost two hours after the males started to call. The males called positioned with the scapular girdle above the water surface, the forelimbs stretched and the snout pointed upwards, exhibiting the black coloration of the vocal sac. Males called from the edge or middle of pond, depending on the availability of substrate for support, and presented active search behavior for females and release call. Agonistic interactions between males were not observed. During amplexus, male and female glue themselves together by means of a viscous substance, secreted by the skin. The eggs were laid on the water surface, and there was no parental care. Males and females exhibited a diversified behavioral repertoire of defense and flight. Both sexes burrow with their forelimbs and build a subterranean chamber, where they spend the dry season. During the reproductive period, they shelter under stems or litter, but can build temporary subterranean chambers. As with other fossorial anurans, the burrowing behavior seems to function mainly in the avoidance of extremes of temperature and in maintaining water balance.

23561: Understanding how predation and landscape characteristics interact to affect fish and amphibian communities is important when managing large ecological systems with multiple-use strategies. During February 2001 through July 2002, we surveyed 90 ponds in the Shawnee National Forest, Illinois to determine how local factors including pond surface area, depth and canopy cover interact with the landscape to influence fish and ambystomatid salamander distributions. A GIS was created to quantify large-scale landscape features including forest, wetland, and agriculture within two buffer zones (1.609 km and 0.805 km resolution) surrounding each pond. Predatory fishes were present in forested, wetland, and agriculture areas and most frequent in large (> 1500 m2), deep (> 2 m) ponds with littoral zone canopy cover. Ambystomatids were most frequent without predatory fishes in small (< 500 m2), shallow (< 2 m), forested ponds with complete canopies. Landscape features principally affected suitable habitat for fish and ambystomatids. Ambystomatids were most frequent in small systems in forested areas and predatory fishes were most frequent in large systems in open areas. However, in aquatic systems where predatory fish and ambystomatids co-occur, suitable habitat cannot be distinguished in terms of these large-scale landscape features. It is within these intermediate systems that local scale factors such as predator-prey interactions, pond surface area, depth and canopy cover play major roles in shaping fish and amphibian communities. To successfully implement landscape-level conservation strategies for amphibians and effective fisheries management decisions, appropriate local and large-scale processes must be identified.

23562: Our current knowledge of the mechanism of burrowing in limbless tetrapods is based largely on descriptions of behavior and anatomy. We used a force plate to quantify the kinetics of head-first burrowing in the Tanzanian amphisbaenian Geocalamus acutus. Geocalamus displays an intermediate head shape between the generalized round-headed morphology of most amphisbaenians and the derived keel-headed (laterally compressed) morphology. Round-headed amphisbaenians are thought to thrust the head directly forward during burrowing. In contrast, keel-headed species are believed to utilize a two-cycle mechanism that entails forward thrusts alternated with lateral head movements. It has also been proposed that the costo- and vertebro- cutaneous muscles, that originate on the skin and insert on the ribs and vertebral column, are the primary muscle generating forward forces. These muscles would build momentum, by accelerating the skull and axial skeleton, which would be dissipated as the head penetrates the substrate. This would be analogous to using a battering ram to build tunnels. To test these hypotheses, animals were induced to push into vials of substrate attached to a force plate from artificial tunnels of varying lengths. Results indicate that the costo- and vertebro-cutaneous muscles are responsible for forward force production. However, momentum is not built up and dissipated with each forward thrust. Instead, the anterior half of the trunk of Geocalamus functions like a pinnate muscle. Force is applied directly to the substrate as the axial skeleton is pulled forward relative to the skin which is braced against the tunnel wall. This mechanism allows Geocalumus to produce about ten times the forward force of a caecilian of similar body cross-section and twenty times the force of a snake with a similar cross-section. Two-cycle burrowing was not observed. However, this behavior may only be seen in species with more extreme lateral skull compression (i.e. Anops and Ancylocranium).

23563: Socially controlled sex determination in the Midas cichlid is believed to be homologous with the various forms of protogyny found in other Labroids, including some other cichlids. It is believed that large body size relative to group-mates causes male differentiation in juveniles because it predicts large size as an adult, which may provide greater fitness payoffs for males than for females. In this study, sex determination was hypothesized to be controlled by size-ratio induction, as opposed to suppression, based on the comparison of the natural social structure of juvenile Midas cichlids to social structures of known sequential hermaphrodites. Juvenile Midas cichlids raised in isolation should lack conspecific stimulus needed to differentiate as males. For fish in social groups, an association between dominance index (aggression performed / aggression received) and male differentiation would provide evidence for an encounter rate mechanism. One brood of juvenile Midas cichlids was divided into 13 groups, each containing seven like-sized individuals. One fish was removed from each group and completely isolated, the other six remained together. All fish were then fed until satiation once daily until maturity. Attacks and displays performed and received were recorded for fish housed in groups. As predicted, a significantly high proportion of socially isolated fish (10/13) differentiated as females. Dominance index was not associated with male differentiation. However, in groups, a significant proportion of alpha individuals (10/13) differentiated as males, and a notable proportion of omega individuals (7/10) as females. It is concluded that the presence of smaller conspecifics stimulates juvenile Midas cichlids to differentiate as males, but relative aggression is not an indicator of sex differentiation.

23564: Systematic studies on the Bothrops atrox complex showed that several distinct populations can be recognized within this clade. We studied the diet of four morphologically distinct Brazilian populations of the Bothrops atrox complex: two populations of Bothrops atrox from forests of eastern and central Amazon, B. leucurus from the Atlantic forest of eastern Brazil, and B. moojeni from gallery forests in savanna areas of central Brazil. We found a total of 406 prey or its remains in the gut of museum specimens of these populations. We measured (snout-vent-length) and weighed both snakes and intact prey. We considered that a species shows ontogenetic shift in prey types when the size of individuals that consumed endothermic prey was significantly larger than those that consumed ectotherms. We considered that a species shows ontogenetic shift in prey size when the slope of the regression line for prey size on snake size was significantly different from one. All species studied are diet generalists and feed primarily on mammals (33- 54% of prey found), frogs (24-39%), and lizards (12-26%). Ontogenetic shift in prey type (from ectotherms to endotherms) occurs in all species, as well as ontogenetic shift in prey size. Mean mass ratios were relatively high (0.19-0.27) in all species. As expected by their phylogenetic relatedness, the populations studied show a high similarity in characters related to feeding habits, despite the fact that they inhabit relatively distinct forests. The lack of marked changes in feeding habits during the evolution of the B. atrox complex may reflect similarities in prey availability among habitats and the opportunistic feeding habits that characterize most species of Bothrops.

23566: The coast of Rio Grande do Sul is part of a large plain constituted by mobile sand dunes and depressions that are flooded during periods of higher rainfall. The vegetation is scarce and composed mainly of grasses. During last decades, this region suffered great modifications due to the fast urbanization process, which covers the flooded areas and removes the dunes. We have developed this study since July 1998 in a 333 ha area located in the municipality of Balneario Pinhal (30o 21'S, 050o 17'W). Data on diet and feeding behavior of 14 species recorded in the area were collected by observing individuals as they were feeding in natural conditions, inducing specimens that had evident gut content to regurgitate, and dissecting specimens from the area (deposited in scientific collections). Adult forms of anuran amphibians are the most used food resource; they were recorded in 125 individuals of seven species (53 Lystrophis dorbignyi, 41 Liophis poecilogyrus, 17 Philodryas patagoniensis, 7 Liophis miliaris, 4 Liophis jaegeri, 2 Liophis flavifrenatus and 1 Helicops infrataeniatus). Fish were recorded in eight individuals of L. miliaris, two individuals of H. infrataeniatus and one individual of L. poecilogyrus. Lizards were recorded in seven individuals of P. patagoniensis. Rodents were recorded in five individuals of Bothrops alternatus and three individuals of P. patagoniensis. Tadpoles were recorded in three individuals of L. poecilogyrus and two individuals of H. infrataeniatus. Snakes were recorded in three individuals of P. patagoniensis. Eggs of lizards were recorded in two individuals of L. dorbignyi, and eggs of anurans in one individual of L. poecilogyrus. Philodryas patagoniensis is the most generalist species, feeding on four of the eight prey categories recorded. Lystrophis dorbignyi is a specialist anuran eater, and Bothrops alternatus feeds exclusively on rodents.

23567: The genus Corydoras, with 142 known species, account for more than 80% of all species of the family Callichthyidae. Cytogenetic studies have shown that there is a great karyotipic diversity among Callichthyidae, mainly in the genus Corydoras, whose diploid numbers range from 2n=40 chromosomes in C. nattereri to 2n=134 in C. aeneus. In the present study, twelve Corydoras species were karyotyped, with the main purpose of evaluate the pattern of karyotypic evolution in this group. The cytogenetic analysis involved the use of Giemsa staining, silver staining of Nucleolus Organizer Regions (NORs) and C-band techniques. Diploid number ranged from 2n=44 (Corydoras ehrhardti, C. nattereri and C. paleatus) to 2n=102 chromosomes (C. pulcher). A great diversity of chromosome formulae was observed. NORs were found at a terminal position in one up to five chromosome pairs. Single NORs were found in the chromosomes of Corydoras ehrhardti, C. nattereri, C. cf. nijsseni, C. pulcher, C. robinae, C. sodalis, C. difluviatilis and C. zygatus. Multiple NORs were observed in C. araguaiensis, C. barbatus, C. paleatus and C. undulatus chromosomes. C-band positive segments were mostly restricted to centromeric and pericentromeric regions in most chromosomes of C. ehrhardti, C. nattereri, C. cf. nijsseni, C. paleatus and C. undulatus; additional terminal and interstitial C-bands and/or heterochromatic arms were observed in C. barbatus, C. pulcher, C. robinae, C. sodalis and C. difluviatilis. C. zygatus exhibit a reduced amount of centromeric and pericentromeric C bands. The data obtained confirm the occurrence of a wide karyotypic diversity in the genus Corydoras. This extensive karyotypic variety may be related to a particular mode of evolution, in which a high number of chromosomal rearrangements, including events of poliploidy, have been fixed in the evolutionary history of this group. The importance of chromosome changes in the genus diversification will be discussed.

23568: Benthic skates and Pacific sleeper shark play an important role in ecosystems of the North Pacific basin. They are a significant element of food webs in benthic communities. Elasmobranchs consume commercially important fish, cephalopods and shrimps. These species themselves have some commercial importance. For example, skates are processed into fish meat jelly and dried skate wing. Pacific sleeper shark does not support a fishery now. The diets of some northern Pacific skates were described only in few papers. Feeding habits and trophic relations of elasmobranchs inhabiting the western Bering Sea were never previously considered. Stomach contents of elasmobranchs brought aboard Japanese trawler Kayomaru No. 28 during summer 1997 were analyzed. The stomach samples were selected without known bias from bottom trawl hauls carried out around the clock in the western Bering Sea between 170° E and 178° W. Stomachs examined and those with food were as follows: 125/102 Pacific sleeper shark Somniosus pacificus, 139/123 Aleutian skate Bathyraja aleutica, 19/18 Matsubara skate B. matsubarai, 68/58 whitebrow skate B. minispinosa, 113/86 Alaska skate B. parmifera, and 189/179 Okhotsk skate B. violacea. The diet of predatory elasmobranchs (Pacific sleeper shark, Alaska skate, Aleutian skate, Matsubara skate, and whitebrow skate) consisted of large crustaceans, cephalopods and fishes. Benthophage elasmobranchs (Okhotsk skate) consumed mainly worms, amphipods and shrimp. Diets of male and female elasmobranchs differed, probably due mostly to the effect of size. The consumption of worms and crustaceans (especially small) in diets of predators declined with increasing their size, whereas proportion of cephalopods and fishes in diet increased. The consumption of worms and small crustaceans by benthophage Okhotsk skates declined with increasing skate size while consumption of crabs and squids increased. Among the species examined, three elasmobranch pairs had a medium level of dietary similarity: Aleutian and Alaska skates, Alaska and whitebrow skates, and whitebrow and Okhotsk skates. Diets of other species differed considerably
23569: The liparid fish Careproctus jordani was collected throughout the Aleutian Islands during recent resource assessment surveys conducted by the U.S. National Marine Fisheries Service, and these collections represent the first documented records for Alaska. The species ranges from north of Umnak Island in the eastern Aleutians, west to the Kuril Islands, and south to Sagami Bay, Japan, where the holotype was collected. Depths of capture range from 210-495 m in the Aleutians to as shallow as 75 m in the Kuril Islands. Eggs of C. jordani containing late-stage embryos were also collected from the vicinity of Seguam Pass, where they had been laid in masses surrounding limbs of the octocoral Primnoa sp., the first know example of Careproctus spawning outside of lithodid crabs. The egg masses were about 40 mm along the deposition axis and contained about 267 large eggs, up to 6.8 mm in the largest dimension. We have retained C. jordani in Careproctus and discuss our rationale for not recognizing the recently erected monotypic genus Allocareproctus. Based on our examination of holotypes, C. pycnosoma appears to be a valid species and not synonymous with C. jordani. A new species is also described, similar to C. jordani but differing from it primarily in body and peritoneum color, pyloric caeca, and body depth.

23570: Competing morphological cladistic hypotheses of the Scombroidei position the swordfish plus billfishes (Xiphioidei) as either sister to the Scombridae, or sister to Acanthocybium within the Scombridae. A published molecular hypothesis based on mitochondrial (cytochrome b) sequences was unable to resolve scombroid relationships. Our novel phylogenetic hypothesis, based on 511 bp of the single copy nuclear locus TMO-4c4, does not recover a monophyletic Scombroidei as previously proposed. There is no support for a close relationship between the xiphioids and the scombroids, and thus, none for a sister relationship between the wahoo (Acanthocybium) and the billfishes. In addition, there is no support for a close relationship between barracudas (Sphyraenidae) and the Scombroidei.

23571: Pachitea River watershed, located at the Peruvian central east, are as arteries of the rainforest. They bring water and provide habitat and food. Much aquatic life depends upon them. As this area is developed and more people and human economic activity move into the basin, these watery lifelines could be compromised. This ichthyological study carried out with the support of San Marcos University and Earthwatch Program through five teams of volunteers, three expeditions (July, 2001 and July-August 2002). Were surveyed 32 different water bodies and more than 5000 specimens were deposited at the Museo de Historia Natural UNMSM in Lima. The results show a list of 158 species, 114 genera, 24 families and 8 orders. Are dominants Characiformes (90) and Siluriformes (44 species). 23572: Established populations of Asian swamp eels within the genus Monopterus (Synbranchidae) have been found near Atlanta in Georgia as well as near Tampa, and North Miami in Florida. In 1999, a population of eels was discovered in Florida near Everglades National Park (ENP). Swamp eels are large (up to 1 m) air-breathing predators capable of short overland movement. Burrowing behavior and copious mucus secretion permit eels to survive periods of drought. These characteristics have raised concerns over the potential impact of swamp eels on native species and ecosystems. We use phylogenetic analyses of two mitochondrial genes (12S and 16S rRNA) and two nuclear encoded genes (RAG2 and LDHA6) to determine (1) the number of lineages introduced in this morphologically conservative group, (2) the geographic origin of lineage(s), (3) the pathways of introduction, and (4) the potential for hybridization among lineages. Samples were collected from each introduced population, countries within the native range, and both domestic and international fish markets. Our results to date indicate that the four introduced populations represent at least three lineages derived from different native source populations. In Florida, North Miami and Tampa are most closely related to Chinese populations while the population near ENP is most closely allied with samples from Indonesia, Vietnam and Malaysia. The Atlanta population groups with Japanese and Korean populations. In addition, we have identified a fourth genetically and morphologically distinct synbranchid eel lineage being sold live in U.S. markets that has not been found in open waters in the U.S.. 23573: Paternity analysis was used to examine the reproductive success of 54 male Blanding’s turtles captured on the University of Michigan’s E. S. 23574: It has been hypothesized that emerging infectious diseases may be contributing to the global decline of amphibian populations. In particular, chytridiomycosis, a cutaneous fungal infection of amphibians caused by the chytrid Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, attracted attention in the 1990s as an apparently new pathogen. This fungus has been implicated as the causative agent of widespread mortalities among wild amphibians in geographically disparate parts of the world. To begin to investigate the global distribution and infectiousness of this pathogen, we examined 3371 postmetamorphic and adult amphibians which had been collected between 1895 and 2001 from 25 countries for the presence of chytrid fungi in the epidermis. In North America, chytridiomycosis was diagnosed in 383 of 2931 (13.1%) specimens of 12 common amphibian species from five Canadian provinces and seven American states, including 30 of 69 locations examined in the St. Lawrence River Valley of Québec. The earliest cases were recorded in two green frogs (Rana clamitans) collected in 1961 from Saint-Pierre-de-Wakefield, Québec. In recent studies, morbidity and mortality were not encountered in infected amphibians from Québec despite a 17.8% (302/1698) prevalence of the infection during the period 1990-2001. In view of this evidence that infection by B. dendrobatidis is widely distributed and enzootic in apparently healthy amphibians, lethal outbreaks of chytridiomycosis among amphibian populations likely have complex causes.

23575: Advertisement and aggressive calls are two types of calls that influence fitness in male frogs. Advertisement calls increase fitness through mate attraction, and aggressive calls indirectly increase fitness through warding off competitors. Comparisons among closely related species of frogs and other groups of animals suggest that aggressive signals are more similar in structure than advertisement signals. This may be due to the lack of directional selection on aggressive calls or to convergent evolution. No comparisons of aggressive calls in frogs have been done in a phylogenetic context. Chorus frogs, genus Pseudacris, have a well supported phylogeny making them an excellent group for studying the evolution of advertisement and aggressive calls. Advertisement calls are diverse in chorus frogs, evolving from single note calls in basal species to trilled calls in derived species. Previously, aggressive calls were only known in one species, and I have described them for five more species. All aggressive calls documented so far have a trilled structure. Distance and phylogenetic contrast methods both suggest that advertisement and aggressive calls are evolving at similar rates in this group and are not evolving independently. In each species, the aggressive call appears to be derived from the advertisement call, and this may result from a neural program common to the clade. This pattern of signal evolution has been observed in other animals that communicate acoustically.

23576: The Rio Ribeira de Iguape basin is one of the larger river basins in southeastern Brazil, being the Juqui river its main tributaries. An important aspect is that this river system is totally included inside one of the largest remains of Atlantic Forest of the southeastern Brazil. Fishes are probably the less known vertebrates in Atlantic Forest, partly due to a lack of taxonomic and systematic information. During ichthyological surveys lead by MCP and inventory field studies related to the project ‘Fish diversity of the streams and headwaters of the rio Ribeira de Iguape in State of São Paulo’ (Fapesp No. 00/04300-9), the upper portions of this basin was extensively sampled. Among Loricariidae, specimens of the genus Isbrueckerichthys Derijst (1996) were regularly collected in several small tributaries. The genus Isbrueckerichthys was proposed by Derijst who transferred Pareiorhaphis duseni (Miranda Ribeiro, 1907) and P. alipionis Gosline (1947) to the new genus. The proposal was justified based on the discovery of an earlier type-species designation by Regan (1920), which had fixed Hemipsilichthys calmoni as the type species of genus Pareiorhaphis, making Pareiorhaphis a synonym of the former. Two species of Isbrueckerichthys are currently recognized in the Rio Ribeira de Iguape drainage, I. duseni from the upper reaches of that basin in Paraná State, and I. alipionis, from the Rio Betari, Rio Iporanga basin. Isbrueckerichthys sp.n., from tributary of the Rio Juquiá in São Paulo State, displays an unique sexual dimorphism in which mature males are distinguished from its congeners by having a well-developed soft fleshy area and a clump of the hypertrophied short odontodes directed forward or slightly upward on anterior portion of snout. 23577: The Rio Ribeira de Iguape Basin, situated at coordinates 23° 45′S / 46° 45′W e 25° 30′S / 49° 48′W, in the states of São Paulo and Paraná, Brazil, is inside the greater remnant of the Atlantic Forest of Southeastern Brazil, in which nine Conservation Units are stablished. Besides, deforestation and many other kinds of human activities cause the reduction of allochthonous food present in the riparian vegetation, increase of the sun light, and silting of the streams reducing the habitats for fishes. As in other brazilian hydrographic systems, the fish fauna of the main river of Ribeira de Iguape is relatively well known. The great gap in the knowledge of the Ribeira, as well as in the other hydrographic systems in South America, is the streams and headwaters, which are inhabited by small size fish species. The immediate results of this project will be: a) ichthyological knowledge of one of the least known regions of the São Paulo State; b) production of scientific publications such as: new taxa description, revisionary monographs, catalogs; c) production of a handbook and field guides dedicated mostly to non scientific people. 23578: Priapichthys annectens and Phallichthys amates are sister clades of livebearing fish from Central America. Samples collected from more than 30 sites from Bocas del Toro Provience, Panama and the Atlantic versant of Costa Rica, where representatives of the two clades are often found together, reveal striking differences between the two clades in number of haplotypes, haplotype diversity, and population substructure. 23579: We determined the effects of differing levels of human exploitation on nesting female size in the slider turtle, Trachemys scripta callirostris, from five locations in the Mompos Depression in northern Colombia. We characterized and quantified habitat available for nesting and examined the number of nests ovoposited in locations with differing characteristics, their hatching success rates, the natural causes of egg mortality, incubation temperatures, and sex ratios of the hatchlings produced. Clutches obtained from harvested females also were incubated under varying semi-natural and artificial incubation conditions. Preliminary results indicated that the majority of nests were oviposited within the first 20 meters from shoreline in sites with sandy or clayish textured substrates with moderate humidities that often were covered by herbaceous vegetation. Invertebrates were the greatest source of mortality to natural nests, although hatching success in the focal study population was high compared to other reports for this species. Only in the site with the highest hunting pressure was a negative correlation found between daily harvest rates and the time elapsed since the beginning of the nesting period, suggesting that the excessive extraction of females there significantly affected the pool of available adult females. 23580: A systematic study of the genus Lamontichthys was undertaken. 23581: Turtles and tortoises are among the most endangered vertebrate groups. Conservation of many species will depend upon successful captive breeding programs. These efforts will benefit from understanding turtle reproductive physiology. Unfortunately, the reproductive endocrinology of many species has not been thoroughly investigated. Most studies have focused only on the major steroid hormones of mammals, namely estradiol, progesterone and testosterone. We have developed a novel methodology utilizing High Performance Liquid Chromatography (HPLC) to investigate the reproductive endocrinology of turtles and tortoises. The advantage of this technique is that multiple steroids can be simultaneously quantified from a single, small sample of plasma. In this study, we examined concentrations of 11 steroid hormones from common aquatic turtles (snapping turtles, Chelydra serpentina and map turtles, Graptemys geographica) and captive specimens of threatened turtles and tortoises (spiny turtles, Heosemys spinosa and pancake tortoises, Malacochersus tornieri). Plasma samples were collected within 20 min of capture for wild specimens. Plasma samples were extracted with methanol, dried under nitrogen and analyzed using Nova Pak C-18 columns on HPLC. The steroids estradiol-17β, estriol, estrone, progesterone, 17α-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, testosterone, 5α- dihydrotestosterone, 17α-hydroxypregnenolone, pregnenolone and corticosterone were identified and quantified. Results for snapping turtles indicate that males had significant levels of testosterone, dihydrotestosterone, progesterone and estriol during the spring. In females, estradiol, testosterone, progesterone and estrone were elevated. An additional unidentified peak indicates that significant quantities of a steroid not included in the 11 standards is present in females. This study is the first to our knowledge to investigate levels of 11 steroid hormones any turtle. This technology will further our understanding of chelonian reproduction and assist in the captive breeding of endangered species. This technique should be easily adaptable to virtually any vertebrate species. This research was sponsored by a University of Kentucky Research Committee Award.

23582: The goal of this study was to examine timing of recruitment and habitat usage of age-0 gray snapper collected from 1990 through 2001 in the northern IRL. Growth rate estimates were also made using fish collected between 1999 and 2001. Age-0 gray snapper recruit to the northern IRL beginning in July, and subsequent peaks in recruitment occur from September to October. 23583: The giant garter snake, Thamnophis gigas, is a threatened species endemic to California’s Central Valley. Historic hydrology resulting in current watershed boundaries suggests there may be genetic differentiation among populations of T. gigas. We tested the hypothesis that T. gigas is a single panmictic population. We sampled 14 populations throughout the current geographic range of T. gigas and amplified 859 bp from the mitochondrial gene ND4 and one nuclear microsatellite locus. DNA sequence variation from the mitochondrial gene indicates there is some genetic structuring of the populations, with high FST values for ND4 with unique haplotypes occurring at high frequency in several populations. We found a correlation of watershed boundary with mitochondrial structuring using AMOVA. However, analysis of allele frequencies at the microsatellite locus NSU3 reveals a pattern of panmixia (FST = 0.07, p-value < 0.001). We propose that the discordance found between mitochondrial and microsatellite data may be explained by components of molecular evolution and T. gigas life history characteristics. Differences in effective population size between mitochondrial and nuclear DNA result in a lower migration rate of mitochondrial haplotypes relative to nuclear alleles. Furthermore, male-biased dispersal may exacerbate this effect. Smaller effective population size for mitochondrial DNA will also increase genetic drift, resulting in lower within-population genetic variation relative to autosomal loci. Genetic subdivision may reflect a recent and short-term fragmentation followed by secondary contact. The mitochondrial nucleotide sequence data supports conservation practices that identify six management units for T. gigas.

23584: Gonad morphology at the gross anatomical or histological levels has long been studied by fisheries biologists to identify annual reproductive cycles and length of breeding season, among other goals. Comparative surveys across vertebrate taxa have not been detailed enough, however, to describe fully the differences and similarities among gonads of bony fishes and other vertebrates, and to use gonad morphology in phylogenetic systematic analyses. These are our aims. First, an emerging constant among vertebrates is the presence of a germinal epithelium. Almost all osteichthyans have a germinal epithelium composed of somatic and germ cells in male and female gonads. Arrangement of the male germinal epithelium into compartments varies among osteichthyans: basal taxa have an anastomosing tubular testis, whereas derived taxa have a lobular testis. The annual reproductive cycle is hypothesized to be the source of morphological variation among testis types. Egg and ovarian characters also vary among osteichthyans: basal taxa release eggs into the coelom; whereas derived bony fishes release eggs into an ovarian lumen. Here, we focus on atherinomorph fishes and their putative close relatives to illustrate the utility of gonad characters in phylogenetic analyses. In all male atherinomorph fishes surveyed to date, spermatogonia are restricted to the distal termini of lobules rather than being distributed along the lobule; there is an epithelioid arrangement of Sertoli and germ cells. Further, atherinomorphs have a distinctive egg with fluid, rather than granular, yolk, among other characters. Variation among germinal epithelia is interpreted in a developing phylogenetic framework to understand the evolution of gonad morphology and also to propose gonad characters to be used in phylogenetic analyses.

23585: The midget faded rattlesnake, Crotalus viridis concolor, inhabits a relatively extreme environment in Wyoming. Their active season (when they leave the den, until they return) is as short as 3 or 4 months. Shedding, building fat reserves, and finding mates occupies most of the active season for adult males and non-gravid females. In 2001, we observed 6 transmittered midget faded rattlesnakes from 3 den sites within one population to migrate to a discrete area as far as 2km from their den during July and August. In 2002, we decided to investigate small mammal prey abundance (believed to be the primary diet of adult midget faded rattlesnakes that have moved away from the den) to see if there were differences that could explain this congregation. We set 3 trapping grids of 36 small mammal traps in 4 different populations of midget faded rattlesnakes. We placed one grid at the den, one over a transmittered snake, and one at a randomly chosen site during the congregation period. We recovered 3 of the 6 snakes from 2001 and followed them for a second season. Two of these snakes returned to the same congregation area allowing us to confirm the habit and period. The results do not clearly point out a reason for the migration and congregation. In fact, one snake spent most of the active season at a site with a density of zero small mammals per hectare. Either the snakes are seeking alternative prey (likely birds) or there are other reasons for the migration and congregation.

23586: The supergenus Bolitoglossa is formed by 13 genera, with distribution ranging from Mexico to Brazil. Mitochondrial DNA supports the monophyly of the supergenus. 23587: Ecologists increasingly recognize pathogens as playing significant roles in community dynamics, yet few experimental studies have documented quantitative patterns of disease impacts on natural systems. I studied the effects of a pathogenic fungus (Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis; Chytridiomycota) on community interactions between two sympatric North American anurans, the gray treefrog Hyla chrysoscelis and Woodhouse's toad Bufo woodhousei. Recent studies have characterized chytridiomycosis as an emerging infectious disease, whose suspected rapid range expansion and widespread occurrence pose a significant risk for amphibian populations worldwide. I manipulated the presence of chytrid fungi in replicated experimental ponds and examined how infections of fungi during development could influence recruitment and competitive interactions between larval Hyla and Bufo. Ponds were followed throughout larval development, and I recorded survival, mean body mass at metamorphosis, and time to metamorphosis. I also tested the effects of competitive and pathogen-mediated stress on developmental instability by measuring fluctuating asymmetry (FA) of surviving metamorphs. The presence of chytrids reduced metamorphic body mass and increased larval period length, but had no significant effect on survival. Chytrid differentially affected metamorphic body mass according to competitive environment; in the presence of the pathogen, both Hyla and Bufo metamorphosed at smaller body masses when reared together compared to when reared alone. Bufo also had strong negative effects on Hyla development, but only in the presence of chytrid. FA of limb length was significantly higher for metamorphs from chytrid ponds, but was not associated with density or competitive environment. These results suggest that chytrid fungi may impact Hyla and Bufo directly by reducing life history performance and increasing developmental instability, and indirectly by exacerbating the negative effects of interspecific competition.

23590: Silver arowana Osteoglossum bicirrhosum are top-level carnivores in the Amazon basin. While close relatives of this species have been shown to exhibit a unique prey processing mechanism, prey capture in this clade has been largely ignored. Several members of this family regularly leap out of the water to capture prey, in addition to feeding on prey at or just below the water's surface. Crickets were offered to four individuals at approximately one-half of a fish's total length above or below the surface of the water. Capture events were recorded at 500 fields per second by two synchronized video cameras. Kinematic variables relating to the feeding apparatus, pectoral girdle, and entire body were measured to quantify prey capture movements. Results indicate that aquatic capture is characterized by ram ingestion at an average attack velocity of 42.3 cm/sec, whereas during aerial capture a higher velocity of 146 cm/sec is attained. Fish also strike from a greater distance and with greater acceleration during aerial (6.27 cm, 20852 cm/sec2) than aquatic (0.85 cm, 8704 cm/sec2) capture. Aerial capture is further characterized by more rapid mouth opening (18 ms) and a larger maximum gape (3.2 cm) than aquatic capture (99.7 ms and 1.9 cm). Thrust generation during aerial capture is characterized by greater body coiling (26.1% TL) compared to aquatic capture (16.8% TL) and more extensive pectoral fin depression (77.3 degrees aerial vs. 38.9 degrees aquatic). 23591: Among the species of poison dart frogs (family Dendrobatidae) known for Costa Rica, the chocolate-mint poison dart frog, Dendrobates auratus, has the widest distribution. 23592: Sand beaches are ephemeral habitats in tropical freshwaters, emerging along river banks during the dry season and usually inhabited by loosely structured fish assemblages. The present study aims to analyze the structure of fish assemblages in sand beaches of Araguaia River, in the Cantão State Park, Tocantins, Brazil, which are present almost all year round, maybe holding more complex fish assemblages. Also, morphological and behavioral characteristics of the main species according to the occupation of sand beach habitats were observed. 129 species were recorded, mostly small sized Characiformes. Only eight species had high frequencies and abundances along the year and were considered core species: Moenkhausia aff. lepidura, Knodus sp., Geophagus aff. altifrons, Bivibranchia velox, Bivibranchia fowleri, Anchoviella sp. Exodon paradoxus and Triportheus albus. Yet, the turnover rate of fish species among hydrological periods was found to be high (55 – 80%). During the low water, beaches constitute well defined habitats occupied by few specialized fish species. The main characteristics of these core species are the feeding habits (benthivorous or surface pickers) and the counter shading or cryptic coloration, which reflect the shallow, exposed and weak structured habitat of sand beaches. In the rising water period number of species increase but with small population numbers. This possibly reflects the opportunistic occupation of the shallow habitats by several species exploiting the increasing food supply and structural complexity at the river banks. We conclude that these habitats hold rich fish assemblages constituted by a small number of core species and many opportunistic, less abundant ones that utilize that environment during limited periods along the year.

23593: The identity of larval cetomimid whalefishes has long been a mystery, as has that of adult mirapinnid tapetails. Recent molecular analyses (Miya, et al., 2003) found that total mtDNA sequences of the tapetail, Parataeniophorus cf gulosus, are nearly identical to those of the whalefish, Cetostoma regani, both 16,508 base pairs long with only 7 nucleotide differences (0.04%). Gosline (1971) was the first to propose a close relationship between the Mirapinnidae, Cetomimidae, and Megalomycteridae, placing the three families in his Group 1 of the order Cetomimiformes. The possibility that tapetails are larval whalefishes has been suggested, and the two do share some notable similarities in the axial skeleton, including posterior dorsal and anal fins, second preural centrum usually with double neural and haemal spines, and certain caudal skeleton features. There is also striking meristic concordance between some taxon pairs of the two groups, especially the mirapinnid Parataeniophorus gulosus and the cetomimid Cetostoma regani. Still puzzling, however, is the fact that mirapinnid juveniles up to 53 mm sl and individuals of one cetomimid species as small as 27 mm sl are known. Furthermore, a significant conflict is that mirapinnids have pelvic fins and short oblique jaws, whereas cetomimids have no pelvic fins and long jaws. Remarkable metamorphoses have been documented in the ontogeny of other fishes (e.g., Rosaura - Gigantura), but in the absence of a single transitional specimen, we think that further morphological and molecular studies are required to resolve the longstanding question of mirapinnid-cetomimid identity. If mirapinnids are larval cetomimids, identification of the big-nose/mosaic scale fishes (Megalomycteridae) as macrosomatic male cetomimids is likely. In addition to similar axial skeleton structure and meristics, some megalomycterids also have long horizontal jaws and pelvic fins, although their possession of external, non-imbricate scales is problematic. Megalomycterids appear to be adult males of larval mirapinnids. Our preliminary conclusions, based on further comparative studies, will be discussed.

23594: In recent years, molecular genetic data have shown that multiple paternity occurs in groups of offspring in many taxa. In turtles, multiple paternity has been found in almost every species examined. However, there are a wide range of reported frequencies of multiple paternity among species, and data on variation in paternity patterns among populations of the same species remain limited. In addition, few data exist on the distribution of paternity among males within multiply sired clutches. Here we present paternity data from 32 clutches of the Giant River Turtle (Arrau, Podocnemis expansa), from the Orinoco River in Venezuela. The large clutches of this turtle permit sample sizes sufficient for accurate assessment of multiple paternity, as well as skew in paternity within multiply-sired clutches (mean sample size = 28.7, range, 10 - 76). Results from the present study extend previous research on paternity in turtles and add to the growing body of knowledge on turtle mating systems.

23595: The Giant Amazon River Turtle, Podocnemis expansa, like marine turtles, is a large, colonially- nesting species that may migrate long distances between nesting and feeding grounds. In the past 100 years, populations of P. expansa have been severely reduced by hunting. Few data are available on the movement or ecology of this species outside of the nesting season, so knowledge of the demographic and evolutionary independence of disjunct populations is lacking. Here we present an analysis of microsatellite DNA data on population differentiation throughout its Amazonian range and the Orinoco River in Venezuela. Data on genetic differentiation across this broad geographic range is compared with previous studies detailing genetic structure of P. expansa at much finer scales (within individual river basins). In addition we address the issue of inter-basin connectivity via an unusual waterway, the Brazo Casiquiare.

23596: The Amazonian tropical rain forest, divided by the Amazonas river and its tributaries, presents both permanently and temporarily flooded areas, the igapo and the varzea. There are forests in non flooded areas, called floresta de terra firme, where we may find small areas with a typical vegetation called savanna. In these areas there are lizards which cannot be found in the forest. There are species of the terra firme forest and species of lizards living in sunny, open areas, on river shore and sandy river banks, such as the open areas of the large tributaries, Tapajos and Negro river. Also, in the upper Amazonas and Solimoes, just above Parintins, the river banks are of clay, no sand shores, with a different vegetation. All this environmental heterogeneity will be a very important factor related to diversity of species. Previously, we described some karyotypes of Amazonian species, from different geographic areas, especially the open area lizard Cnemidophorus lemniscatus group populations. Also, we have been analyzing and increasing the number of metaphases analyzed for the species collected by fauna rescue operations near the hydroelectric power plants of Balbina, Amazonas and Tucurui, Para. The samples do not represent all of the lizard fauna. Preliminary data indicate that this study will be a contribution to the Brazilian cytotaxonomy of lizards, especially for those species from Amazonia. Chromosome preparations were processed from tissue samples of bone marrow, testis, spleen and epithelial cells of intestine. Conventional staining by Giemsa and AgNOR banding. Karyotype description of 18 species of lizards showed variation in the diploid number from 30 to 50 chromosomes, with variation in the number and morphology of chromosomes. In some species there is a geographic variation in the karyotype and chromosomal mechanisms of sex determination. Polymorphisms in the patterns of chromosomal nucleolar organizers, AgNORs, were observed. Data suggest that in open areas there is a higher diversity of species and karyotypes.

23597: The Atlantic Forest is complex with a gradient of several types of vegetation: seasonal semideciduous, ombrophylous dense and the restingas. Restingas include highly diversified vegetation: low restinga, bush restinga and forest restinga, where the type of vegetation is an important factor related to the density of lizard species. Also, in mountainous regions, there are species from high altitudes and those exclusively from low altitudes. In the southeastern Atlantic Forest there is a high degree of endemism and there are species with population distribution restricted to very small geographic areas. This particular configuration of Atlantic Forest indicates a large and very special potential for research on genetic diversity and evolutionary mechanisms on species and population levels. The heterogeneous fauna distribution in the Serra de Paranapiacaba, Serra do Mar and restingas is evidenced, so far, by the karyotypes of 16 species from 7 families of Sauria and one species of Amphisbaenia. Chromosomal preparations were obtained from tissue samples of bone marrow, testis, spleen and epithelial cells of intestine. Conventional staining with Giemsa and AgNOR banding techniques were used. Comparative chromosomal studies between restinga species from Sao Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Espirito Santo States and those from high altitudes from Serra de Paranapiacaba and Serra do Mar, indicate that those species from restingas show a higher diversity of species as well as a higher diversity in the number and morphology of chromosomes. There is no geographic variation for the same species, however there is a high interspecific chromosomal variability. There are common species in high and low altitudes as Tupinambis merianae and Placosoma glabellum. There are endemic species in restingas as Liolaemus lutzae and Cnemidophorus littoralis. There are three population groups: 1. species of both high and low altitudes - 5; 2. high altitude species - 5; 3. low altitude species - 7. Some species show chromosomal mechanisms of sex determination and mutations related with speciation which suggests recent evolutionary processes.

23598: The testes of 5 species from three closely related genera (Xenurobrycon, Tyttocharax and Scopaeocharax) of the Xenurobryconini were examined using electron microscopical techniques. In each species, fully-formed, unencapsulated sperm packets (spermatozeugmata) were found within the lumens of the efferent ducts. The organization and number of spermatozoa within each sperm packet varied among the genera. In Tyttocharax and Scopaeocharax the spermatozoa within an individual spermatozeugma are tightly packed in a similar pattern. The anterior part of each packet is formed by elongate sperm heads and flagella which run alongside the nuclei, whereas the posterior part consists of free flagella. The flattened sperm heads appear to be attached to one another along their entire lengths by electron-dense material. Spermatozeugmata in T. tambopatensis and T. cochui contain 16-54 spermatozoa (mean=28; n=15) within a single packet, whereas in Scopaeocharax sp. and S. rhinodus they contain 55 - 160 (mean=102.8; n=9). The mean length of a packet was 22.7µm (n=11) in Tyttocharax and 21.9µm (n=9) in Scopaeocharax, in each case being approximately equal in length to that of a single spermatozoon with its free flagellum. In Xenurobrycon macropus, on the other hand, the sperm packets are much larger, varying in length from 120-190µm (mean 158.4µm, n=8) and the spermatozoa are arranged in a unique manner. As seen with SEM, elongate sperm heads were visible only in the anterior part of the packet. The flagella, however, not only form the posterior part of the packet, but also cover the outside of the packet. Several levels of sperm heads were visible within a packet.

23599: Gymnodactylus darwinii is restricted to the Atlantic Forest domain of eastern Brazil, and ranges from the northern state of Rio Grande do Norte south to the northern coastal regions of state of São Paulo. Forty-four specimens were sampled throughout this range and used to infer a mtDNA phylogeny. Sequence data were corroborated by karyotypes where possible. Phylogenetic analyses (parsimony and model-based criteria) using multiple outgroups, demonstrated monophyly of the complex, and recovered three geographically coherent clades, coincident with major rivers systems reaching the Atlantic coast. The southern island-mainland complex of populations formed a clade, with very low levels of genetic divergence (about 0.3%), and lack of population structure. This pattern, expected in a scenario of recent dispersal, might reflect the effects of fluctuations in sea level related to the last marine transgression (11,000 ya), when these islands were isolated from the mainland. The deep split between this southern clade (2n=38) and the two northern clades (2n=40), with sequence divergence around 8%, coincides with Rio Doce. The Bahia de Todos os Santos, which receives the drainage of Rio Paraguaçu and other less important rivers seems to account for significant divergence found between the two major northern clades; within them there are strongly supported monophyletic groups, with ranges coincidental with São Francisco and Jequitinhonha rivers. Our data agree with studies on morphological character variation in Gymnodactylus. Although these data suggest that major Atlantic coastal rivers act as potential barriers among Gymnodactylus populations, we need a better geographical coverage of the area. All the Atlantic Forest and the sandridge habitats along the coast where populations of Gymnodactylus occur are above sediments of Barreiras Formation. Estimates of divergence times based on mtDNA reptilian rates revealed that the split between southern and northern clades, and the opening of Rio Doce, took place 17 - 6 Mya, which is compatible with the presumable time for deposition of Barreiras Formation (Miocene/Pliocene). Present data offer a baseline towards the understanding of the comparative history of the major river systems in Atlantic Forest.

23600: During the breeding season, tree frogs (Hylidae) usually move to suitable water bodies for mating. The time they spend at these locations varies among species and depends on several different factors. Male frogs of species with short breeding seasons may stop feeding for that period to concentrate on their mating efforts. The subtropical Northeast of Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, shows a high diversity of anuran species which is associated with strongly differing habitats. 29 of the 71 recorded species are tree frogs. To study the feeding behaviour of different tree frogs we examined the stomach contents of 250 male specimens belonging to five species (Hyla faber, H. minuta, H. pulchella, Scinax granulatus and S. perereca). The frogs were collected in spring and early summer (November 2002 to January 2003) at their typical calling sites, usually at night. Their stomachs were emptied as soon as possible after collecting by stomach flushing, a simple and frog-sparing method that provides data of surviving animals. Half of the examined frogs had empty stomachs, though there were significant differences between the species: The percentage of stomachs with content ranged from 38% (H. faber) to 84% (H. pulchella). Animal items were found in only 8% of H. faber stomachs, whereas in H. pulchella every filled stomach contained at least a single prey item. Among the examined species, the breeding season of H. faber is the shortest (about two months), while H. pulchella stops mating activity only in winter for about three months. Thus our data suggest a correlation between feeding behaviour and duration of breeding season. The stomach contents included not only animal items, but quite frequently remains of plants. The number of stomachs containing plants did not show any significant difference between species (percentage ranged from 18 to 34), although a significant difference could be observed when concerning animal prey items. Presuming that plants are occasionally devoured along with prey, but remain in the stomach for lack of digestion, plant remains might be no indicator for actual feeding.

23601: The objective of the present study was to analyze the diet of nine species of fishes of the Três Irmãos reservoir. Five species were characterized as carnivorous (Plagioscion squamosissimus, Serrassalmus spilopleura, Hoplias malabaricus, Rhamdia quelenand Cichla sp.), the majority with predominance of crustaceans on diet. Vegetable was predominant on diet of two species, Metynnis maculatus and Schizodon nasutus, considered as herbivorous and algivorous. Geophagus brasiliensis and Astyanax altiparanae were characterized as insectivorous and herbivorous-insectivorous. The niche breadth of Geophagus brasilensis, Hoplias malabaricus, Metynnis maculatus and Plagioscion squamosissimus characterized them as specialists and the one of Serrassalmus spilopleura, Rhamdia quelen, Astyanax altiparanae and Cichla sp. as generalists.

23602: Ambystoma andersoni is an endemic amphibian of the Laguna de Zacapu, Mich. Mexico. Furthermore ecological relevance, this species has a meaning in local culture by its medicinal and economical properties. Unfortunately, the fresh water ecosystems have a huge damage because of anthropogenic activities like pollution and fishing pressure, for this kind of reasons this amphibian species could be considered endangered of extinction (NOM-Ecol-059-2001). Due to these deeds, aquaculture is one link for conservation of native species, because breeding obtained already, might to omit the fishing activity. However standard amphibian aquaculture techniques have identified a high mortality in early stages of life, which is considered the most critical period, mainly by appropriate feeding lack. This work pretend founding a food that can be available and with a considerable nutritional level. Different diets efficiency in growth have been studied with different live food species, which Daphnia pulex, Hyalella azteca, Artemia franciscana, Tubifex sp., Eissenia foetida, and beef heart, mixes of D. pulex plus H. azteca, D. pulex plus A. fransiscana, offered ad-libitum (the feeding was along the first nine weeks). Growth was observed with one individual isolated and with three individuals together, both in a constant temperature of 21 ° C with a variation of 1.5 ° C, individuals were measured weekly. A. andersoni has a better growth with diets which includes zooplankton rather with the other kind of diets, where growth was lower. Although there is not a range of difference, among treatments with one individual isolated and with three individuals together, in treatments with three individuals was observed cannibalism the nine weeks long.

23603: Lampropeltis triangulum elapsoides is reported to intergrade with neighboring subspecies of milk snakes (L.t.triangulum, L.t.syspila, and L.t.amaura) in portions of their overlap range while in other areas of range overlap they appear to exist in sympatry with little or no gene flow. As part of a larger study to investigate the degree of gene flow between subspecies of milk snakes in the eastern United States, a putative intergrade zone between L.t.elapsoides and L.t.syspila in western Kentucky and Tennessee was analyzed for gene flow. Milk snakes from this appear superficially as either L.t.syspila, or as somewhat aberrant L.t.elapsoides (leading some to call these intergrades). Recent morphological analysis by Armstrong et al. suggests however that these aberrant L.t.elapsoides are true to type with little or no syspila influence. To test this hypothesis mitochondrial 16s rRNA gene sequence was used as a character to delineate sub species and as a marker to test for gene flow. A comparison of DNA sequence from Reference L.t.elapsoides (Florida, Georgia and South Carolina) and L.t.syspila (Missouri and Tennessee) with L. triangulum specimens from the zone of sympatry in western Kentucky supports the conclusions of Armstrong et al. with all phenotypically syspila like animals showing syspila sequence, and all phenotypically elapsoides like animals showing elapsoides sequence. We suggest that other reported areas of intergradation of L.t.elapsoides with either L.t.triangulum (along the Atlantic coast = L.t.temporalis), L.t.syspila, or L.t.amaura may also have been miss-identified in this regard, and require further study.

23604: A recent discovery of an Amazonian semi-fossorial Otophysan fish, apparently not related to any of the taxa known for the region, has raised much speculations. The fish was collected in pools in the Rio Negro basin near Manaus during the low water season. The taxon can be diagnosed by a series of unique external morphological features such as: maintenance of a notochord extension over the caudal fin; larval paddle-like pectoral fin in almost fully grown juveniles; very elongate body; numerous scales (more than 240); absence of lateral line pores along body and head; spatulated caudal peduncle with dorsal and ventral soft-tissue expansions and minute eyes located anteriorly on the head. Internally, it has a long swim bladder subdivided in several constricted chambers; a well developed weberian apparatus with the distal process of the third supraneural directed straight anteriorly not articulating with the supraoccipital and an apparent reminiscent second supraneural; enlarged quadrate-metapterygoid fenestra; absence of laterosensory canals on the neurocranium; anterolateral processes of the mesethmoid articulating with a deep ventral recess of the premaxilla; numerous pleural ribs (41 or 42) and vertebrae (68) and significant fusion of caudal fin elements. It seems to be highly paedomorphic with larval features being retained in specimens over 30 mm SL. Adaptation to semi-fossorial habits may have caused the loss or great reduction of many anatomical structures, including certain bones and portions of the latero-sensory canal system. The fish represents a new family, genera and species. Preliminary hypotheses on its phylogenetic relationships within Otophysans will be discussed.

23605: Gelanoglanis are minute Auchenipterid catfishes that occur in the Amazon and Orinoco river systems and until recently has been poorly known. In recent years several new collections have yielded a diversity previously unsuspected in this taxon. In this paper we will present four new species of Gelanoglanis from the Amazon basin. Three species are from southern slope drainages of the Guyana shield, two being syntopic in the Tacutu river, and the third species is found in the Demeni river. The fourth species occurs in western Amazonia in the Nanay river drainage in Peru. Two groups of species are recognized based on the presence or absence of dorsal and pectoral fins spines and adipose fin. Species are diagnosed based on morphological differences of the anal fin in sexually dimorphic adult males, body proportions, size and relative position of pelvic fins and coloration patterns.

23606: How rapidly can a species adapt to changes in its environment? Cane toads (Bufo marinus) were introduced into Australia > 65 years ago. The cane toad is a large anuran and is extremely toxic to most species of Australian snake. A recent estimate suggests that more than 49 species of Australian snake are likely to be adversely affected by the presence of toads. For most species of Australian snake the toad thus represents a novel and very strong selective force. Are snakes showing an adaptive response to toads? There are a number of ways in which a population may respond to toads, a population may: become more resistant to toad toxin, change prey or habitat preferences and/or may exhibit morphological change (particularly in relative gape width). We present data that explore these possibilities. We have used comparisons across populations to assess changes in toxin resistance and prey preferences. We have assessed changes in morphology using museum collections and information derived from GIS layers. Preliminary results suggest that some species are exhibiting adaptive response to cane toads despite the relatively short time since exposure.

23607: Following attainment of sexual maturity, correlation between body size and age in lizards is weakened, and may be entirely absent, which decreases the reliability of ordinary allometric methods. The annual growth in amphibians and reptiles is cyclical, which results in the production of growth lines in bones. Less dense layers are associated with periods of rapid, and narrower ones, with periods of decreased growth rates. In this study we analyze the contribution of skeletochronology as a tool to determine age and growth patterns in three species of lizards, as to improve ecological studies. The species studied are sympatric and sintopic from Patagonia steppe: Liolaemus elongatus and Phymaturus patagonica (Tropiduridae, Liolaeminae), which are viviparous and diurnal, and Homonota darwini, which is nocturnal and oviparous. Femurs, humerus and phalanges were decalcified in 5% nitric acid and cut in 15 µm slices. The sections from the midshaft of the dyaphysis were stained in Tricromic of Masson dye. Endosteal bones resorption in humerus and femurs occurred in all the adults studied, but intensity varied related to the size of the bone and to the age of the animal. Cross sections of the three types of bone show cellular and vascular tissue mainly built of a compact parallel fibered bone of periosteal origin, and reduced medullar cavities in phalanges. Annuli in adults are more distinct in femurs. Young individuals do not show endosteal resorption, neither annuli before the first year. In the diurnal species there are no differences between the number of annuli in humerus and femurs, however being more distinct in femurs. L. elongatus phalanges do not show growth marks. In H. darwini there are no differences between the number of growth marks in humerus and femurs but in phalanges there are one or two less. This technique will allow us to perform improved population and reproductive field studies of these species.

23608: Physalaemus aguirrei occurs in the Atlantic Rainforest of the states of Espirito Santo and Bahia, Brazil. Tadpoles on stages 36 and 37 were obtained from a foam nest collected in a temporary pond at PARNA Descobrimento (17°06′ S, 39°20′ W), Prado Municipality, Bahia, Brazil. Mean total length is 20.6 mm. Nostrils large, nearly round, located and oriented dorsally, closer to eyes than to snout; internostril distance 35% of interocular distance; eyes located dorsolaterally; eye-nostril distance 89% of eye diameter; spiracle single, sinistral, short, projected, opening at the end of the second third of body length, posterodorsally oriented; vent tube medial, wide, long, attached to ventral fin, with opening oriented posteriorly. 23609: Recent collections on floating meadows along a small Solim Ões-Amazonas region close to Manaus uncovered a large number of fish species and, in particular, two loricariine species absolutely absent in fish collections and museums. Rineloricaria castroi Isbrücker and Nijssen, 1984, was described from Lower rio Trombetas (Pará State) and it is only known by the holotype, deposited in the Museu de Zoologia da USP (São Paulo). 23610: The genus Mabuya has viviparous and oviparous species and seasonal or continuous reproductive cycles. All 15 Brazilian species are viviparous and appear to reproduce seasonally. However, there are differences in clutch size, correlation between female SVL and clutch size, and age of sexual maturity. Although Mabuya guaporicola is considered a rare species, the Tapiti Fauna Rescue collected about 500 individuals in the APM Manso dam - Chapada dos Guimaraes, MT, Brazil - between December 1999 and January 2001. To evaluate the reproductive cycle of M. guaporicola we used 456 animals from Manso. We measured their SVL, identified sex and reproductive condition via dissection. Macroscopic examination of female gonads revealed ovules, vitelogenic follicles, embryos, fetuses and young through the year. We indirectly measured male reproductive activity by the volume of the left testicle (VT). SVL varied from 28.7 to 96.6 mm. Females were larger than males and the recruitment occurred between December and January (rainy season). Females apparently can become gravid within couple of months of life; probably produce just one clutch per year, and the gestation lasts 9 to 12 months. Clutch size ranged from 3 to 7, was directly related to female SVL and the presence of vitelogenic follicles and small embryos was concentrated from December to February. The male VT varied with SVL, but the residuals of VT and SVL for males larger than 50 mm were lower during the dry season. The species reproductive cycle is seasonal and synchronic as both sexes present mature gametes simultaneously. Mabuya guaporicola has a reproductive strategy similar to the other Brazilian congeners, corroborating the hypothesis that Mabuya reproductive patterns are conservative.

23611: By means of skeletochronology, we have determined the age distribution of the frog species Rana luteiventris in central Nevada over the years 2000 to 2002. Through analysis of the number of lines of arrested growth (LAG) in the toe bone of clipped frogs (one LAG is equivalent to one year), skeletochronology can be used to determine the age of a frog. Of the 12 sites studied, random samples of 20 frogs from each were analyzed to determine age distribution. Fewer juveniles were reported in 2001 compared to 2000 indicating less reproduction due to drought. The wetter sites (located further north) contained more juveniles than the drier (southern) sites. Otherwise, age distributions among all sites were similar, with one exception. The exception is a beaver pond that contains trout. It appears that recruitment has not been successful at this site in recent years. Only the older age classes are represented. All the other sites are free of trout.

23612: Information on the utilization of fish resources by local peoples is necessary in order to both assess the impact of human activity on local fish ecology and also to plan and implement successful conservation policies. To gain a better understanding of the utilization of fish resources by traditional populations in and around the Caxiuanã National Forest, data were collected from 37 fishing trips between August and December 2002. Data collection included: time allocation in fishing activities, time traveled and location of fishing activity, fishing method, number and weight of individual fish caught and household composition. All fish caught were consumed in the household. A total of 40 different species were registered. In all cases travel to the fishing location was by canoe and in 60% of the cases travel time was 30 minutes or less. A positive correlation was found between distance traveled and total capture weight (r = 0.48). The most common fishing technique was floating gill net (49%) followed by trident (30%), hand-held line (14%) and spear/mask (9%). In terms of total number, the most commonly caught species were traíra (Hoplias malabaricus) (10%), acará-pixuna (Heros severus) (8%), acará-borroló (Acaronia nasa) (8%) and acará-tinga (Geophagus surinamensis) (6%). In terms of weight the most important fish in the diet were traíra (Hoplias malabaricus) (9.5%), acará-pixuna (Heros severus) (9.3%), piranha-branca (Cyphocharax abramoides) (8.5%) and acareua (Aequidens spp.) (8.3%). Fish is the most reliable and important source of protein in the local diet and local fishing techniques do not appear to be sufficient to disrupt fish ecology in and around the national forest. However, community elders have noticed a decrease in fish availability, which may be due to local population growth and the presence of commercial fishing vessels just outside the national forest.

23613: The specimens of piramutaba (Brachyplatystoma vaillantii) analyzed in this research were obtained from experimental fisheries in the amazon estuary. For the study of age determination pectorals and dorsal spines, opercules, otoliths (lapillus) and vertebrae were analyzed. This is so because the vertebrae showed good resolution in annulus (59%), and it also has a significant exponential relationship (r2 = 0.9889 and P<0.05) between the radius of the vertebrae and the fork length of fish. The seasonal rings were validated using length frequency analysis. Two annual rings are formed on the vertebrae of piramutaba. The weight-length relationship seen in piramutaba describes its growth as allometric and the equation that describes its growth is: Wt = 6.1 * 10-6 * Lf3.1129. The sexual proportion of piramutaba observed was not 1:1, as the number of females was superior to the males. On vertebraes of piramutaba a maximum of ten rings were observed. The von Bertalanffy growth model was utilized in this research to estimate the length and weight equations. The growth parameters (k, t0 and L infinit) were estimated through four different methods: rings reading, backcalculation, rings modal progression and length frequency analysis. 23614: This work reports different aspects of the reproduction of the colubrid snake Liophis miliaris in four regions of Brazil: (1) northern Atlantic forest in Bahia state, (2) southern Atlantic forest in São Paulo-Paraná states, (3) inland Atlantic forest in São Paulo state and (4) inland Atlantic forest in Paraná state. Females have a larger snout-vent length (SVL) than males in all these regions. In northern Atlantic forest - where there is litlle climate variation - reproductive cycle is continuous whereas in the other regions it is seasonal, related to warmer and more rainy season. Sperm production seems to occur all through the year in all these places. Where the reproductive cycle is seasonal, mating seems to be dissociated from vitellogenesis; thus, females must store sperm overwinter. Clutch size is similar in all populations increasing with maternal length. In northern Atlantic forest newborn snakes had a smaller SVL than in the other regions studied. Reproductive frequency is lower in northern Atlantic forest and, different from the other regions, tends to increase with female length. Prey items are similar in all populations and gravid females do not feed. Ophidiascaris sp. (Nematoda) and cystacanths of Oligacanthorynchus spira (Acanthocephala) were found equally in both female and males, fewer in snakes from Atlantic forest in Bahia. Apparently, these parasites do not impede reproduction, but females attacked by nematodes in inland Atlantic forest in Paraná show a smaller clutch size than non-attacked ones. The activity pattern of adult snakes is associated with the reproductive cycle and climate variation in all sites. The reproductive pattern of L. miliaris differs from other Xenodontini species which tend to reproduce continuously even in areas with seasonal climate. Thus, L. miliaris seems to be more sensitive to some climate variables than other species of Xenodontini studied.

23615: In tropical areas, the reproductive cycles of lizard species can be continuous or seasonal. Studies on reproductive biology are highly limited to a few families and do not include species in the family Anguidae. Ophiodes striatus (Anguidae) is a common limbless lizard in southeast Brazil; it probably represents a complex of species. In addition, to the taxonomic confusion, information about its reproduction has been not available. This study presents data on sexual maturity, adult body size, newborn body size and mass, fecundity, male and female reproductive cycles of one population of Ophiodes cf. striatus from São Paulo-Paraná states, southeast Brazil. Females are larger and attain sexual maturity with a larger SVL than males. The female reproductive cycle is highly seasonal with secondary vitellogenesis starting in February. Embryos in early stages of development occur in June and birth from August to December (end of the dry season and onset of the rainy season). Due to the long gestational period it is improbable that females can reproduce annually. Clutch size averages 7-8 newborn and it is not related to the mother’s size, as in other lizard species. Newborns average 44.1 mm in SVL and 0.69 g in mass. In males, the residual volume of the testes does not vary along the year, suggesting a continuous spermatogenic cycle. The diameter of deferent duct is greatest from January to March, suggesting that males store sperm until the mating season.

23616: As part of the National Park Service Inventory and Monitoring program, eight national parks and monuments on the Northern Colorado Plateau in Utah were surveyed for herpetofauna in 2001 and 2002. The primary objective for this project was to document 90% of the species present. 23618: Over the last years, several programs have been launched on Brazilian rivers to restore and protect migratory fish populations. These programs involve building upstream fish passage facilities, but little attention has been paid to problems associated with downstream migrations. The possibility of downstream passage in Santa Clara Power Plant structures was assessed using a mark-recaptured program. Its powerhouse contains three Kaplan turbine units. The three conventional spillway gates are 11.5 m wide and 15.8 m deep. Fishes were captured below the dam with casting nets from October 2002 to February 2003. A total of 15.376 marked fishes were released upstream on reservoir. During this period, 29 fishes were recaptured immediately below of the dam. Most of them (85%) were migratory species (Prochilodus vimboides, Leporinus conirostris, L. steindachnerii and Brycon ferox). In average, the downstream fishes were recaptured 47 days after the releasing, and have 19.5 centimeters mean standard length. A relatively small number of fish were injured (7%). However, very injured and dead fishes are hard to capture by casting nets. The spillway must be the main route of fish downstream passage. Although spills had occurred in 30% of the study time, 93% of the recaptures had happened during these periods. The Santa Clara spillway seems to be useful to provide downstream migrations. 23619: The coast of Rio Grande do Sul is part of a large plain constituted by mobile sand dunes and depressions that form water bodies during periods of higher rainfall.
