23712: The ontogeny of diet changes of 836 whitemouth croaker, Micropogonias furnieri, collected in the Baha Blanca estuary (Argentina) between March 2000 and February 2001 was investigated. Diet shifts were examined in relation to changes in habitat use, foraging behaviour, and morphology. Also, the relationship between diet and abundance of the main prey was studied. Juvenile M. furnieri prey heavily on chaetognaths (Sagitta friderici), white shrimp (Peisos petrunkevitchi) and polychaetes. Two size-related dietary shifts, at 4.00 cm and 7.00 cm total length (TL) were found. Small juveniles (1.00 - 3.99 cm TL) were pelagic feeders and prey heavily on chaetognaths. Electivity index indicated strong positive selection towards this prey item. Medium-sized juveniles (4.00 - 6.99 cm TL) switched to demersal-pelagic (mysid shrimps, mainly Neomysis americana) and benthic prey (polychaetes). Finally, large juveniles (7.00 - 15.99 cm TL) shifted to demersal-benthic prey and fed almost exclusively on epibenthic crustaceans (primarely P. petrunkevitchi). Although mysids were an important prey item in the diet of medium-sized juveniles, they were consistently selected against. P. petrunkevitchi and crutaceans Penaeoidea (Artemesia longinaris and Pleoticus muelleri) were positively selected by both medium and large juveniles. Increased mouth gape was associated with increased size spectrum and mean size of the most important prey items consumed for M. furnieri. Juveniles < 12 cm TL ate prey almost as wide as their mouth opening, whereas juveniles > 12 cm TL were capable of feeding on larger prey than were found in their stomachs, indicating that the maximum size of prey eaten was not constrained by mouth gape. Consequently, size spectrum and relative abundance of prey of various sizes was probably determining larger juveniles’ diet.

23713: Snakes of the Micrurus nigrocinctus complex are distributed in almost all-major ecosystems of Middle America. These monad coral snakes are the most important elapids in the region from the point of human envenomation. Currently, six subspecies are recognized: M. n. nigrocinctus, M. n. mosquitensis, M. n. divaricatus, M. n. babaspul, and M. n. coibensis, mainly based in locality and color patterns. Despite their wide distribution, little is known about the morphological and molecular variation of those populations, and the taxonomical status of the subspecies remains controversial. Furthermore, the phylogenetic relationships among populations of the M. nigrocinctus complex have never been established, making difficult to understand the historical events that shaped their distribution. In this study, we investigate the phylogenetic relationships within populations, and evaluate their position in relation to other monad species. To reconstruct phylogenies, we employed external morphological characters and sequences of the mitochondria genes ND4 and Cyt b from ca. 35 individuals from 14 localities. All sequences from individuals included in the complex constituted a monophyletic clade, sister to Micrurus fulvius from North America. Within the complex, snakes from the South Pacific lowlands of Costa Rica, previously described as M. n. nigrocinctus, have higher affinities to the M. n. mosquitensis forms from the Caribbean lowlands. The affinities of M. nigrocinctus populations is revised under the new evidence, but the inclusion of insular forms is necessary to elucidate the taxonomy within the complex

23714: Population decline or extinction of over 26 species of anurans had been reported from pristine environments of Costa Rica. Despite this fact, very few projects have been established to monitor long term changes in amphibian communities in the region. Here, we present data for the first fifteen months of one of such projects conducted at La Selva Biological Station. Visual encounter survey was established once per month in two transects: Cantarana (150 m length) and Holdridge trail (1000 m). Both sites include breeding places for swamp dwellers, and a proportion of primary forest. In 15 visits, we recorded 740 individuals of 11 genera and 27 species of amphibians, a figure that represent 54% of the species known to the station. Composition and abundance of species are different at each site, probably reflecting their structural differences. Fluctuations in species abundance observed during this period are discussed in terms of seasonal rainfall pattern and forest flooding. Long-term monitoring programs are necessary to understand the complex dynamics of amphibian populations, as well as to establish null models to compare fluctuations of suspected declines. We suggest that long term monitoring projects should be incorporated as exercises for students in the academic agenda of OTS.
23715: Trichomycteridae, which comprises about 200 species distributed among 35 genera and eight subfamilies, is represented by small-sized catfishes that are widely distributed throughout South and Central America. In the present study DNA sequences of a partial segment of cytochrome oxidase I and tRNAAsn were analyzed. Molecular data were obtained for 21 species of Trichomycterus and 4 species of other Trichomycteridae genera. The size of analyzed sequences range from 947 bp in Pseudostegophilus sp. to 965 bp in Trichomycterus sp. The species Nematogenys inermis was used as outgroup. In 966 bp aligned sequences, 591 showed to be conserved, 373 variable and 294 phylogenetically informative. The phylogenies were obtained by maximum parsimony using the software Mega 2.1. Bootstrap resampling was applied to assess support for individual nodes using 1000 replicates with 20 random additions and TBR branch swapping. Two threes were obtained with tree length of 1125, consistence index of 0.497 and retention index of 0.630. In these trees the species of Stegophilinae (Pseudostegophilus and Henonemus) and two samples of Vandelliinae (Vandellia) were separated as well supported natural groups. All the species of Trichomycterus were placed together, forming a monophyletic group with 99% of support in the bootstrap analysis. It is considered that the study of other Trichomycteridae species and genera will complement the available information for a better understanding of the evolution of the family.

23716: The dorsal scale rows of alethinophidian snakes are oriented at an acute angle, rather than being aligned along the transverse axis of the body. A lower angle of the dorsal rows corresponds to greater offset between adjacent rows of scales. In general, macrostomate snakes are characterized by relatively oblique rows, and we hypothesize that the macrostomate condition reflects variation in the distribution of intersquamous skin along the length of individual scales. Highly folded intersquamous skin is more abundant toward the tip of each scale than at the base. We propose a model that describes the distribution of intersquamous skin around the circumference of the body as a function of scale row angle. The model predicts the effect of scale row angle on the degree of integumentary stretch. Scale rows that are vertically aligned result in a limited degree of stretch compared to oblique scale rows. The model permits investigation of the effects of scale row angle and other integumentary variables and yields testable predictions. Broadly speaking, variation in scale row angle in snakes appears to reflect differences in prey diameter and gape.

23717: Analysis of the shape of species accumulation curves is a straightforward method to evaluate the performance and behavior of methods for sampling species richness. We compared four methods used for sampling the snake fauna of a Cerrado fragment in southeastern Brazil (Itirapina Ecological Station) between September 1998 and March 2002: incidental encounters (IE; sampling effort 446 days), pitfall traps with drift fence (PTDF; 18,360 bucket-days), captures by local collectors (LC; 167 collector-months), and time constrained search (TCS; 900 person- hours). We used species accumulation curves to compare the performance of methods. Curves were generated by EstimateS 5.1 software, with 1000 ressamplings. We captured a total of 731 snakes of 33 species: 156 individuals of 27 species through IE, 381 individuals of 25 species through PTDF, 114 individuals of 19 species through LC, and 80 individuals of 14 species through TCS. No curve reached an asymptote, indicating that none of the methods captured all the species possible, despite the relatively high sampling effort. IE resulted in a curve with slow and constant growth and was the only one that made possible a reliable estimation of species richness by Jacknife (33 ± 3 spp.); however, the sampling effort was very high (446 days of fieldwork). Pitfall traps resulted in a curve with relatively fast growth until 100 samples and 16 species (aprox. 50% of total richness), indicating that the method is useful for short-term studies to capture the most common species. The curves of LC and TCS grew slowly and constantly, indicating they are useful only as complementary methods. Each method was biased and limited to certain species. These results indicate that only a combination of methods, associated with a high sampling effort, would result in a good sampling of snake species richness in the Cerrado. Funded by FAPESP.

23718: Western diamondback rattlesnakes co-occur with timber rattlesnakes in the eastern part of their range. In the Ouachita Mountains of west-central Arkansas, western diamondback rattlesnakes occupy a relict distribution associated with rocky outcrops on south-facing slopes. Timber rattlesnakes are generally distributed in more forested habitats. Though there was considerable overlap, telemetry studies comparing habitat use between the two species indicate that western diamondback rattlesnakes occur more often in areas with less canopy closure on higher and steeper slopes. This more open habitat had slightly more ground level foliage, rock cover, and burrows. Timber rattlesnakes were found more often on lower mountain slopes in areas with greater canopy closure due to slightly greater numbers of canopy trees. Western diamondback rattlesnakes appear to occupy habitats in the Ouachita Mountains that most closely resemble habitats used throughout its extensive range in the southwestern United States. Timber rattlesnakes were more closely associated with closed canopy forests as is characteristic of this species throughout its range in the eastern United States.

23719: The subfamily Lithogeninae was erected by Gosline in the now classic 1947 paper, Contributions to the Classification of the Loricariid Catfishes. Lithogenes villosus Regan, 1909 was the sole representative of the subfamily, being known until recently from a single specimen collected in 1908 from Kaieteur Falls, Guyana. Additional specimens were collected at the type locality in 1998. A new species, L. valencia, was recently described from Lago de Valencia, an isolated endorrheic lake situated in the Caribbean coastal region of north-central Venezuela. A third species, presently undescribed, was discovered in a tributary of the Orinoco River in a remote region of western Amazonas State of Venezuela. In this study, evidence is presented that serves to diagnose the three species and determine their relationships. They uniquely share a number of derived specializations among the Loricariidae, thus confirming the status and monophyly of the Lithogeninae. All three species are known from single localities, without populations in the intervening regions. Lithogenes therefore represents yet another example among a growing list of neotropical fishes that display widely disjunct Guyana Shield distributions.

23720: To encourage tourism, commercial dive boat operators often offer shark feeding excursions and provide video footage of the dives to participating SCUBA divers. We conducted a longitudinal study of Caribbean reef shark (Carcharhinus perezi) feeding dives occurring at a single location off West End, The Bahamas. We analyzed video tapes of 36 dives recorded over the period of November 1992-September 2001. Data was collected on the following variables: water visibility; human activity; number of sharks and humans per dive; shark parasite load; gender of shark and male maturity; and frequency of feeding attempts, acts of antagonism, and yawning. Site fidelity of individual sharks was investigated by documenting, when possible, markings and scars on each shark. We found that the minimum number of female and male sharks per dive, as well as the parasite load on both sexes, increased temporally. Parasites were most frequently found near gill openings. Bumping of the camera, presumably an act of antagonism, was observed more often in females than in males. The frequency of shark feeding attempts was correlated with the technique of the human feeder. The number of divers and water visibility had no significant affect on the recorded shark behaviors. No seasonal trends concerning recorded behaviors, parasite load, or clasper size were observed. Females and males did not differ significantly in frequency of feeding attempts. Nine individual females and eight males were identified in more than a single dive. Although one individual had a hiatus of 4.5 years between sightings, most of the reappearing individuals were repetitively observed on site over periods of several months. Such site fidelity may be attributable to feeding-induced conditioning of the sharks.

23721: The endemic Lake Tanganyika cichlid genus Lepidiolamprologus was erected by Pellegrin in 1904 for Lamprologus elongatus Boulenger, 1898, largely on the basis of its being more elongate than most Lamprologus and having smaller and more numerous scales. In 1906, Boulenger synonymized Lepidiolamprologus with Lamprologus, and the genus was subsequently ignored for almost 80 years. Then in 1985, Colombe and Allgayer resurrected Lepidiolamprologus, and included in the genus six superficially similar elongate piscivores removed from Lamprologus. Under closer scrutiny, however, Lepidiolamprologus sensu Colombe and Allgayer does not appear to be monophyletic. This study uses morphological and molecular characters to examine the species composition and intrarelationships of Lepidiolamprologus. A diagnosis for the genus is provided.

23722: One environmental gradient that dramatically influences freshwater species distributions and community composition is the hydroperiod gradient. Species capable of colonizing temporary ponds are exposed to small predation risk but are under severe developmental time constraint. Conversely, developmental time constraints are relaxed, but predation pressure increases, in species colonizing ponds of increasing permanence. Using a system of ranid tadpole species distributed across the hydroperiod gradient in lower Michigan, I demonstrate that time- constrained species grow and develop faster because have higher foraging rates and larger areas of gut epithelium, but lower maintenance costs, than time-unconstrained species. These observations are consistent with the species ability to colonize ponds of different hydroperiod. I also examined the fundamental behavioral tradeoff that arises because activity rates in these species are simultaneously correlated with resource acquisition and predation risk. Supporting theoretical predictions, I demonstrate that growth is positively correlated with activity rates. Furthermore, whereas time-constrained species display steep activity reductions with increasing food availability, time-unconstrained species are comparatively inactive and largely unresponsive to variation in food availability. These findings support the predictions that activity rates should decline with increasing food availability, because the energetic demands of the forager can be met with reduced activity, and as such, reduced predation rates. Moreover, they are consistent with alternative adaptive solutions to a foraging rate/mortality rate tradeoff in habitats varying in duration and predation risk, and with selection favoring phenotypic plasticity in species experiencing greater temporal and spatial habitat heterogeneity. Finally, the observation that maintenance costs are lower in highly active species suggests that the metabolic costs of activity are negligible and as such, any increases in fitness gained by reducing activity results from reduced predation rather than increased energy conservation.

23723: Generalized pond tadpoles have long been considered herbivores and detritivores with no or little food discrimination other than that based on particle size. Consequently, the role of resources in structuring anuran communities has been downplayed. Following my research findings that food type, quality and quantity can drive major patterns of anuran habitat segregation, I conducted a comparative study of the feeding ecology of four ranid tadpole species across a productivity (canopy-cover) gradient in lower Michigan. Based on field sampling and transplant experiments, I quantified the identity and C:N ratios of gut contents, as well as the 15N/14N, 13C/12C stable isotope composition of tadpoles and their putative food. Whereas gut content analyses provide information on the identity, proportions, and quality of food ingested, isotopic analysis indicates trophic level and actual nutritional sources integrated over the lifetime of the organism. Isotopic signatures of wood frogs and leopard frogs transplanted to bottomless cages in open- and closed- canopy ponds indicated very different diets across habitats, but similar diets in each habitat. Isotopic and gut content analyses of free-ranging wood frogs indicate nutrition based on high- quality periphyton in open-canopy ponds, and on low-quality detritus in closed-canopy ponds. Carbon isotopic signatures of bullfrogs and green frogs transplanted to open-canopy ponds dramatically differed from those of wood frogs and leopard frogs, either indicating reliance on different resources, or seasonal changes in the isotopic signature of primary producers. Surprisingly, the nitrogen isotopic signature of free-ranging bullfrogs and green frogs spanned that expected for four trophic levels; furthermore, in some ponds tadpole nitrogen signatures equaled those of dragonfly naiads, suggesting that carnivory significantly contributes to nutrition of these species. Overall, my results suggest that coexisting tadpole species with archetypical generalized morphology may consume different resources, and support the hypothesis that the food web role of tadpoles may have to be reconsidered.

23724: Southamerican herpetofaunal lowland communities can present more than 180 species. Longterm studies on the ecology of Amazonian anuran communities are known from Belem, Brazil, Santa Cecilia, Ecuador, Manaus, Brazil, and Panguana, Peru. Herpetological communities with focus on the upper Amazon Basin have been reported from Ecuador (Santa Cecilia), Peru (Panguana, Dpt. Loreto, Cocha Cashu, Cuzco Amazonico, Serrania de Sira, Rio Curanje, Pakitza, Manu National Park, from Bolivia (Puerto Almacen). The Rio Llullapichis is an eastern confluence of the Rio Pachitea. Total anual rainfall is about 2000 - 3000 mm. The wet season (October to April), which comprises 80 % of the rainfall, is followed by a distinct dry season. The temperature is mostly between 22 and 30 centigrades. The species diversity of the investigated area reflects the typical caracters of an upper Amazonian herpetofauna. Widespread species and those showing restricted occurrence represent an overlap of highly variable distribution patterns in that area. Long term studies since 1977 reveal data on taxonomy, habitat, diel activity and food. 23725: Many aquatic organisms rely on chemical cues (produced during predation events) for making phenotypic decisions, and these cues may differ when predators consume different prey diets. Two possible explanatory mechanisms for this pattern are phylogenetic relatedness and ecological similarity of target species to different predator diets. More distantly-related diets did not consistently produce weaker responses than more closely-related diets. Further, heterospecific diets that typically coexist with the target did not consistently induce stronger responses than heterospecific diets that do not coexist. These results suggest that the chemical cues released during predation events provide specific information about the species being consumed, and that the pattern of response cannot be accurately predicted by either phylogenetic similarity or ecological similarity alone.

23726: The family Synbranchidae has a broad, native distribution, known to occur in fresh and occasionally brackish or estuarine habitats. In the laboratory experiment, swamp eels were held at 0.2 (freshwater control), 12, 14, 16 and 18 ppt for 80 days. 23728: The dourado is considered to be one of the most mobile long distant migrating fresh water fishes of the Neotropics. 23729: In this study, the historical relationships among gopher tortoise (Gopherus polyphemus) populations in peninsular Florida and southern Georgia were inferred using nine microsatellite loci. 23731: Family Emydidae is a diverse group of aquatic, semiaquatic, and terrestrial turtles native to the New World, except for the Eurasian genus Emys. They have been a common subject for physiological, behavioral, and ecological research. Those studies which have taken a comparative approach often reveal differences among genera. 23732: Depending upon the species, salamanders possess various groups of exocrine glands that are sexually dimorphic and implicated in courtship and mating activities. These glands secrete either onto the surface of the skin or into the cloaca. Skin glands are most highly developed in the Plethodontidae and include nasolabial glands, mental glands, and caudal courtship glands. Caudal courtship glands independently evolved in some salamandrids, and cloacal glands involved in pheromone production are more highly developed in the Salamandridae than in other families. Males of Rhyacotritonidae have a pheromone-producing gland that originated as a cloacal gland and secondarily became a skin gland. Phylogenetically, production of sex pheromones is the ancestral function for cloacal glands in both sexes, and cloacal glands involved in male spermatophore production and female sperm storage evolved in the common ancestor to the Salamandroidea, and are synapomorphies for the group. Mental glands evolved once in the common ancestor to plethodontids and have been secondarily lost in some taxa (Houck-Sever hypothesis) or origin and loss of mental glands has occurred independently several times in the Plethodontidae (Beachy hypothesis).

23733: The snapping turtle, Chelydra serpentina is currently considered to be one of the most broadly- distributed turtle species on earth, ranging from southern Canada to Columbia and Ecuador. Four morphologically-defined subspecies are currently recognized, with considerable debate centered on their validity and proper rank. To shed light on this problem, we conducted a molecular analysis of all four currently recognized taxa within C. serpentina, with particularly deep sampling across the continental U.S. Consistent with previous work, we found virtually no mitochondrial (mt) DNA variation across the entire U.S. portion of their range for the often- rapidly evolving control region. However, the two forms from Mexico/northern Central America (C. s. rossignoni) and southern Central America/South America (C. s. acutirostris) are divergent, well-supported clades. Taken together, these results indicate that there are no absolute constraints on mtDNA evolution in these turtles, yet the U.S. populations contain no measurable variation. To differentiate between a rapid invasion of all of the U.S. by snapping turtles, and the alternative interpretation of a selective sweep on the mitochondrial genome, we sequenced two nuclear genes for a broad subset of our original sample. To our surprise, we found that both nuclear genes show considerably more variation than the mtDNA, consistent with the selective sweep hypothesis for reduced variation. We discuss these results both in terms of our views on species boundaries in the snapping turtle complex, and the implications of natural selection, in addition to phylogenetic history, shaping variation in the mtDNA of these animals.

23735: Here we report on communal oviposition involving the common house gecko (Hemidactylus frenatus), tropical house gecko (H. mabouia), ashy gecko (Sphaerodactylus elegans), and Florida reef gecko (S. notatus), and remark on their reproduction and microhabitats of oviposition sites in the lower Florida Keys, Monroe County, Florida, USA. 23738: In the coast of Paraná State there are a series of isolated hydrographic basins with apparently similar species compositions of freshwater fish assemblages. 23741: Courtship and mating in snakes are generally viewed as co-operative endeavours between the male and female, but our studies on red-sided garter snakes (Thamnophis sirtalis parietalis) in Manitoba suggest a more sinister scenario. Intuition suggests that it would be impossible for a (small) male garter snake to forcibly inseminate a (large) female. Her elongate flexible body is difficult to physically restrain, males do not display any overt aggression during courtship, and a male cannot intromit until the female gapes open her cloaca. Nonetheless, males do obtain forcible matings in this system, by exploiting specific features of snake anatomy, physiology and behaviour. The snake lung extends along most of the body, with the large posterior section (the saccular lung) lacking any respiratory exchange surface. Rhythmic caudocephalic waves by courting male garter snakes push anoxic air from the saccular lung forward and across the respiratory surfaces, such that females cannot obtain oxygen. Their stress response involves cloacal gaping, which functions in other contexts to repel predators by extruding feces and musk, but in this situation permits male intromission. Thus, superficially benign courtship behaviors may involve cryptic coercion, even in species for which intuition dismisses any possibility of forcible insemination. Understanding such conflicts may be critical to interpreting the diversity in mating systems and courtship behaviours among snakes.

23743: Little is known about the habitat parameters that influence amphibian and reptile communities, and even less is known about their landscape-level environmental influences. 23747: Caecilians are some of the least known of all herpetofauna. 23750: Hylomantis aspera was described by Peter in 1872 and the syntipes were probably collected at Caravelas, State of Bahia. 23751: The phenomenon of communal nesting has been observed in a wide variety of reptile taxa. Although the decision of where an oviparous female lays her eggs is recognized as a critical determinant of her reproductive success, there remains little known about the mechanisms and significance behind the apparent convergence of nesting decisions among multiple females in communally nesting species. We propose a new framework for developing an understanding of communal nesting in reptiles. In doing so, we differentiate between independent nesting decisions of females converging simply because high quality nest sites are rare, and non-independent nesting decisions arising because females gain some benefit from matching their nest site choices with those already made by other females in the population. We examine published accounts of communal nesting among Australian lizards to determine the phylogenetic and ecological distribution of the behavior within this group. Accounts of the timing of nesting and hatching, and the availability of alternative nest sites will be used to provide a preliminary test of our proposed framework for explaining the incidence of communal nesting in reptiles.

23752: More than 70 parthenogenetic (all-female) species of reptiles, amphibians, and fishes have been reported, and of those that have been carefully studied all appear to have originated via interspecific hybridisation. One of the most critical questions about unisexuals is how they originated, which has important implications regarding the roles of genetic variability and sex in evolution. Two competing (but not exclusive) hypotheses are that they arose strictly as a result of selection acting on mutational changes or that unisexuals originated by interspecific hybridisation. Evidence supporting hybrid origins has continued to mount, but perhaps the best remaining vertebrate candidate for a non-hybrid origin of parthenogenesis are the tropical night lizards, Lepidophyma. The limited evidence available from morphology, karyotypes, and allozymes suggests that the all-female populations of Lepidophyma flavimaculatum did not arise via hybridisation. In this study we reconstruct a phylogeny of the genus Lepidophyma, using mitochondrial and nuclear gene sequences to determine the origin of the unisexual populations of L. flavimaculatum and L. reticulatum in Costa Rica and Panama. Conformation of a non-hybrid origin will provide insight into other evolutionary mechanisms for the origin of parthenogenesis. Another important contribution of phylogenetic hypotheses is that they provide unambiguous frameworks for prioritising conservation actions for endangered taxa. Since many of the species within this genus have extremely restricted distributions, in some cases known form only a single locality, this work will also provide information on the evolutionary distinctness of lineages and hence aid in identifying those taxa requiring conservation actions.

23753: Lepisosteidae (gars) comprises three extant species in Atractosteus and four in Lepisosteus. 23757: William A. Gosline was born in Toledo, Ohio, on December 20, 1915. His father owned the Toledo Coal Company and was president of the Toledo Art Museum. Bill had an adventuresome boyhood, canoeing and exploring natural history of the lower Maumee River and western Lake Erie, and even Hudson Bay with a group of 16-year-old friends. He completed his undergraduate education at Harvard, spending considerable time in the MCZ fish collection. Against his parents' wishes, Bill decided to become and ichthyologist and went to Stanford to study under George S. Myers, whom he regarded as a genius. At Stanford he met and married fellow Natural History Club member Alice Rundle, who assisted him by translating Russian fish papers until her death in 1997. Their two children, George and Ann, are successful professionals and environmentalists. After wartime service as an ambulance driver in North Africa, Bill served as a "fisheries engineer" and studied systematics of South American catfish in Brazil for 2 years. His brilliant 1944 paper on African and South American ostariophysans argued for a freshwater connection (before plate tectonics). He joined the faculty of the University of Michigan for 3 years before moving to the University of Hawaii where he began his work on higher classification of fishes and reef fish ecology as well as writing the Handbook of Hawaiian Fishes (1960) with V.E. Brock, and the Functional Morphology and Classification of Teleostean Fishes (1971). His outstanding doctoral students at Hawaii included Jack Randall and Gareth Nelson. Bill retired (because he hated administration) and returned to the Michigan fish collection as an adjunct curator in 1971, to work on higher classification and (informally) guide graduate students. Despite the times and location, he rejected cladistics--like others of his generation, he couldn't believe that a computer could sort out primitive from advanced characters as well as a trained ichthyologist. Bill is remembered for his dedication to fishes, his Spring mint julep parties, his wit, liberal wisdom, and for frequently walking into the fish lab, surveying people at their computers, and barking: "Doesn't anyone in this goddamn place study fish anymore?" Bill Gosline died peacefully in his beloved 60-acre woods outside Ann Arbor, June 25, 2002.

23759: Generalized patterns of distribution among marine species of the Western Central Atlantic (WCA) were sought by combining individual species range maps for hermatypic corals, azooxanthellate corals, stylasterid hydrozoans, mollusks, crustaceans, fishes, sea turtles, and marine mammals. 23763: Freshwater fish species density is determined by Cenozoic history of continents and river drainage basins--geologically stable, large drainage basins have the most species. Origination and extinction of species both depend on degree of isolation and connections among drainage basins and sub-basins, but the present patterns are determined primarily by extinction, which is most frequent on active continental margins, high latitude (cold) areas, and subtropical high-pressure (arid) zones. North America, South America, Eurasia, and Africa demonstrate the dependence of species density on the effects of plate tectonic history on river basin size and stability and on the effects of cold, dry, and seasonal climates on extinction. Australia was isolated, cool, dry, and depauperate throughout most of the Cenozoic. Active continental margins (subduction zones, e.g., the Pacific rim) decrease freshwater fish species diversity by uplift, high elevations, and extreme topographic relief, which reduce basin size, increase gradients, decrease stream volume, and eliminate species by driving energy budgets negative. Passive continental margins have large, stable drainage basins, huge habitat volume, low extinction rates and exceptionally large fish faunas (Amazon, Congo, Mekong, Mississippi). Glaciated regions have not regained their species and high latitude, seasonal climates exclude many species by energetic and growth limitation. River basins harbor fish metapopulations whose dispersal filters consist of fluvial habitat gradients magnified by linear distances (downstream then upstream). Dispersal among habitat types within basins as well as stream captures control speciation and extinction, consistent with predictions of metapopulation theory. Speciation rates are slow in rivers, but sometimes rapid in lakes; extinction rates are slow in stable river basins but high (inevitable) in lakes.

23764: Glanidium, designated by Lutken (1874) for the monotypic Glanidium albescens is recognized as monophyletic and redefined based on four synapomorphies: (1) Presence of a volumous adductor mandibulae section A2 extending caudally to the eye rim, being the muscle origin located in a pronounced concavity between the margins of sphenotic and pterotic; (2) Muscle adductor mandibulae section A3 b with a well developed deep portion originating on orbitosphenoid and pterosphenoid, medially to the articular facett for hyomandibula; (3) Modified anal fin of adult males with higher number of segments on third unbranched anal fin ray (up to 20); (4) Proximal anal-fin radials enlarged and sutured to each other. The taxonomic status of the species is evaluated and the group is found to consist of the following seven species: Glanidium albescens Lutken described for the rio das Velhas and registered to other parts of the rio São Francisco drainage in Minas Gerais; Glanidium ribeiroi Haseman and Glanidium cesarpintoi Ihering both known from the upper rio Paraná system at São Paulo and Paraná; Glanidium melanopterum Miranda Ribeiro with the widest range of distribution among the group, recorded mainly for small coastal river basins in brazilian east, since the Lagoa dos Quadros in Rio Grande Sul to the rio Paraíba do Sul, in Rio de Janeiro; G. leopardus Hoedeman largely disjunct from its congeners, occurring in the Guyana, Surinam and French Guyana; and two new species, one from the rio Doce, at Minas Gerais, and the other from rio Jacuí basin, at Rio Grande do Sul. Glanidium catharinensis Miranda Ribeiro, known only from the holotype, captured at Tubarão, Santa Catarina, is designated as a junior synonim for G. melanopterum. Glanidium comprises the largest forms among the Centromochlinae and represents the only group with occurrence in coastal river drainages of brazilian east. Historical approaches on the biogeography of the group are given.

23765: The mandibular muscles of Glanidium melanopterum Miranda Ribeiro, a typical representative of Centromochlin subfamily, are described and compared to other representative species within the group, namely Centromochlus heckelii (Filippi), C. existimatus Mees, Tatia neivai (von Ihering), T. intermedia (Steindachner) and Glanidium ribeiroi Haseman. Dissections of Centromochlin specimens were provided for anatomical comparison of seven pairs of mandibular muscles: (1) Adductor mandibulae; (2) Levator arcus palatini; (3) Dilatator operculi; (4) Adductor arcus palatini; (5) Extensor tentaculi; (6) Retractor tentaculi; (7) Levator operculi. As observed in Auchenipteridae in general, the adductor mandibulae complex is divided in sections A2 and A3, with no recognised section Aw. The M. Adductor mandibulae, section A2, is well developed in Glanidium and Tatia and "slim" in Centromochlus. The M. Levator arcus palatini is laterally arranged in relation to A3, with differences on the size of crest associated to insertion on hyomandibulae. The M. Dilatator operculi is bipenniform in Centromochlus and penniform in Glanidium and Tatia. The M. Adductor arcus palatini, the most medial mandibular muscle, is associated on its site of origin to a "crest" on parasphenoid, "keeled" on Centromochlus. The M. Extensor tentaculi is a single muscle in Glanidium e Tatia, but in Centromochlus is subdivided to two sections. The M. Retractor tentaculi presented variation on its relative position to eye. The M. Levator operculi is uniquely associated to an opercular process, in Glanidium and Tatia. Both Glanidium and Tatia catfishes have depressed heads with broad adductor muscles, and similarities between other mandibular muscles were observed. On the other hand, in Centromochlus species several modifications on the mandibular muscles were identified, possibly in association to its pelagic habits.

23766: Centromochlus was created by Kner (1858) based on Centromochlus megalops and C. aulopygius. Actually, the species remaining on the genus are no clear. Ferraris (1988), Soares-Porto (1997) and Royero (1999) shown the difficulty in the delimitation of the genus and some species of Tatia and Gelanoglanis have been placed in it. In the present study the genus Centromochlus is redefined and found to consist of five species: C. heckelii (Fillipi) largely distributed through Amazonas and Orenoco river drainages; C. existimatus Mees from the Amazonas and Orenoco; C. megalops Kner endemic for Orenoco; C. steindachneri Gill from upper Amazon and a new species, C. microphthalmus, known from the rio solimoes. The genus is recognised as a monophyletic assemblage diagnosed on the basis of the following synapomorphies: (1) outer mental barbels reduced in size, half the lenght of mentals; (2) posterios nuchal plate rounded, expanded caudally in the horizontal plane; (3) dorsal profile of opercle curved, with semicircular shape; (4) pectoral fin spine very long, more than 35% in SL; (5) cleithral process with a longitudinal groove for the resting of the maxillary barbel; (6) coracoid process partially exposed externally; (7) dorsal fin spine elongate, more than 30% in SL; (8) quadrate interposed between metapterygoid and hyomandibula; (9) distal tip of mullerian ramus produced posteriorly, extending deeply in the lumen of the swimbladder; (10) anal fin base very narrow, with less than 9 rays. The cladistic analysis indicated that both Gelanoglanis Bohlke and the sister species Tatia perugiae (Steindachner) and T. romani Mees are closely related to Centromochlus.

23767: Physalaemus lisei is a small frog (SVL 21-33 mm) inhabiting forests in the Brazilian states of Rio Grande do Sul and Santa Catarina. To study the diet of this species, we collected 57 adult males at a small temporary pond near the research and conservation station Pro-Mata, located on the Planalto das Araucarias, municipality of Sao Francisco de Paula, Rio Grande do Sul. All frogs were captured at night between 21:00 and 24:00, taken to the laboratory to undergo stomach- flushing and released the next day. In 43 specimens the flushed stomachs contained food. All prey items were stored in 70% ethanol, measured and identified to the level of class or order except for Hymenoptera, which were classified into Formicidae and non-Formicidae. The volume of each item was estimated using three formula: 2*length(π*width2) for larval Coleoptera and Lepidoptera, 4π length*width2/3 for Gastropoda and the formula for a prolate spheroid, 4/3π(lenght/2)(width/2)2, for all other items. On average 2.45 prey items per flushed stomach were obtained. The most consumed prey type by number were Formicidae (27.16 %), followed by Diptera (16.49 %) and Araneae (14.55 %). Although proportionally small percentages of the number of prey items were Diplopoda (3.88 %) and Isopoda (2.91 %), these items represented 34.42 % (286.84 mm3) and 16.43 % (136.93 mm3) of the prey volume. On the other hand, Formicidae and Diptera only represented 6.86 % (57.17 mm3) and 5.82 % (48.49 mm3) of the prey volume, respectively. Stomach flushing, a method that we have been used and tested over the last four years, was found to be the most appropiate method to obtain stomach contents, even from small frogs as P. lisei. A photographic documentation showing each step of the flushing procedure and a list of the materials needed will be presented.

23768: Position of the pelvic fins in teleost fishes varies from relatively posterior in primitive teleosts to anterior, and in association with the pectoral fins in the most derived acanthomorphs. Migration of the pelvic fin through body segments during development has called into question homology of the pelvic fins, although their homology has never been seriously challenged. Further, recent data on gene expression patterns and development of the pelvic fins indicates that the same gene networks are responsible for pelvic fin development in all osteichthyans. This similarity of genetic control of pelvic fin development invites the comparison of the sequence of development of muscle, bone and nerve characters among taxa. We identify a hierarchy of character systems -- nerve, bone, muscle and connective tissue which can be compared to phylogenetic hierarchies. Morphological variation among these character systems in the pelvic fins of gobioid and other acanthomorph fishes will be used as examples to test the relationship between developmental and phylogenetic hierarchies.

23769: Fishery is one of the most traditional activities in the Amazon Region. There has been fishing exploitation in this area for over 2000 years. The Amazon lake systems are part of a mosaic of elements that compose the floodplain systems - varzeas, periodically interconnected with the main rivers. No studies yet established the relationship between the lake fisheries with aquatic environments explored by the commercial fishery of Manaus fleet in the Amazon. The present study aims to determine the aquatic habitats explored for commercial fisheries of the Manaus fishing fleet from 1996 to 2000. All the information was collected daily with fishermen using questionnaires at the main Manaus landing site. The answers obtained from the follow variables were used: type of environment, fishing region, fishing location name, nearest city name. Based on the information supplied by the questionnaires, the environment explored for fisheries was determinate. The frequency of the fishing ground was obtained using 22956 records of the commercial landings. The different responses of the fishermen were listed and clustered in five categories: LAKE, RIVER, INDETERMINATE and MIXED. In 1996, 50.4% of the fishing grounds explored by the commercial fishery could be clustered in the LAKE category; in 1997, 55.9%; in 1998, 5.91%; in 1999, 4.76% and 2000, 2.56%. For the RIVER category in 1996, 25.87% could be clustered in this category; in 1997, 28.29%; in 1998, 41.24%; in 1999, 48.56%; in 2000, 3.62%. For the MIXED categories in 1996, 2.30%; in 1997, 0.77%; in 1998, 1.26%; in 1999, 3.82% and in 2000, 0.62%. To the INDETERMINATE category corresponded 21.37% in 1996; 14.26% in 1997; 51.59% in 1998; 42.83% in 1999 and 93.20% in 2000. The results demonstrated that there was a tendency to the exploration of the lake systems by commercial fisheries along 1996-1997, but in 1998-1999 the main environment explored was the river. In 2000, the aquatic habitats explored were indeterminate. A characterization of the main fishing grounds has been done using remote sensing images and in situ evaluations to find responses to the patterns found. Apparently, the aquatic habitats explored for the commercial fisheries have change annually and indicate a modification in the fishery strategies of exploration.

23770: Physopyxis lyra Cope, 1872 is a minute Doradidae species described from the río Ampiyacu, Peru. Among doradids, this fish can be distinguished by the huge pectoral girdle with a very long postcoracoid process that reaches the base of the pelvic fin and is longer than the humeral process. Since Cope’s description, no taxonomic work has been done with the genus. This study aims to review the taxonomic status of Physopyxis specimens recently collected as well as the material already deposited in several museums, including the holotype. A preliminary analysis revealed morphological differences between specimens from some river drainages and provided the distinction of three morphotypes. The main characters that allow to separate the different species are the height of the lateral plates and the number of hooks present on them. Physopyxis lyra has intermediate-sized plates with only one series of spines on each plate; Physopyxis n. sp. 1 has high plates and shows a wide variation in the number of series of spines in the plates, whereas Physopyxis n. sp. 2 exhibits at most ten reduced plates on its lateral series. Physopyxis lyra has been found in the Upper and Medium rio Amazonas (rio Negro not included). Physopyxis n. sp. 1 was found in the Medium and Lower rio Amazonas, rio Negro and río Essequibo, and Physopyxis n. sp. 2 was found only in the rio Negro. These findings change the monotypic status presumed for the genus and expand the distribution for Physopyxis in the Amazon.

23771: Maryland and other state monitoring programs have determined that fish indicators are ineffective in headwater streams, where stream salamanders may replace fish as top predators. Because of their life history, physiology, abundance, and ubiquity, stream salamanders are likely representative of biological integrity in these streams. The goal of this study was to determine whether stream salamanders are effective indicators of ecological conditions across biogeographic regions and gradients of human disturbance. During the summers of 2001 and 2002, we intensively surveyed for stream salamanders at 76 stream sites located west of the Maryland Coastal Plain, that were also monitored by the Maryland Biological Stream Survey (MBSS) and City of Gaithersburg. We found 1,584 stream salamanders, including all eight species known in Maryland, using two 15x2-m transects and two 4-m2 quadrats that spanned both stream bank and channel. We performed removal sampling on transects to estimate salamander species detection probabilities, which ranged from 0.71-0.85. Stepwise regressions identified 15 of 52 non-salamander variables, representing water quality, physical habitat, land use, and biological conditions, that best predicted salamander metrics. Indicator development involved (1) identifying reference and degraded sites (using percent forest, shading, riparian buffer width, aesthetic rating, and benthic macroinvertebrate and fish indices of biotic integrity); (2) testing 17 candidate salamander metrics (representing species richness and composition, abundance, species tolerance, reproductive function, and trophic function) for their ability to distinguish reference from degraded sites; and (3) combining metrics into an index that effectively discriminated sites according to known stream conditions. Final indices for Highlands, Piedmont, and non-Coastal Plain regions were comprised of four metrics: number of species, number of salamanders, percentage of intolerant salamanders, and number of adult salamanders, producing classification efficiencies between 80% and 90%. Partial validation of this stream salamander index of biotic integrity (SS-IBI) was obtained when a test of the number-of-salamanders metric produced an 82% correct classification of 618 MBSS sites surveyed in 1995-97.

23772: Amphisbaenians are generally considered to utilize one of four mechanisms of head-first burrowing that are each associated with distinct cranial characteristics. Species with a dorso- ventrally flattened skulls (spade or shovel-snouted) are thought to utilize a derived two-cycle burrowing mechanism that involves temporally separate forward thrust and head-lifting phases. It is hypothesized that the forward thrust involves the dissipation of momentum after the acceleration of the axial skeleton and skull by muscles that originate in the skin and insert on the ribs. The head lifting phase is mediated by a pair of large, pinnate muscles originating on the tops of the vertebrae and inserting on tendons that themselves insert on the top of the skull. We tested this functional hypothesis in Leposternon infraorbitale, a spade-snouted amphisbaenian from central Brazil, using kinetic data gathered while animals attempted to burrow on a force plate. Experimental manipulations of tunnel length indicate that the costo-cutaneous muscles of the trunk play only a small role in generating forward-directed forces. The duration and size of the forward forces, combined with the size of the animals, excludes a prominent role for the storage and dissipation of momentum. No two-cycle behavior was observed. Instead Leposternon utilizes an upward rotation of the skull to simultaneously generate both thrusting and lifting forces during burrow construction. Large Leposternon can generate well in excess of 100 N of force during burrowing. However, approximately one-half of the total force generated is directed dorsally rather than forward.

23773: Species of the genus Atractus are poorly represented in museum collections. Consequently, our knowledge on the natural history, morphological variation, and geographical distribution of most species of Atractus is far from satisfactory. Atractus albuquerquei is one of the many species belonging to this genus that have been recorded only sporadically after its formal description in 1983, based on a specimen from the state of Pará, Brazil. According to this study, the hemipenis of the holotype is bilobed, with a bifurcated sulcus spermaticus, and an undifferentiated pattern. However, comparative analyses of eight completely everted and fully expanded organs (including the left hemipenis of the holotype) revealed a differentiated organ, significantly different in several aspects from that described in 1983. After its original description, A. albuquerquei was reported only three times, in the states of Rondônia and Acre, resulting in a disjunct distribution along the southern border of the Amazon basin with a wide gap between the westernmost and easternmost parts of the Brazilian Amazon. We here report on 14 additional specimens of Atractus albuquerquei from the states of Goiás, Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul, and present new data on the morphological variation of the species. These new records extend significantly the distribution of the species to the southernmost limits of the Amazon basin, and give us a better knowledge on the intraspecific variation of A. albuquerquei.

23774: The genus Colostethus is a basal group in the family Dendrobatidae and represents 50% of species in the group, but little is known of the reproductive behavior of most of the species. Only a few species had their courtship and oviposition studied and in these cases oviposition occurs in leaf-litter, plant stems, or bromelias. We report a new reproductive mode for Colostethus observed in a population of Colostethus sp. in Acre (Brazil). Eggs were laid on the undersurfaces of living (95%) or raised dead leaves. Clutches were located 1 to 23 cm above the ground (mean = 7.9; N=139). Reproduction in occurred between December and January. Courtship and oviposition occurred in the morning (between 05:00 and 12:00) and lasted 27 to 262 min (mean = 85 min; N=24). Tactile interactions between male and female occurred under the leaves and lasted approximately 10 min. The pair faced each other and touched snouts before initiating oviposition, during which the male remained behind or besides the female and touched her belly and/or head with his front leg. The eggs were white and clutch size varied from 4 to 15 eggs (mean = 8.4; N=139). After oviposition the pair left the leaf but the male returned to the clutch after 30 to 40 min and remained over (probably hydrating) the eggs for 20 to 37 min (mean = 26; N=16). Clutches were visited by the male several times until he transported the tadpoles to pools, about 30 days after oviposition. Some males transported more than one clutch at a time. Only males were observed visiting clutches, and most clutches were transported by males. However, one female transported tadpoles from a clutch that had been abandoned by the male. The mating system in this population is promiscuous; males mated with more than one female and females mated with more than one male.

23775: We studied the composition of amphibians in two areas in the Brazilian Amazonian forest (Reserva Extrativista do Alto Juruá - REAJ and Parque Nacional da Serra do Divisor - PNSD), located in the southwest part of Acre State, Brazil. The sampling and observations for this study were carried out between October 1993 and December 2000 (ca. 3,140 hours of observation). A total of 126 species, 32 genera, and 10 families of amphibians were recognized. In the order Anura we found 5 species of Bufonidae, 1 Centrolenidae, 10 Dendrobatidae, 57 Hylidae, 40 Leptodactylidae, 8 Microhylidae, 2 Pipidae, and 1 Ranidae. We found one species in the order Caudata (family Plethodontidae) and one species of Gymnophiona (family Caeciliidae). Of the 113 species recorded in REAJ and 125 in PNSD, 112 species were common to both sites. Nineteen species were not identified at the specific level; three species are endemic to the State of Acre, and 14 are new findings in Brazil. The amphibian fauna at both sites is composed by species adapted to both open and forested environments. The amphibian fauna of REAJ and PNSD are composed of species distributed throughout the Neotropics, species with a wide distribution in the Amazon Basin, species restricted to the Upper Amazon Basin, and species distributed in the Andean and Sub-Andean regions, along with species distributed in central and southeast Brazil. The high biological diversity found at the two sites may be related to their geographical proximity to the proposed forest refuges, and the relationship between biotic and abiotic factors in the region. Additional studies are necessary for a better knowledge of the amphibian fauna of the region.

23776: The purpose of this work is to perform a taxonomic revision of the genus Aphyocharax, which includes small characid fishes with a wide distribution in tropical South America. The monophyletism of this group has been corroborated. It includes only one genus, Aphyocharax, which is currently defined by the reduction of the second infraorbital and the enlargment of the third and fourth infraorbital bones, which together cover the whole cheek. This work elucidates the taxonomic confusion that has always been associated with Aphyocharax. Twenty-two species were originally described as belonging to this genus, and additional species have been later attributed to it: three from the genus Cheirodon, one from Notropocharax, and another from Phoxinopsis. However, the genus is so poorly defined that in the past many of the species described on it belonged to other genus that are not even close related, and Aphyocharax was clearly polyphyletic before the removal of these species to other genera. The analysis of specimens from the entire range of geographical distribution areas has shown that only 8 of the 26 nominal species are considered valid. Three species occur at the Paraná basin (Aphyocharax anisitsi, A. dentatus, A. rathbuni), others are from Amazon and Guiana Basins (A. colifax, A. erythrurus, A. gracilis, A. pusillus), and A. nattereri occurs in both Amazon and Paraná Basins.

23777: Phylogenetic relationships of the endemic Malagasy rainbowfishes (Bedotia and Rheocles) are investigated using morphology and nucleotide characters from five mitochondrial loci. Results indicate that Bedotiidae (Bedotia + Rheocles) and Bedotia are monophyletic, whereas Rheocles is paraphyletic. An assemblage comprising the Australasian melanotaeniids, telmatherinids, and pseudomugilids is monophyletic, and recovered as the sister-group to Bedotiidae. The biogeographic disjunction between Malagasy bedotiids and this latter clade, restricted to Australia, New Guinea, and Sulawesi, is congruent with Gondwanan fragmentation. Vicariance, not trans-oceanic dispersal, can most parsimoniously account for the current distribution of rainbowfishes and their relatives.

23778: We investigated the genetic structure of wood frog (Rana sylvatica) populations in a woodland habitat around Lake Itasca, Minnesota. Wood frogs are philopatric and dispersal studies have suggested that genetic subdivision may be seen at distances of 2-3 km. We used microsatellites to examine population structure at distances from 95 m to 9.6 km. At larger distances we found evidence for genetic differentiation though allele frequencies remained very similar between locations. When the Minnesota and North Dakota locations, separated by over 200 km, were compared, however, the two groups were significantly different, though again the overall pattern of allele frequencies remained similar at most loci.

23779: Mating system studies that have utilized molecular tools have revealed unexpected patterns of paternity, owing to the diverse behavioural tactics of individuals. These alternative mating strategies appear to be widespread among many groups of animals, however there remain large gaps in our understanding of the evolution and maintenance of these strategies. Alternative male strategies may be facultative, meaning individuals can switch between tactics or may be genetically hard wired. In the latter, the alternative strategies may be indicative of an overall difference in the behavioural phenotype or personality of the individual. In this sense males with different mating strategies may also have different behaviours outside of the mating context. To investigate this I used a combination of field and laboratory based studies to test if males of the southern water skink (Eulamprus heatwolei), which adopt different mating strategies, also differ in behaviours not related to mating. During the field study I identified male mating strategies and measured their reproductive success using molecular markers. Following this I measured male exploratory and predator avoidance behaviours in the lab to test for correlations between mating and non-mating behaviours, and to identify if male mating strategies are linked to a broader male personality.

23783: We provide a synthesis and extension of some 20 years of studies on fish assemblage patterns in the Napo River basin, a major headwater tributary of the Amazon. Assemblage patterns were analyzed by applying detrended correspondence analysis (DCA) and two-way indictor species analysis (TWINSPAN) to a species by locality matrix of abundance data. Large river habitats were found to have at least four main assemblages: lowland blackwater, lowland whitewater nearshore, lowland whitewater deepwater, and upland whitewater. Lagoon habitats were distinct between lowland and piedmont regions. Analyses of small-stream habitats are still in progress, but at least three assemblages are evident: lowland, piedmont and upland. General patterns that appear to cut across the diverse assemblages include: 1) increasing species richness from upland to lowland; 2) consistently high species diversity across all habitats; 3) faunal turnover between major assemblages of 80-90% or more, often over very short distances; 4) within assemblage turnover between nearby sites of about 50%, reflecting extremely patchy distributions for many species; and 5) at least in the lowlands, assemblages experience significant seasonal changes due to migrations. The overall effect of having at least nine discrete assemblages in the basin is extremely high regional species richness, with close to 590 species in a drainage area of only 20,000 km2. These baseline studies provide a solid foundation for future analyses of anthropogenic effects in this region and a basis for broader-scale studies on Amazonian biodiversity.

23784: Microsternarchus bilineatus is widely distributed throughout the Amazon basin, yet it is restricted to smaller tributaries. 23785: Disease from chytrid fungal or ranaviral infections likely plays an important role in global amphibian declines and extinctions. Both of these pathogens are emerging infectious diseases, but for different reasons. Originally, we hypothesized that chytrid infections are a new disease because die-offs were severe and among many amphibian taxa in given locations, indicating a lack of coevolution of pathogen and host. Phylogeographic data support the recent global spread of a single species of chytrid fungus. In contrast, we hypothesized that salamanders and viruses showed an older co-evolutionary relationship, because salamanders most often recover 1-2 years after a ranavirus die-off. Ranaviruses were isolated from tiger salamander populations ranging from Arizona to Saskatchewan, Canada, areas that experience frequent epizootics and consequent extreme population fluctuations. To investigate coevolutionary patterns, I generated gene genealogies for both ranavirus isolates and salamander populations from these sites. I reconciled a viral gene genealogy based on 1086 bp from the capsid protein and two intergenic spacer regions, with that generated from 900 bp of mtDNA sequence from tiger salamanders from the same localities to test for concordance . Overall, the trees were non-concordant, suggesting a lack of coevolution. However, I also have genetic evidence that non-native salamanders have been introduced in some sites because of their use as fishing bait. These data, in concert with discovery of infected salamanders from bait shops, support the possibility of anthropogenically-enhanced viral spread that may disturb natural coevolutionary dynamics of salamanders and viruses. Thus, the virus is deemed an emerging pathogen, with recent spread likely attributable to human activities.

23786: We investigated the role of red-footed tortoises (Geochelone carbonaria) and yellow-footed tortoises (G. denticulata) as seed dispersal agents in the terre firme forest of Maracá Island Ecological Reserve, Roraima, Brazil from 5 January to 26 January 2002. Ficus sp. was the most abundant species recovered (n = 400), followed by a Bromeliaceae sp. (n = 88), and Genipa americana (n = 59). Based on visual examination of the embryos from a subset of recovered seeds, 100% of Ficus sp. appeared viable, followed by 93% Bromeliaceae sp., and 91% G. americana. Mean minimum retention time (time of capture until time of defecation) was 1.6 days, with a range of 0 to 4 days. Based on recaptured tortoises (n = 9) and thread-trailed individuals (n = 2), the mean daily distance moved was 51 m, with a range of 0 to 400 m. 23787: The use of information obtained from biotelemetry studies assumes fish behavior is unaffected by the attachment method and presence of the transmitter. 23788: Species phylogeny in molecular studies is usually estimated by reconstruction of a single, or at best a few, gene lineages. This approach can be especially problematic in phylogenetic studies among species of a species flock, in which diversification has been recent and rapid. We investigated the phylogenetic relationships among 62 specimens of a monophyletic riverine species flock of mormyrid electric fishes collected in Gabon, West Central Africa in an analysis of an amplified fragment length polymorphism (AFLP) dataset consisting of hundreds of independent molecular markers and in a separate analysis of complete sequences of the mitochondrial cytochrome b (cyt b) gene. Ten AFLP primer combinations yielded a total of 2208, 1579 and 1326 informative binary characters at the three peak detection thresholds employed. We analyzed the AFLP data using Nei-Li distance, Wagner parsimony and Dollo parsimony methods and the aligned cyt b sequences by Wagner parsimony. AFLP tree topologies recovered by all three methods and at the three thresholds were largely congruent with each other. Recovered basal relationships in the group are similar between cyt b and AFLP analyses, but differ substantially at many other nodes. By comparison to the cyt b results, many more of the clades recovered with the AFLP characters are consistent with the morphological characters used to designate operational taxonomic units in this group. We interpret these results as support for our earlier hypothesis that the mitochondrial gene tree differs from the overall organismal phylogeny among these taxa due to the effects of mitochondrial introgession among lineages and incomplete gene lineage sorting. Mapping the two forms of electric organ found in this group onto the AFLP tree suggests that posteriorly innnervated electrocytes with non-penetrating stalks have independently evolved from anteriorly innervated, penetrating-stalk electrocytes at least three times. In a case in which study of a single molecular marker yielded a misleading estimate, we find AFLP characters to be a powerful tool for resolving organismal phylogeny within a clade of closely related species.

23790: In the Corumba River, a tributary of the Paranaiba River, occur two species of Steindachnerina, S.insculpta, widely distributed in the Parana River basin, and recently described S.corumbae, a new species, restricted to the upper Paranaiba River. 23791: We compared the effects of predation and habitat complexity, on juvenile red snapper, Lutjanus campechanus, recruitment to artificial nursery habitats. 23792: Captive propagation of animal populations relies on accurate determination of both sex and maturity in order to be successful. 23795: The Southern California Bight (SCB) is located at a plate collision boundary with a wide continental margin containing multiple dramatic basins and sills. These islands and submerged banks provide shallow habitat amidst the cold and warm water masses and mesoscale eddies ('the southern California eddy' and the 'Santa Barbara Channel gyre') associated with the biogeographic boundary at Point Conception. My goal was to assess connectivity among patches in the SCB and throughout the range of the depth-limited (<200m) kelp rockfish (Sebastes atrovirens). I assessed patterns of genetic diversity for 8 coastal and 5 island sampling locations from central California to central Baja. Nine microsatellite loci and 650 adult individuals were screened to estimate scales of realized dispersal in the context of sea surface temperature during the pelagic dispersal stage. No significant population structure was detected among all collections treated separately (Fst = 0.0001) but significant differences were found when sampling populations were pooled based on common average sea surface temperature at the time of spawning and pelagic dispersal (Fst = 0.002). A significant isolation by distance signal was found for pairwise comparisons among six well- sampled populations at extremes in the range for the species (Mantel test, p = 0.02); however, when data for central SCB populations (e.g., Anacapa Island, Santa Barbara, San Nicolas Island, etc.) were included, the relationship was not significant. Since the kelp rockfish has been exploited by the live finfish fishery and is almost exclusively associated with fragile kelp forest habitat, understanding the connectivity of its populations is a critical step in ecosystem-based management and understanding the functioning of marine reserve networks.

23796: The physiological processes of desert reptiles may be limited by the availability of food. 23797: Testosterone (T) is responsible for sexual size dimorphism (SSD) in numerous animal species. 23800: The main channel of the Rio Negro basin is characterized by high concentrations of dissolved organic matter, low nutrient levels and low primary productivity. Natural variations in the stable carbon isotopes ratios (δ13C) and mercury (Hg) concentrations in fish and plants were used to identify the energy sources and trophic levels of fish. 23801: Many fish have ocelli, or false eyespots, near the caudal portion of the body. It has long been suggested that the eyespot misdirects attacks away from the head toward a less vulnerable part of the body; however, there are few direct tests of this hypothesis. Using the defensive attacking behavior of parental convict cichlids, Archocentrus nigrofasciatus, on a predator model, we tested the misdirection hypothesis. By manipulating the presence or absence of eyespots on the model, we found that the percentage of bites given to the head is greater without the presence of an eyespot, compared to the percentage of bites given to the head with the presence of an eyespot. 23802: Small streams and seepage areas in the foothills of the southern Appalachian Mountains, along the junction of the Blue Ridge and Ridge and Valley Physiographic Provinces, are inhabited by populations of dusky salamanders (Desmognathus) whose taxonomic affinities are poorly understood. 23803: The Atlantic Sharpnose Shark, Rhizoprionodon terraenovae, and the Caribbean Sharpnose Shark, R. porosus are small coastal-temperate and tropical sharks of the continental shelves that overlap in distribution along the Gulf of Mexico, Florida and around the Yucatan Peninsula to the Caribbean Sea. 23804: The relationship between standard metabolic rate (SMR) and body mass is one of the most controversial and complex, yet unresolved, issues in comparative animal physiology. For Squamata, SMR increases at the power of 0.67 and 0.75 of body mass, in inter and intraspecific comparisons, respectively. These values, however, are variable and deviating figures ranging from 0.5 to 0.9 are not odd occurrences. Complicating the matter, body size may interact with other variables (e. g., hormone level, temperature, season), which may influence SMR. The tegu, Tupinambis merianae, exhibits a remarkable increase in body mass, from hatchling (about 10 g) to fully-grown individuals (up to 5000 g). Such features, makes this species an appropriate candidate for the study of scaling in metabolism. Moreover, tegus exhibit a marked circannual cycle of activity and have their metabolism affected by temperature. The present study investigated the scaling of metabolic rate with body size in T. merianae and ascribed the influence of two extrinsic variables (temperature and seasonality) on such relationship. SMR was determined from oxygen consumption rates (VO2) measured in 80 animals with body mass varying from 10 to 3700 g. The VO2 was measured at 17, 25, and 30°C along four seasons. The relationship between SMR and body mass was influenced by temperature and seasonality. Mass exponent (b) varied among the three experimental temperatures: b (17°C) = 0.78; b (25°C) = 0.79; and b (30°C) = 0.81, independently of season; and among seasons b (winter) = 0.84; b (spring) = 0.83; b (summer) = 0.74 and b (fall) = 0.76, independently of temperature. Even thought the fact that all these values fall within the range usually reported for intraspecific comparisons in reptiles, they also show that the magnitude of the effects exerted by temperature and season on metabolic rate are influenced by body size.

23805: Community studies bring information of great relevance about the natural history of a species. 23806: The 15 species currently included in the genus Acestrorhynchus have been traditionally grouped on the basis of color pattern, but these groupings are yet to be diagnosed as monophyletic units. In addition, four species show reduction in body size (although they are not miniatures) when compared to congeners, but a better understanding of this phenomenon is not possible with available phylogenetic data. Although characters from the orbital region, jaws, suspensorium, and neurocranium, so far analyzed, do not completely solve the relationships among all Acestrorhynchus species, they do provide evidence for the monophyly of an assemblage formed by the lacustris and falcatus species groups, and the nasutus group, therefore corroborating at least partially the traditional groupings. The monophyly of Acestrorhynchus is also corroborated by additional synapomorphies, and the geographic distribution of all species is updated.

23807: The California sheephead, Semicossyphus pulcher (Labridae), is a temperate, rocky-reef/kelp-bed fish that is sought by recreational and commercial fishermen. No-take marine reserves may be an effective management strategy that could protect and increase stocks, but first, it is necessary to determine the movement patterns and site fidelity of this fish. We use acoustic telemetry tracking and long-term acoustic monitoring to ascertain fine-scale movement patterns of S. pulcher and the stability of their home ranges over time. Sixteen adult sheephead (26 to 40 cm SL) were surgically fitted with small acoustic transmitters and manually tracked during multiple, 24-hour periods within the Catalina Marine Science Center Marine Life Reserve (CMLR). A Geographic Information System (GIS) was used to calculate home range sizes (95% Kernel Utilization Distributions) and habitat use. Home range sizes of fish varied greatly, ranging from 938 to 82,070 m2. Variability in home range sizes between fish was primarily attributed to differences in habitat shape and to natural habitat boundaries in adjacent areas within the reserve. Larger sheephead within the CMLR were found within sand habitat significantly more often than smaller fish. On average, sheephead used rocky reef areas 54% of the daytime and high-relief areas of the reef were used most often. Sixteen additional sheephead were fitted with long-term (~ 1 year) coded transmitters and their presence in the reserve was monitored. Sheephead exhibited high site fidelity; however, two of the smaller females shifted location of home ranges during the study. Based on the relatively small home ranges observed for S. pulcher and the persistence of their home ranges over time, no-take reserves, if containing appropriate habitat, may provide adequate protection for stocks of adult sheephead.

23809: Schizodon fasciatum, Rhytiodus microlepis and Leporinus friderici (Characiformes: Anostomidae) are anostomid species commonly known as aracus in the commercial fisheries of central Amazonia. This single common denomination includes species that may respond differently to some environmental variables affecting biological processes such as reproduction, feeding and migratory movements. Thus, this study aims to find possible temporal and spatial variation of population parameters of those species in relation to environmental variables. Samples were taken from three varzea lakes in Central Amazonia during different years: Lago do Rei (1986, 1987 and 1988), Lago do Inácio (1990 and 1991) and Lago do Catalão (1999 and 2001), using gillnets of different mesh sizes (30-120 mm), for 24 hours at each site. In general, Schizodon fasciatum and Rhytiodus microlepis showed biological responses closely related to the flood pulse, probably due to a strong seasonal autochthonous feeding pattern exhibited by these two species. Leporinus friderici, on the other hand, did not present such a clear variation and it seemed to depend more on the availability of allochthonous food. From all parameters considered, length at first sexual maturity showed the strongest variation among lakes while the others exhibited variation that could be linked to the extent and characteristics of the area used by each population. Even though R. microlepis is not important in the local commercial fisheries, its biological parameters seems to reflect the results of the fishing effort upon the other two species and the direct impact produced on it is own population by the fisheries. These results indicate that the three aracus present different biological responses to the environmental variables analyzed and deserve distinct fishing management strategies.

23810: The genus Ambystoma in Mexico had around a total of 17 species confined to mid to high altitudes, of above 1600m elevation in the north and central regions (Shaffer, 1989), 15 of these species (Ambystoma altamiranoi , A. amblycephalum, A. andersoni, A. bombypellum, A. dumerilli, A. flavipiperatum, A. granulosum, A. lacustris, A. lermaensis, A. mexicanum, A. ordinarium, A. rivulare, A. taylori, A. velasci and A. zempoalaense) were located only in the Transverse Neovolcanic Axis (Huacuz-Elias, 2001; Uribe-Pena et al, 1999), who are an east-west oriented chain of mountains that extends from western Veracruz to Jalisco where mountains merge with the Sierra Madre Occidental. In this region of central Mexico, the ambystomatid salamanders found their major diversity in an amazing conglomerate of vegetation types and micro-environmental situations, where these species evolve and become endemic to these mountains and in the case of some non-transforming species (A. andersoni, A. dumerilli, A. mexicanum and A. taylori) to single lakes located in the states of Michoacan, Mexico, Puebla and Distrito Federal. But this area also is one of the most densely populated regions on earth, and is under severe pressure from urban development, intensive agriculture, deforestation, draining or filling of lakes, channeling of rivers and streams, pollution and introduction of exotic species (like Carassius auratus).
