23813: Anura is an ancient and speciose amphibian Order comprising over 30 currently recognized families. Relationships among these families have been previously estimated with morphology as well as nuclear and mitochondrial rRNA sequence data. Recent mitochondrial rRNA studies from our lab have found nonmonophyly of Archaeobatrachia, and relationships among archaeobatrachians largely concordant with those derived from morphological data. These mitochondrial studies have also resolved some relationships within the problematic Neobatrachia. However, there has been no independent confirmation of these findings using protein-coding sequence from the nuclear genome, and many neobatrachian relationships have yet to be satisfactorily resolved by any data set. I will present results from a phylogenetic study using the nuclear gene RAG-1, a 3-kb intronless protein-coding nuclear gene. Taxon sampling for this study spans the diversity of extant anurans, with specific sublineages sampled more intensively to address particular questions at a variety of hierarchical levels. I will compare RAG-1 results with mitochondrial results, and test specific hypotheses suggested by existing mitochondrial data (e.g., nonmonophyly of Archaeobatrachia, Leptodactylidae, and Microhylidae; Heleophryne as the sister taxon of all other Neobatrachia).

23814: Information on habitat use and activity of the Neotropical rattlesnake, Crotalus durissus, are scarce. However, after correcting frequencies of captures with the area occupied by each habitat type, rattlesnakes were more frequently found in shrubby grasslands with trees, the formation which occupies the smallest area of the reserve. 23815: We studied the behavior in the laboratory of four cave balitorids (Nemacheilus troglocataractus, Schistura oedipus, S. jaruthanini, and S. spiesi), that show different degrees of troglomorphy in eyes and pigmentation, and of a cave cyprinid (Poropuntius speleops), compared respectively to the epigean balitorids, S. mahnert, S. similis and Acanthocobitis zonalternans and an epigean cyprinid P. deauratus, from Thailand. 23816: The population ecology of Ancistrus cryptophthalmus was studied by mark-recapture technique in stream reaches of three caves (Angelica, Bezerra and Passa Tres Caves) from the São Domingos karst area, State of Goiás, during the dry seasons of 1999 and 2000. 23817: In a recent paper, we noted that the abundance of non-native fishes was generally low in freshwater marshes of the Everglades at sites distant from canals, but was relatively high in some habitats bordering that ecosystem. Further, we reported a negative correlation over a 10-year period between the numbers and biomass of native fish and the same parameter for the non-native Mayan cichlid, Cichlasoma uropthalmus, in mangrove habitats. Since that publication, we have observed an expansion of Mayan cichlids into Everglades wetlands adjacent to the mangrove zone. These data permit us to estimate a rate of spread of this species. At present, we can identify no statistical evidence for effects from any non-native taxa on native fish communities in freshwater wet-prairie habitats. However, in the mangrove zone on the northern fringe of Florida Bay, the native species sheepshead minnow (Cyprinodon variegatus) and marsh killifish (Fundulus confluentus) decline in abundance in periods when Mayan cichlids are common, and increase following cold weather that decreases cichlid abundance. Two other small, abundant native fishes, sailfin molly (Poecilia latipinna) and rainwater killifish (Lucania parva), appear to be unaffected by the changing abundance of Mayan cichlids. Our work indicates that Mayan cichlids have altered the community structure and dynamics of native fishes in some habitats in southern Florida, but not in others. We use our data to develop a predictive model of the spread of Mayan cichlids into wetlands of the Everglades, as well as their impact on freshwater fish communities there. Further, we discuss the ability to generalize our observations to other expansions and evaluate if predictions can be made early enough to intervene once a new fish species is detected.

23818: Three extraordinary craniofacial anomalies are documented and described, based on samples of metamorphosing larvae or young from natural populations of Rana pipiens and R. clamitans. 23819: The preferred body temperature of Chinese green tree viper, Trimeresurus stejnegeri stejnegeri was measured in a linear thigmothermal gradient. 23820: Although high body temperature enables snakes to digest their food quickly, the metabolic cost is also entail with it. We found the postprandial preferred body temperature of Chinese green tree viper, Trimeresurus stejnegeri stejnegeri was 25.8 ± 1.0 °C (N = 40). By measuring food energy (Efood), digestive efficiency (De), specific dynamic action (SDA), digestive rate (Dr) and resting metabolic rate (Erest) in temperatures of 15, 20, 25, 30 and 35 °C, we can estimate the net energy gain (Enet) in different temperature. The equation for Enet is following: Enet = (Efood De - SDA) Dr - Erest. If snakes can eat and digest their food continuously, the net energy gain was increased from 15 °C to 25 °C and decreased thereafter. However, if food is limited, the optimal net energy gain will shift to lower temperature when snakes have less food ration.

23821: In the Northern Hemisphere, various glacial relict species are found to survive only in the coldest places, usually at high altitudes in mountain ranges. Similarly, in Taiwan, the Palearctic faunas inhabit mostly in the highlands whereas the animals from Oriental regions are commonly found in the low lands. The species that are restricted to high mountain regions are frequently endemic species of Taiwan. Although many factors may interact to limit the distribution of these climatic relicts, temperature is often regarded as one of the most important environmental factors. Each snake was acclimated at 10, 20, and 30 °C for more than two weeks before testing its CTMax. The CTMax was risen when acclimation temperature was increased from 10 to 30°C. 23822: Terrestrial, and especially arboreal, snakes can generally span a greater distance than aquatic snakes, which have a relatively short saccular lung. Thus, we hypothesize that the saccular lung provides structural support when snakes form a cantilever. Without subsequent study, the saccular lung has long been proposed as a support for the body of a snake, especially to help span gaps. To test this hypothesis, we determined whether the pressure in the saccular lung was significantly elevated when the snake was spanning a gap. Further, we reduced pressure in the lung to zero to determine whether this manipulation reduced the cantilever ability of the snake. The pressure in the saccular lung increased signficantly as a snake neared its maximal cantilever distance. However, when we prevented the pressure in the saccular lung from rising above atmospheric pressure, the maximal cantilever distance of snake was not affected. Therefore, the pressure increase in the saccular lung as the snake approached its maximal spanning distance was probably caused by the contraction of skeletal muscles needed to support the body. We conclude that the saccular lung does not help snakes span gaps, and probably does not help support the body or maintain posterior body form.

23823: Gopher tortoises (Gopherus polyphemus) are large terrestrial turtles associated with xeric habitats of the southeastern U.S. coastal plain. However, due to habitat loss and degradation, tortoise numbers are declining and populations have become fragmented and isolated. Removal and subsequent relocation of individual animals or populations is commonly practiced as a solution to human development of sites occupied by tortoises. Biologists have criticized current relocation policies because the policies do not recognize the importance of an overall conservation plan for the protection of the species nor do they adequately address the potential associated risks (e.g., disease, genetic mixing). In Fall 2001, approximately 100 tortoises were removed from an industrial development site and repatriated to the Savannah River Site (SRS), South Carolina, USA. The SRS is located within the historic range of the species, but tortoises had been extirpated from the site prior to the 1950s. The goals of the project were to: (1) re-establish a protected, viable population of tortoises on the SRS, (2) test the efficacy of existing relocation methods, and (3) develop a model for relocation of other tortoise species. Results of the first year of post-relocation monitoring will be summarized, including a radio-telemetry study designed to experimentally test the effects of penning and penning duration on movement patterns and site fidelity in repatriated tortoises. Prospects for long-term studies will also be discussed.

23824: We examined prey assemblages consumed by turtles in reaches of free-flowing and dammed riverine habitats for four rivers of south-eastern Queensland. We used a retrospective, blocked design consisting of river habitats compared to impoundments formed by weirs (<5m in height) or dams (>5m in height). The experimental design simultaneously considered prey differences from ontogenetic dietary preference and seasonal shifts of prey availability. Nonmetric multidimensional scaling of the sites identified the dams with backups > 20 km as being relatively similar in losses of biodiversity. Canonical correspondence analysis identified two major factors, habitat alteration and turtle size, as major determinants of underlying variance in the prey consumed. Dietary samples in lakes were substantially reduced in prey abundance, species richness, and dietary breadth relative to the riverine populations. Specialist foragers were more affected by dams than was the dietary generalist. For the generalist turtle, qualitative differences were evident in diets from impoundments and rivers, yet considering its greater dietary breadth; any quantitative effects on diet were minor. Herbivorous turtles in impoundments took fewer aquatic plants and windfall fruits than those living in rivers. For the carnivore, fewer aquatic invertebrates were ingested in impoundments than in riverine habitats but some compensation was achieved by scavenging behaviour in impoundments. 23825: Previous morphological and molecular studies of highly migratory and abundant prochilodontid fishes (Characiformes) strongly indicate that past geological events were important for shaping patterns of genetic diversity in this group of freshwater fishes. We conducted a mtDNA study of four prochilodontid spp. that occur in major drainages of northern South America, and found that the geologically complex landscape of this region explained much of the genetic diversity among species. However, unusual patterns of mtDNA variation were revealed within major lineages. Prochilodus mariae and Prochilodus rubrotaeniatus (Rio Negro lineage) harbored little or no variation at mtDNA markers we studied. This observation was contrary to expectations based on their vast abundance in these systems. Statistical testing revealed weak evidence for purifying selection on mitochondrial genes in P. mariae, but the absence of selection in P. rubrotaeniatus. If purifying selection is an important process affecting genetic diversity then an unlinked, selectively-neutral locus should be highly variable in P. mariae. Characterization of two nuclear gene introns, calmodulin and elongation factor-1 alpha (EF1α), revealed high levels of genetic variation in P. mariae, which is consistent with the operation of selection on the mitochondrion. P. rubrotaeniatus in the Rio Negro was monomorphic for variation at calmodulin and showed little diversity at EF1α. This observation is consistent with a genetic bottleneck, perhaps associated with a relatively recent founder event in the Rio Negro.

23826: The only known population of burbot, Lota lota, outside of Lake Erie in Pennsylvania is restricted to Allegheny River headwaters and tributaries; consequently, the species is listed as threatened in the state. 23827: Federal and state agencies are attempting to project the impact of hydrological restoration on the Everglades ecosystem. Current modeling efforts have focused on primary producers (e.g., macrophytes and periphyton) or higher trophic levels (e.g., panther, deer, birds). Even though amphibians are known to comprise a large portion of the faunal biomass within wetland systems, they remain underrepresented in these modeling efforts. The biphasic life-cycle of frogs makes them extremely sensitive to hydrological change. Therefore, amphibians make excellent organisms to investigate immediate impacts of hydrologic alterations. Unfortunately, there is little known about amphibian abundance, ecology and importance to the Greater Everglades. This study investigates how changes in the abundance of Rana grylio relate to water level, hydroperiod, percent cover of vegetation and climatic variables (e.g., precipitation and relative humidity). A total of 551 one kilometer transects were surveyed at night via airboat, to compare the monthly density of Rana grylio across large areas of long hydroperiod marsh in Water Conservation Areas 3A, 3B and Everglades National Park. Surveys using a double observer method occurred from August 2000 through September 2002. We compared these estimates with capture-recapture techniques that were used within plots at each site in order to estimate abundance and other parameters on a smaller scale. A drought occurred during 2001 which allowed us to assess how this species responds to a prolonged dry-down. Frog abundances were severely affected by this drought, and responded differently in each area. Overall frog abundances quickly returned to pre-drought numbers. This information is useful in projecting how restoration efforts may affect a species with an important role within the Everglades foodweb.

23829: The African frog genus Tomopterna consists of cryptic species that occur throughout Africa. It is one of the few vertebrate taxa that include a polyploid species. 23830: Very little is known about the influence of environmental data on distributional patterns of neotropical lizards in patchy landscapes, although this is basic knowledge for understanding community dynamics and defining conservation strategies. In order to describe lizard community, as well as to identify factors influencing their local distribution in Emas National Park, Brazilian Cerrado, six different habitat types, ranging from grasslands to gallery forests, were sampled with pitfall traps, and habitat structure parameters were measured. A canonical correspondence analysis revealed that lizard distribution in Emas National Park is associated with vegetation and soil type: some species are associated with grassy cover, while others show preference for bushes, leaf litter or sandy soils (F = 10.22; p = 0.01), factors related to microhabitat availability. The greatest richness and diversity indexes were obtained in savannas and grasslands, while forests were the poorest habitats. Differences among sampling sites can be explained by the association between each of the lizard species and some of the environmental parameters, reflecting ecological constraints on the many sympatric lineages. Habitat heterogeneity in Cerrado determines high beta diversity, resulting in great regional diversity as well as differences in faunal composition and abundance among neighboring areas, allowing sympatry among non-syntopic species. These results indicate the importance of preserving heterogeneous areas in order to protect the greatest portion of the regional fauna, and this is applicable to management planning in Emas National Park region as well as to the definition of conservation priorities for the whole Cerrado.

23838: This study focuses on the Florida box turtle, Terrapene carolina bauri, in the sub-tropical Florida Keys at the southernmost limit of its range. 23839: The Amazonian river turtle genus Podocnemis comprises six species. They vary in their geographical distribution, carapace length, body weight, habitat preference, abundance, feeding habits, life-history and behavior. Species also differ in hunting pressure they are subject to. Many species, especially the larger ones, are preferred source of food in the rural sector of the Amazon region. Adult freshwater turtles are captured for food, and eggs are often widely collected, both for local use as well as for the black market. Consequently, some species are considered threatened (CITES). In addition to ecological and hunting information, a direct assessment of the amount and distribution of genetic variation is necessary for management decisions. Therefore we accessed molecularly four different Podocnemis species (P. expansa, P. unifilis, P. sextuberculata, and P. erythrocephala) to study trends between ecological variables and genetic diversity. Clear trends between ecological variables and genetic diversity exist. Proper ecological and genetic management of Podocnemis species will assure they remain a sustainable resource of meat, eggs, shell and oil for the Amazonian people.

23840: Allozyme variation and evolutionary relationship in species of the genus Microlophus of the peruvianus group from 11 localities in Chile and southern Peru were determined. The taxonomic arrangement proposed is according to Rogers genetic identity levels, where the respective dendrogram clustered populations in three nodes, one for each species. 23841: The phylogeny of Iguania has been discussed and showed to be controversial. The number of families changes from three to more than eleven, depending on the character data set used. Morphological data sets have pointed to a more diverse group, while molecular ones showed a more restricted number of families. The sperm morphology has been proposed as an independent source of characters for phylogenetic analyses. Recently, several studies have concerned the morphology of the Squamata and, particulary, Iguania sperm cell, with regards to phylogeny. This work describes the ultrastrcture of the sperm of three genera of the Corytophanidae family, Basiliscus, Corytophanes, and Laemanctus, and does general comparisions of the sperm morphology among Iguanian lizards. Epididymides of two specimen of each corytophanid general were processed through routine methods for transmission electron microscopy. The spermatozoon of three genera shows to be very similar, and no evident differences are observed. The sperm cell consists of three distinct regions: the head, comprising the acrosome complex and the elongate nucleus, the midpiece, containing the centrioles and axoneme surrounded by mitochondria, and the tail, formed by the axoneme surrounded by the plasma membrane solely. The acrosome complex is depressed anteriorly and becomes circular posteriorly. Its most anterior cap, the acrosome vesicle, is subdivided into a cortex and a medulla, with separating cross striations. The midpiece contains three rings of mitochondria, interposed by fragmented dense bodies. Although the results are preliminary, our data and that provided in the literature show that Agamidae, Corytophanidae, Iguanidae, Phrynosomatidae and Tropiduridae possess major similarities among each other, and Polychrotidae and Hoplocercidae could form another group. Complete characterization of the sperm cell of members each iguanian family, compilation of its morphometric characteristics, and the joining with others data sets will confirm or refute the current hypothesis to Iguania relationships.

23842: This paper describes the fish assemblages of Patos Lagoon (10,227 km2) that flows 250 km from the vicinity of Porto Alegre city (30o30 S) to the oceanic end of the jetties (32o12 S) at the city of Rio Grande, RS, Brazil. The shallow waters (< 1.5 m) were sampled using a 9-m beach seine (5 hauls monthly at 17 sampling sites) from March 2000 to April 2001. Deep waters data (> 2.5 m) came from historical data sampled in August and December of 1987 and March and June of 1988 using a 15 m vessel (R/V Larus). In each cruise, a set of 2 randomly-selected stations were chosen from sixteen longitudinal strata, using an 8 m shrimp trawl (1.3 cm bar mesh wings and body with a 0.5 cm bar mesh cod end liner, and a pair of weighted otter doors). A total of 84 species were collected. Beach seine (BS) sampled 64,833 individuals and 59 species and bottom trawl (BT) 35,577 individuals and 58 species. Cluster analysis suggests 3 large strata: a) The estuarine zone (ca 1,000 km2; 68 species; 40 = BT and 50 = BS) and numerically dominated by 3 marine species (Porichthys porosissimus, Macrodon ancylodon, Umbrina canosai), 5 estuarine dependent (Micropogonias furnieri, Lycengraulis grossidens, Mugil platanus, Mugil curema, Brevoortia pectinata) and 3 estuarine resident (Genidens genidens, Atherinella brasiliensis, Jenynsia multidentata); b) The upper-estuarine transitional zone (ca 3,000 km2; 46 species; 33 = BT and 27 = BS) were dominated by 3 estuarine dependent (M. furnieri, L. grossidens, M. platanus), 5 estuarine resident (Achirus garmani, G. genidens, A. brasiliensis, J. multidentata, Odontesthes argentinensis); and 3 fresh-water (Pimelodus maculatus, Parapimelodus nigribarbis, Pimelodella australis); c) The limnic Zone. (ca 6,000 km2; 38 spp; 24 = BT and 28 = BS) were dominated by 2 estuarine dependent (M. furnieri, L. grossidens), 1 estuarine (A. brasiliensis) and 5 fresh-water (P. nigribarbis, P. maculatus, Astyanax bimaculatus, Odontesthes mirinensis, Astyanax fasciatus).
23843: The common name of jaraquis includes two species of Characiformes: Semaprochilodus insignis and S. taeniurus that perform reproductive, trophic and dispersion annual migrations in Central Amazonia. The dispersion takes place during the river flooding periods with the fish occupying several aquatic environments above the main hydrographic subsystems of the area: Purus, Madeira, Solimoes-Amazon and Negro. In this migration the fish schools are exploited intensely by the commercial fishing that lands in Manaus, reaching a production of 6000 annual tons. With the objective of evaluating space and temporary differences among the hydrographic subsystems in relation to relative abundance of both jaraquis species, information concerning the fishing landing was registered between 1996 and 2000 during the period of the dispersion, from March to August. The registered data concerned: number of fisheries; fishery location; closest city to the fishery location, environment type of fishery; subsystem: main river and fork length of the captured samples (cm). The relative abundance was obtained through the number of fish captured per day by fisherman in each fishery. To verify the possible variations of the relative abundance of the two species among the different subsystems an ANCOVA was used, being considered the abundance as dependent variable; the subsystems as factor; the time (years), size of the fish (medium fork length), fry proportion and number of fisheries as covariables. In comparison to fishing locations identified by Petrere (1978) 25 years ago, and the identified ones in this study, it is noticed that most (65%) of the fishing locations have been used traditionally year after year by the jaraquis fishermen during the dispersion period. It was notorious that in 1997 there was little diversity concerning fishing locations, while the following year (1998) a high diversity existed in all subsystems. The ANCOVA model for the relative abundance considering as factor the rivers, revealed significant differences (P < 0.001) in the abundance (F0,05 [5;1156] = 3.17 < Fobs = 4.36) of jaraquis in the different subsystems.

23845: Two species of the genus Pimelodus have been described from the Magdalena River Basin of Colombia: P. clarias and P. grosskopfii. These species have sympatric distributions and carry out annual migrations along the different tributaries. It has been traditionally assumed that each species has a single panmictic population uniformly distributed in the different tributaries. Additionally, the coincidence of their reproductive periods may favor the formation of hybrids at the expense of the parent species. This work aimed at determining whether each species has a single population with a high migration rate or several populations with low migration and sufficient genetic and morphological differentiation distributed among the different tributaries of the Magdalena River Basin. The analysis of morphometric and genetic (RAPDs) data indicate that there is a third group distinct from P. clarias and P. grosskopfii. We suggest that this group represents a third species (Pimelodus A) previously undetected from the Magdalena River Basin. Additionally, we did not find any evidence of hybridization among the two previously recognized species. Finally, significant genetic differentiation was detected among populations of each species, both among the Cauca and Magdalena rivers, and among the high, middle and lower basins of each of these two rivers.
23846: The reefs are complex coastal marine ecosystems of high diversity. They are extremely vulnerable systems to antropogenic and environmental perturbations. Many rocky reefs exist in the Gulf of California; however, there are few studies of the fish communities. In our study we evaluated five locations around San Jose, Island Mexico. The composition, diversity and abundance of rocky reef fishes were analysed in each location from October 2001 - August 2002. These fish communities were recorder through visual censuses using SCUBA equipment, with transects of 50 meters length in two depth levels: 1.5 m and 6 m. A total of 26946 individuals were registered belonging to 84 fish species from 31 families. Fish families with the higher number of species were: Serranidae (10), Labridae (8), Pomacentridae (7), Haemulidae (6) and Scaridae (5). The San Francisquito location presented the highest specific richness; however with the Fisher test no significant differences were found among locations. The index of Biological Value (IVB) determined that dominant species in the rocky reefs were: Stegastes rectifraenum (cortez gregory), Abudefduf troschelii (panamanian sergeant), Thalassoma lucasanum (cortez rainbow wrasse), Scarus ghobban (bluechin parrotfish) and Mulloidichthys dentatus (mexican goatfish). An increase of abundance was shown during months with higher water temperatures (August to October). The fish diversity, were not with significant differences by months, however was between locations and depths.

23847: Two cerrado habitats, approximately 100 m apart, were sampled during 26 continuous days using drift-fence arrays. One site was more open than the other as a result of reduced vegetative cover, primarily trees and shrubs. 23848: The turtles of the Amazon River Basin were an important food source for river people for hundreds of years. They exploited the turtles to their capacity eating what they could and caching live turtles to maintain themselves during periods when hunting other animals was less productive. Turtle populations were able to withstand these user-oriented harvests. But with the arrival of the European settlers, turtle populations began to tumult drastically at the turn of the 19th century. Millions of turtle eggs and adult turtles were rendered annually solely for their oil to light the streets of Manaus. In the last 50 years turtle populations have been exterminated in areas where they were once common for centuries. The best populations of turtles today are found in the most remote and inaccessible regions of Brazil, areas that require 20 to 40 days of boat travel or within reserves, or the environment is so inhospitable that people refuse to venture or live within the realms of the biting bloodsucking and parasitic invertebrates which infest the air and water. Before we can attempt to recuperate populations of turtles on a large spatial scale, we must undertake long term studies of ecology, reproduction, genetics, taxonomy, physiology, and embryology. Only in this way we will be able to recommend what steps need to be taken to increase turtle populations, use them on a sustainable basis, and preserve populations as a national heritage for future generations. Our objective is to study all the aspects of the biology of the freshwater turtles of the Amazon Basin, to discover what methodology must be undertaken to manage this resource correctly in nature. One of the first steps that we are taking is to document the present day distribution, taxonomy, population status, and ecological requirements of all species of Amazonian freshwater turtles.

23849: We had our first freshwater turtle ecology symposium at the ASIH meeting in Williamsburg in 1975 organized by R. Bruce Bury. 23850: Although much is known about the ecological significance of metamorphosis and metamorphic timing, few studies have examined the underlying genetic architecture of these traits, and no study has attempted to associate phenotypic variation to molecular variation in specific genes. Here we report on a candidate gene approach (CGA) to test specific loci for a statistical contribution to variation in metamorphic timing. Three segregating populations (SP1, SP2, and SP3) were constructed utilizing three species of paedomorphic Mexican ambystomatid salamander, including the axolotl, Ambystoma mexicanum. We used these replicated species to test the hypothesis that inheritance of alternate genotypes at two thyroid hormone receptor loci (TRa, TRb) affect metamorphic timing in ambystomatid salamanders. A significant TRa*SP effect indicated that variation in metamorphic timing may be influenced by TRa genotype, however, the effect was not a simple one, as both the magnitude and direction of the phenotypic effect depended upon the genetic background. These are the first data to implicate a specific gene in contributing to variation in metamorphic timing. In general, candidate gene approaches can be extended to any number of loci and to any organism where simple genetic crosses can be performed to create segregating populations. The approach is thus of particular value in ecological studies where target genes have been identified but the study organism is not one of the few well-characterized model systems that dominate genetic research.

23851: The Cuban treefrog (Osteopilus septentrionalis) is an introduced species of treefrog (Anura: Hylidae) in southern Florida, with a distribution that has recently expanded northward from the Florida Keys. Several large populations have been documented in Everglades National Park (ENP). Two native species of treefrogs occur in ENP as well, the green treefrog (Hyla cinerea) and the squirrel treefrog (Hyla squirella). We hypothesized that Cuban treefrogs have a negative impact on the two native treefrog species due to the large size of the Cuban treefrog relative to the native species and the combination of being both a predator of and competitor with the native species. We began a mark and recapture study at five sites in ENP using PVC pipe refugia as a trapping technique to capture the three species of treefrogs. After 15 months of capture-mark- release, we began removing all captured Cuban treefrogs from the populations at our study site, while continuing capture-mark release on the native frogs. We performed survival analysis on the mark-recapture data for each species before the beginning of Cuban treefrog removal and for the two native species since Cuban treefrog removal. Capture rates of native treefrogs at sites with high densities of Cuban treefrogs were low prior to removal, but have increased since removal. Capture rates and survival of native treefrogs at sites with low densities of Cuban treefrogs prior to removal have remained relatively high and constant. The increase in capture rate and apparent survival of the two native species after removal of Cuban treefrogs provides strong evidence that Cuban treefrogs have a negative impact on the native species. We will continue to monitor these populations, and future research will focus on factors that might influence the spread of Cuban treefrogs into the natural areas of south Florida.

23853: Comparative phylogeography of Pacific Northwestern (North America) amphibians reveals similar patterns of divergence into multiple lineages. Phylogenetic trees, using mitochondrial cytochrome b sequences (approx. 500bp), were constructed for five mesic coniferous forest- associated amphibians (Plethodon larselli, Plethodon vandykei, Batrachoseps wrighti, Rhyacotriton cascadae, and Rhyacotriton variegatus). Several deep branching lineages, consisting of sequence differences ranging between 1-4%, have been found within each species. The timing and geographic distribution of divergence among lineages, when compared across taxa, suggest similar geologic events or geographic barriers have led to vicariance in each species. Each species is considered sensitive in Pacific Northwest forests and the patterns of divergence reveal units for conservation. Further, the cross species comparisons provide a model for regional conservation planning in order to preserve biodiversity across forest associated amphibians.

23854: Gulf sturgeon are anadromous and spend 6-8 months of the year in freshwater. They migrate into saline waters where they overwinter and feed on benthic dwelling organisms such as isopods, amphipods, lancets, molluscs, crabs, grass shrimp, and marine worms. Sturgeon spend the cooler months (October or November, through March or April) in estuarine or marine habitats and the balance of the year in freshwater rivers. Gulf sturgeon return to their natal river in the spring, where sexually mature sturgeon spawn. Gulf sturgeon occur in most major river systems from the Mississippi River, east to the Suwannee River, Florida as well as marine waters off the central and eastern Gulf of Mexico, south to Charlotte Harbor. In Florida, Gulf sturgeon are still found in the Escambia, Yellow, Blackwater, Choctawhatchee, Apalachicola, Ocholokonee, and Suwannee Rivers. As Gulf sturgeon require several different factors for survival, sturgeon habitat must be defined in terms of ecosystem conditions. Some important riverine conditions required for sturgeon survival include: large areas of diverse habitat; natural variation in flow, velocity, temperature, and turbidity; a broad prey base; and free flowing sections, which provide suitable spawning sites. An evaluation of programs of rivers and estuary/bay systems within the present and historic ranges of Gulf sturgeon was conducted to determine the presence of suitable habitat for all life history stages and to determine numbers of resident gulf sturgeon populations present. Watersheds examined include bays and major rivers associated with Pensacola Bay, Choctawhatchee Bay, St. Andrew Bay, Apalachicola Bay, Suwannee Sound, and Tampa Bay. Scientists, managers, and policy makers from all Gulf states need to work together to coordinate and facilitate the exchange of information of Gulf sturgeon conservation and recovery activities. Also, biologists and managers need to implement and monitor Gulf sturgeon recovery programs. Management objectives, recommendations, priorities and strategies must be clearly planned out to ensure the system-wide habitat needs of Gulf sturgeon are met. This conservation plan will be used to aid recovery of Gulf sturgeon populations throughout the State of Florida and could be used as a model for other Gulf states.

23855: Many amphibians utilize cutaneous gas exchange when submerged in water. Critical oxygen tension is the minimum amount of dissolved oxygen necessary to sustain metabolic processes. It is often assumed that cutaneous respiration is limited primarily by the ability of oxygen to diffuse through the skin. However, the boundary layer around a submerged amphibian can be an even greater impediment to the absorption of oxygen through the skin. The boundary layer is the layer of still water surrounding the organism through which oxygen must diffuse before it reaches the skin. The thickness of the boundary layer is determined by the rate at which water flows past the amphibian. We monitored the behavior of Rana pipiens in a flow-rate gradient as it gradually reduced the dissolved oxygen in the gradient. We found that as dissolved oxygen was depleted, the frogs spent more time in the parts of the gradient where the current velocity was faster. Our results suggest that current velocity, by reducing the boundary layer, can effectively reduce the critical oxygen tension for amphibians in lotic systems.

23856: The Australian pygopodid Burton's legless lizard (Lialis burtonis) represents an independent evolution of the snake foraging mode; functionally limbless, it subsists via infrequent ingestion of large prey items. Like many of its elapid competitors, Lialis preys largely upon skinks, which tend to have highly developed chemosensory capabilities. I investigated the resolving power of these capabilities in a predator-detection context. Feeding trials suggested that garden skinks (Lampropholis guichenoti) perceive saurophagous elapids as much graver threats than Lialis; skinks often fled or froze when placed in an arena with a snake but rarely did so when confronted with a Burton's. To test this preliminary observation, I presented garden skinks with cotton swabs bearing the scents of Lialis, a sympatric arthropod-eating pygopodid (Pygopus lepidopodus), various elapids, and controls, and scored tongue-flick rates and the incidence of fleeing. Skinks tongue-flicked and fled significantly more in response to elapid scent; Lialis and Pygopus scent elicited reactions statistically indistinguishable from the controls. 23857: The stress response is a highly conserved set of physiological and behavioral mechanisms that are initiated when there is a threat to homeostasis. 23858: The red-eyed treefrog, Agalychnis callidryas, deposits gelatinous egg masses on vegetation overhanging water. Both induced gill regression and exposure to a hypoxic gas mixture stimulate early hatching, indicating that oxygen stress is a hatching trigger. To characterize the respiratory environment of embryos, and assess effects of development and egg surface exposure on oxygen availability, we used a fiberoptic microprobe to measure PO2 in the perivitelline fluid within A. callidryas eggs. Perivitelline PO2 was generally lower later in development, and in eggs with less surface area exposed to air. More surprisingly, there was substantial variation in PO2 within eggs, both spatially and temporally. We observed strong effects of embryo behavior on perivitelline PO2, despite the constant ciliary circulation of the perivitelline fluid. This suggests that embryo movements may serve a stirring function, and so improve gas exchange, and that the position of embryos within their eggs may be important for oxygen uptake. Furthermore, embryos tolerated very low PO2 levels without hatching. For normally and synchronously developing embryos early in the period of hatching competence (4 d old) we measured perivitelline PO2 ranging from 0.2 kPa to 12.4 kPa in the approximate center of the perivitelline space. 23859: Understanding the inter-relationships among morphology, performance, and behavior is fundamental when evaluating links among phenotypic traits and fitness. Fifteen individuals (21%) ignored the predator and continued to chase the prey. Neither body size (SVL range=22-33.5 mm) nor running speed (range=0.32-7.99 m/s) were associated with escape behavior. 23860: The southern United States supports one of the best studied and richest temperate freshwater fish faunas on Earth. I emphasized the total native fauna, faunal subsets (darters, minnows, catfishes, and suckers), and transplanted species. I tested five hypotheses: (1. similarity of native assemblages (and faunal subsets) among drainages is structured in congruence with geographic linkages of drainages; (2. native drainage diversity increases with regional diversity; (3. imperilment is associated with drainage diversity and endemism (4. beta-diversity is decreased via fish transplantation; and (5. native species density in drainages is negatively related to the number of transplanted species. I used distance matrices to compare geo-spatial structuring among faunal subsets and drainage networks and to estimate changes in beta-diversity. Faunal structure (all native and subsets) was significantly and strongly congruent with geographical linkages of drainages, drainage diversity was related to regional diversity, and imperilment was associated with drainage diversity and endemism. The relationship of numbers of transplants to density of native species suggests a saturation boundary that limits numbers of transplants unless native diversity is decreased. 23871: Cooper Creek, Australia's largest dryland river, is highly influenced by variations in flow and is characterised by a boom and bust ecology. 23874: Environmentally-cued polymorphisms are found in a wide variety of species and provide ideal systems for testing ecological and evolutionary hypotheses. 23876: Salamanders, particularly the paedomorphoic Axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum), have provided the classic example of how changes in development influence morphological evolution. We find that paedomorphosis has occurred multiple times among and within salamander families, and that there is surprising diversity among the families of salamanders in the morphological consequences of paedomorphosis for adult morphology. For example, adult morphology among paedomorphic taxa varies continuously from those that are essentially sexually mature larvae to those that are largely "adult." Similarly, few characters are tightly associated with paedomorphosis across lineages, such that different suites of larval traits characterize different paedomorphic lineages. This problem is illustrated in our ongoing phylogenetic studies of the frog family Hylidae and its relatives. Current results are based on parsimony and Bayesian analyses of data from mitochondrial DNA sequences (12S, ND1), nuclear DNA sequences (c-myc, POMC), and non-molecular data (including osteology, larval morphology, karyotypes, and life history), from a sampling of >80 species. Preliminary phylogenetic results suggest that the phylogenetic diversity of hylid frogs in the Neotropics has been concealed at several taxonomic levels. The subfamily Hemiphractinae is distantly related to other hylid frogs and should be recognized as a distinct family. The subfamily Hylinae appears to be a monophyletic group (but includes the Pseudidae), which is the sister taxon of the subfamilies Phyllomedusidinae + Pelodryadinae. The speciose genus Hyla (>300 species) is grossly non- monophyletic and contains considerable cryptic diversity. Two major clades of Hyla, which are not recognized taxonomically, are of similar age to other subfamilies of Hylidae. Both clades are highly diverse in the Amazonian rainforests. One corresponds to the "30-chromosome clade" of some authors, whereas the other includes the gladiator frogs and their relatives. Most other species of Hyla seem to belong to a clade that reaches its highest diversity in Middle American and that also contains most North and Middle American genera of hyline frogs. Several lineages of Hyla in this clade appear to be as old as many of these genera. Unfortunately, much of the recognized and unrecognized phylogenetic diversity in this clade may be lost as amphibian species decline and disappear in the montane Neotropics. The revealed patterns of lineage age and distribution also have implications for explaining global patterns of species richness, and reinforce the importance of the South American rainforests as a "museum of diversity."

23878: In August, 2002, over 100 scientists surveyed the flora and fauna in the Calumet region of Illinois and Indiana. The goal was to see how many species could be identified within a 24 hour period. The purpose was to demonstrate to the public how scientists approach conservation work. Public participation was encouraged. The Calumet region, specifically Wolf and Powder Horn Lakes, has been an area of active change for the past 100+ years. Wolf Lake was once shallow with extensive marshes. Fishes were minnows, catfishes, etc. typical of such environments. In the 1950's, the lake was dredged to provide fill for a highway, then subsequently stocked. Game fishes dominate now. The artificial Powder Horn Lake was also a source of fill for a highway, and did not exist prior to the 1950's. Four Illinois state endangered/threatened fishes have been reported from the area. The blacknose (Notropis heterolepis) and blackchin (Notropis heterodon) shiners were extirpated from Wolf Lake sometime during the last century. The banded killifish (Fundulus diaphanus) can still be found in both lakes. The Iowa darter (Etheostoma exile) has been collected recently in Wolf Lake, but was not collected during the BioBlitz. It is probably being out competed by the invasive round goby (Neogobius melanostomus). It is unclear what impact the invasive bighead (Hypophthalmichthys nobilis) and silver (Hypophthalmichthys molitrix) carps will have when they arrive. Wolf and Powder Horn Lakes are currently very popular with local fishermen and recreationists, but are not what they were 100+ years ago.

23879: High species richness of fishes inhabiting structurally complex habitats is hypothesized to be associated with ecomorphological diversification and niche partitioning. To test this idea, we examined relationships between habitat structural complexity in river littoral-zone habitats and morphological diversity of tropical fishes. We quantified 16 habitat attributes in 45 littoral sites spanning a range of structural complexity in the Cinaruco River, Venezuela. We performed standardized collections of fishes during the day and night, and estimated species richness, abundance, and diversity for each site. We measured 22 morphological variables on specimens of each species collected. Principal components analysis (PCA) of habitat data yielded two axes that modeled >80% of variation across sites. PC 1 described a gradient that separated habitats with high water velocity and low habitat complexity from habitats with low current and high complexity. PC 2 described a gradient contrasting sites with low versus high complexity as defined by structural density, rugosity, and substrate porosity. Regression analysis revealed that species richness during both day and night, and species diversity during daytime, were negatively associated with high flow/low complexity habitats (i.e. habitat PC scores). PCA of morphological variables modeled >70% of variation on the first two axes. PC 1 indicated a gradient contrasting larger fish with relatively elongate dorsal fins, shallow caudal peduncles, and small mouths and eyes versus fish with the opposite suite of attributes. PC 2 described a gradient contrasting fish with relatively elongate snouts and caudal peduncles, shallow body depth, and ventrally-oriented mouths with fish having the opposite characteristics. Regressions of the standard deviation of morphological PC scores of assemblages within sites against habitat PC scores for sites revealed that morphological variation was positively associated with habitat structural complexity during both day and night. This finding suggests that high species richness in structurally complex habitats is facilitated by morphological diversification associated with niche compression/segregation of individual species and/or expansion of total niche space.

23880: Intraspecific geographic variation in turtle morphology and behavior has been well documented in many freshwater turtle species. Growth rates, sexual size dimorphism, and mean population body sizes have been shown to vary significantly among localized geographic populations and often such differences have been attributable to local environmental effects in diet and abiotic factors associated with habitat type. We will present data on morphological and behavioral variation in the northwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata marmorata, using both mark/recapture and radio telemetry data collected over a three year period from three study sites in northern California. These three sites differ in several habitat characteristics. Morphologically, adult turtles differ among sites in several characters such as carapace length, body height, and body width. We hypothesize that size differences may be a result of variation in prey availability, water temperature and/or microhabitat structure among sites. Within sites, it appears that males and females are similar in carapace length but differ in body height and body width. These data coincide with hypotheses that through ontogeny females become more domed or boxier than males to increase internal volume for egg storage and maturation. Behaviorally, adult turtles differ in movement patterns and choice of hibernacula which may be a result of variation in water temperature and/or water velocity among sites. We currently are studying diet, reproductive output, and microhabitat use of pond turtles at these three diverse sites, to gain a better understanding of the plasticity observed in pond turtle morphology and behavior.

23881: Back-calculation methods yield a time series of sizes for individuals and have proved to be valuable tools for both fisheries research and fish ecology. A variety of models have been proposed, each making different assumptions about the relationship between otolith and fish growth. It is difficult, however, to test these assumptions for many fishes. Yet we know that erroneous assumptions can lead to biased estimates of, for example, size-at-age, growth rates, or size-selective mortality. In this study we tested two key assumptions of back-calculations models: 1) that otolith increments are deposited on a daily basis; and 2) that fish growth is proportional to otolith growth. Recently settled gobies, Gobiosoma evelynae and G. prochilos, were kept in the lab for 3 months under variable food conditions. Otoliths were tagged with Alizarin at the start of, 1 month, and 2 months into the experiment to validate daily increment formation. Body length measurements were also taken every two weeks for 3 months. At the end of the experiment, we were able to reconstruct otolith and fish sizes and then compare these sizes to estimates based on back-calculation models. Our results show that 1) G. evelynae and G. prochilos produced daily increments up to three months post-settlement; 2) otoliths increased in size more slowly than fish length, resulting in a weak correlation between relative otolith and somatic growth; and 3) five different back-calculation models (i.e., Biological Intercept, Modified-Fry, Body Proportional Hypothesis, Time-Varying Growth, and an Age-Effects model) provided biased estimates of back-calculated size-at-age. Surprisingly, this bias was present even in models that incorporated disproportionate otolith-fish growth. The Modified-Fry model provided the least biased estimates and suggested that a mixed-model allowing variation among individuals and an underlying allometric relationship between otolith and fish size would be a more appropriate model for these species.

23882: The Casiquiare River flows from the Upper Orinoco to the Upper Rio Negro which should permit biotic exhange between these two great river systems, yet several Amazonian faunal elements are absent from the Orinoco Basin (e.g., Osteoglossidae, Symphysodon spp.) and many allopatric sister taxa are divided between the basins (e.g., Pygocentrus cariba, P. nattereri). The Casiquiare Basin contains diverse aquatic habitats, and water quality varies from clearwater to extreme blackwater conditions. We examined fish assemblage structure relative to 11 habitat characteristics with a dataset containing 215 samples and 454 species from surveys catalogued in the Museo de Ciencias Naturales in Guanare, Venezuela. We performed canonical correspondence analysis based on species presence/absence using two dataset versions: one that eliminated sites having <5 species, and species occurring at <5 sites; and another that eliminated sites having <10 species, and species occurring at <10 sites. Results from both analyses were the same qualitatively. The dominant environmental axis contrasted sites with blackwater versus clearwater conditions. Longitudinal position on the mainstem Casiquiare was correlated (r2= 0.30) with CCA axis-1 scores, indicating blackwater conditions nearer the mouth and clearwater nearer the origin. The second CCA axis was most strongly associated with habitat size and structural complexity. Species were clustered using the centroid method and pairwise squared Euclidean distances calculated from species loadings on CCA axes 1-4. Seven ecological groupings were identified: (1) species normally associated with clearwater in large habitats, (2) species associated with structured habitats in blackwater, (3) species associated with a variety of mostly shallow habitats in blackwater, (4) species associated with channel shoreline areas mostly in clearwaters, and (5-7) three large, relatively ubiquitous species. High fish species richness in the Casiquaire Basin appears to be a function of historical biogeography, high habitat diversity, and semi-permeable barriers to regional dispersal.

23883: Over the past 20 years, an isolated, subalpine population of tiger salamanders (Ambystoma tigrinum nebulosum) in central Colorado has fluctuated dramatically. Historical data and anecdotal observations at this study site suggest repeated population cycles. For the past 13 years, we have closely monitored recruitment, mortality, and life history trajectories of individuals in this stage-structured population (metamorphic adults, paedomorphic adults, multiple year classes of larvae) through an intensive mark-recapture program. Our results suggest that the fluctuations are related to the cyclic production of dominant cohorts that subsequently suppress recruitment for a decade or more. We are currently constructing individually based models to test alternative hypotheses about the generation of these cycles including 1) the role of cannibalism in suppressing recruitment, 2) prey resource depression by dominant year classes, 3) population fluctuations in key prey species, and 4) fluctuations in the physical environment of both the terrestrial and aquatic habitats. Data on salamander life histories and prey resource (benthic and planktonic invertebrates) abundance are used to parameterize the model. Understanding the mechanisms that underlie natural population cycles is critical for distinguishing them from anthropogenically induced amphibian declines.

23884: Observations on the courtship, mating behavior, and mating success of the leaf-frog Phyllomedusa rohdei population were conducted in a site of Atlantic Forest, southeastern, Brazil. This species was classified as prolonged breeder, although male-male competition takes place and there was no evidence for female choice. 23885: In the wet tropics of Queensland, Australia at least 8 species of stream dwelling frogs have experienced population declines, and individuals have been found with fungal infections of Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis, an emerging infectious disease of amphibians. We examined the spatial and temporal pattern of infection prevalence in a sample of extant populations and found differences between species, increased prevalence during the dry season (May to September), and increased prevalence at high elevations (600-800 m). Litoria genimaculata, a recovering species, had the highest prevalence observed (maximum 27%, mean 7.7%). The following hypotheses regarding the underlying causal mechanisms of disease emergence were evaluated: (1) frogs were healthier at sites with low prevalence, (2) tadpoles metamorphose in the dry season and provide and influx of susceptible hosts, (3) disease transmission is density dependent, (4) environmental conditions affect pathogen growth and virulence, (5) environmental conditions affect host behavior and disease transmission, and (6) environmental conditions affect host immune function including antimicrobial skin peptides. There was a lack of evidence for hypothesis (1) and (2), but disease transmission appears to be host density dependent (3) and environmental conditions (4 - 6) are important in all aspects of disease ecology. Thermal environment affects pathogen growth and disease progress, and high temperatures (37°C for 16 hours) can clear frogs and enclosures of chytrid fungus; this has important implications for disease treatment and for explaining the impact of thermoregulatory opportunities and behaviors on disease incidence in the wild. The difference in innate immune function between species and life stages is a useful tool in predicting disease susceptibility. We found that patterns of infection prevalence, and potentially disease emergence, are the product of an interaction between pathogen growth, environmental conditions, and host ecology.

23886: The catfish family Trichomycteridae is a highly diverse group of Neotropical siluroids, distributed over most of South America, from Costa Rica to Patagonia, on both sides of the Andes. In the present paper are being analyzed specimens of Trichomycterus hasemani, T. johnsoni (both currently includes in Trichomycterinae), a new species related to these, and specimens of Copionodontinae, Trichomycterinae, Glanapteryginae, Sarcoglanidinae, Tridentinae, Stegophilinae and Vandelliinae as outgroup. The systematic methodology employed for proposing hypotheses of relationships is cladistic or phylogenetic. The strict parsimony was employed to choose a hypothesis in the presence of character incongruence. The framework for out-group comparisons varied according to the level being discussed. The analysis includes 28 characters, and resulted on a single most parsimonious cladogram. A new subfamily of Trichomycteridae will be described. It comprises one new genus, including the species T. hasemani (as new combination), T. johnsoni (as new combination), and a new species. The new subfamily is hypothesized as monophyletic by the presence of 2 exclusive derived features, and it is sister group of Tridentinae, Stegophilinae and Vandelliinae, by sharing the presence of three derived features. This is an important contribution for the systematic of Trichomycteridae, specially for the better understanding of the classical but polyphyletic group “Trichomycterinae”.

23887: Brain serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT) generally serves an inhibitory role in aggressive behavior. But little is known about how 5-HT works during aggressive interaction and where the related works take place in the brain. Paradise fish has regular and ritual process of aggressive interaction which can be separated into three phases, namely, initial phase, threatening phase, and fighting phase. In initial phase, two fish encounter and swim close to each other. In threatening phase, two fish display shaking, head-tail swimming to threat their opponent. In fighting phase, two fish bite each other. The separation of the behavioral phase makes paradise fish to be a good animal model for study aggressive behavior. This research is divided into two parts. Results of the first experiment indicate that the brain neurons utilize 5-HT to inhibit biting in the threatening phase. When 5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan; serotonin precursor) was depleted in the telencephalon and 5-HT turnover rate in the brain stem decreased, the inhibitory effect of 5-HT declined. Then harmful bites started and the fighting phase took place. According to a report on paradise fish, PCPA (p-chlorophenylalanine; 5-HTP synthesis blocker) treated fish fight earlier. Results of the second experiment indicate that after PCPA treatment synthesis of 5-HTP became insufficient. Subsequent declines in 5-HT cause the inhibitory effect of 5-HT on bite to decrease. Consequently, fighting phase took place earlier after PCPA treatment. In conclusions, paradise fish utilizes 5-HT to inhibit biting and fighting phase starts when the synthesis of brain 5-HT is insufficient. The control center of aggression in the brain of paradise fish may be located in the telencephalon and brain stem.

23889: Among the fishes inhabiting flooded areas, the genus Triportheus due to its wide distribution and adaptability to different biotopes, accounts for a significant amount of the total landings in Manaus. 23890: Leptodactylus validus belongs to the melanonotus species group of Leptodactylus and exhibits an unusual distribution inhabiting Trinidad, Tobago, and the Lesser Antilles, but not the mainland of South America. This distribution is inconsistent with other distribution patterns observed for these islands. Furthermore, slight variation in adult morphology has been observed between the populations in the Lesser Antilles and those from Trinidad and Tobago. However, call data suggested a single species present in Trinidad, Tobago, and the Lesser Antilles. Moreover, calls of Leptodactylus pallidirostris from Venezuela suggested that this taxon might be conspecific with L. validus. Herein, we assessed the genetic diversity among populations of Leptodactylus validus to understand the current status of this taxon. Forty-six specimens of L. validus from Trinidad, Tobago, and the Lesser Antilles islands of Grenada and St. Vincent were included in the analyses along with two other members of the melanonotus group, L. pallidirostris (northern Brazil) and L. wagneri. Leptodactylus chaquensis and L. ocellatus (ocellatus species group) were included as outgroups. A total of 871 base pair positions were collected from the 12S mitochondrial rDNA gene. Sequences were aligned using Clustal X and run under maximum parsimony and maximum likelihood criteria using PAUP*. The results obtained suggest that Leptodactylus validus is not a species complex but represents a single species; with genetic differences among these samples between 0.0 and 0.58%. The sample of L. pallidirostris does cluster within the L. validus clade indicating that, at least for the sample included, L. pallidirostris represents the same species as L. validus (greatest genetic difference between pallidirostris and validus = 0.69%). Leptodactylus wagneri differs in about 8% of its sequences from validus- pallidoristris samples, whereas the outgroups diverge about 9-10% from the ingroup.

23891: As part of the Global Amphibian Assessment, we used the Red List criteria version 3.1 of the World Conservation Union (IUCN) to assess all currently recognized amphibians of Mesoamerica for extinction risk. A total of 27 herpetologists contributed to the assessments of 771 species known from Mexico through Panama. Of the 550 species for which enough information is available to allow an assessment, 52% fall into one of the IUCN Red List threatened (Critically Endangered, Endangered, or Vulnerable) or extinct categories. Four species fell in the extinct category: the Costa Rican toad Bufo periglenes, the Honduran frogs Eleutherodactylus milesi and Eleutherodactylus chrysozetete, and the Mexican salamander Ambystoma lermaens. Overall, the endemic, highland species with small distributions were the most threatened whereas the widely distributed lowland species had the most secure populations. Taxonomically, salamanders were the most threatened order (72% of species threatened), followed by anurans (43%). Caecilians are virtually unknown with only three of the 13 species in the region studied sufficiently to allow classification. On a national basis, Mexico has the most threatened fauna (55% of species threatened) whereas Belize has the most secure fauna with just 8% of its species threatened. Habitat destruction is the single most important factor causing populations to decline, although a substantial number of montane species have disappeared from regions where seemingly suitable habitat remains. In addition to documenting the conservation status of these species, this exercise produced a valuable compendium of previously unpublished data summarizing recent fieldwork on amphibian populations throughout the region and producing digital range maps for each species. These data will be published together with data from the rest of the world in late 2003. Web access to the data will be via www.redlist.org and www.natureserve.org (species from the Americas only).

23892: Previous studies of spitting in cobras have focused on the specialized morphology of the fangs exit orifice. This dentitional morphology explains the unusual directionality of the venom stream, but not the actual mechanics of spitting. Spitting cobras are unusual among venomous snakes in that they routinely expulse venom without making physical contact with their target. This suggests that the different species of spitting cobras all possess a specialized form of release mechanism for venom flow. The kinematics of the spitting behavior were explored using still photography and high-speed digital videography. This analysis revealed a consistent deformation of the palate immediately prior to the release of venom, commonly accompanied by an upward rotation of the snout. Examination of preserved and skeletal material suggested that the palatal deformations were caused by ventral buckling of the pterygoid-palatine and ectopterygoid- maxilla joints; rotation of the maxilla and palatine in the sagittal plane would also explain the observed rotation of the snout. Of the muscles attaching to the palato-maxillary arch in elapids, the Protractor Pterygoideus appears to be best positioned to cause the observed deformations. We hypothesize that the rotations of the maxilla deform the fang sheath, and underlying soft tissues of the distal venom delivery system, thereby permitting venom flow. This hypothesis was explored using a variety of experimental techniques including: stimulation of the Protractor Pterygoideus to replicate the displacements of the palato-maxillary arch; recordings of venom pressure from the fang and venom duct concurrent with stimulation of the Protractor Pterygoideus and the Adductor Mandibulae Externus Superficialis (which surrounds the venom gland); and electromyography of these two muscles. The results are consistent with the Protractor Pterygoideus functioning in Asiatic and African spitting cobras as a release for venom flow, specifically by causing deformation and displacement of the soft tissues associated with the fang sheath.

23893: The analysis of fish species richness within a geographical area is useful to solve biogeographical and ecological questions, particularly in groups such as goodeids, that have most of their diversification within a basin. The Goodeidae comprises 2 subfamilies of viviparous fishes of Nearctic origin occurring in North America. The Goodeinae contains approximately 40 species and is entirely endemic to the Mesa Central of Mexico. Within this area, the Lerma-Santiago River Basin is the major hydrographic system, and is where most of the goodeins are found. Geographical distribution of freshwater fishes can be analyzed based on their capacity of survival and establishment considering their particular ecological conditions. The Genetic Algorithm for Rule-Set Preditcion (GARP) is a machine-learning system designed to find non-random associations between species point occurrences and environmental information, to build predictive models of ecological niches of species. GARP has proved a useful tool to generate robust ecological niche models of species, which can be then used to predict geographic distribution of species. We used GARP to build distributional niche models for 37 species of goodeids. Our findings suggest that conditions in the Lerma Basin clearly define a nested pattern of areas capable to host different number of species, with the highest species richness in the middle part of the basin, progressively decreasing toward the borders. Conditions become unsuitable for goodeids in the neighbor basins (Balsas and Panuco). This suggest that these regions represent geographical barriers that have constrained the dispersal possibilities for these species, explaining why although goodeids diversified about 11.5 million years ago they have not established into other regions ecologically suitable. Finally, the middle part of the Basin seems to be a hot-spot for this group and deserves more attention for biogeographical, conservation and resource management studies.

23894: Osteological and soft anatomical systems in the African characiforms previously recognized as the Alestidae and in outgroup taxa were examined to determine whether that family as previously defined was monophyletic and to advance a hypothesis of relationships within the Alestidae. The overall most parsimonious hypothesis of relationships based on 200 characters indicates that the Alestidae as previously delimited (the African Characidae of many previous authors) is the closest relative of Chalceus, a genus of South American characiforms previously assigned to the family Characidae. Chalceus is consequently shifted into the Alestidae and that family, thus, becomes the only Trans-Atlantic family-level group within the Characiformes. The intrafamilial phylogenetic analysis permits a resolution of the suprageneric relationships within the Alestidae. This hypothesis indicates that various previously proposed suprageneric assemblages within that family do not delimit monophyletic groups and are consequently not recognized. Two separate episodes of miniaturization and one episode of gigantism are hypothesized to have occurred within the evolution of the Alestidae. That family demonstrates the greatest proportional range in body sizes of any comparably speciose clade within the Characiformes. The presence of members of the Alestidae in the freshwaters of South America and Africa indicates a minimum age of the Alestidae of 90, and perhaps 112, million years. Evaluation of fossil alestids within the context of the final most parsimonious phylogeny indicates that the ancestors of Alestes, Arnoldichthys, Brycinus, Bryconaethiops, and Hydrocynus evolved prior to the early Eocene (Cuisian of Upper Ypresian), 49 to 54.8 million years ago. The fossil genera Alestoides and Sindacharax appear to be most closely to Alestes and Bryconaethiops, respectively.

23895: The association of colour polymorphism and ecological aspects of Enyalius sp was investigated in two gallery forests of Cerrado from Brazil Central. The follow aspects were appointed as possible maintenance mechanism of colour polymorphism in this specie: sex, sexual maturity, reproduction activity, climatic sazonality, growth rate and permanence rate. The general association Mantel-Haenszel (QCMH) test and Bayesian network was used to investigated the association between ecological aspects and colour polymorphism. The permanence and growth rate were calculated from capture-mark-recapture study, 22 month long. I identify 10 colour pattern from a sample with 268 individuals, with the combination of dorsal colour elements: bars, circles, lozenge, paravertebral stripes. There are signifcative diferences between male and female, but there are no exclusives pattern, what is in disagree whit the hypothesis that the colour pattern is used to intraspecific communication. Juveniles shows much more bar, probably as a predation scape mechanism, since the lateral coloration turns in to a disruptive effect. There are no significative association of sexual maturity, reproductive activity or climatic sazonality with colour pattern. The morphs doesn't show performance differences, seen as CRC or growth rate, or permanency rate. The chromatic polymorphism could increase the camouflage efficiency in species subject of visual oriented predator, reducing the individual predation risk, what represent one advantage in relation with monomorphic species. The main lizards predators are birds and diurnal snakes, visual oriented species. , a direct selection over colour polymorphism through the predation seems to be the most plausive maintenance mechanism in Enyalius sp.

23896: The frog Leptodactylus labyrinthicus is widely distributed throughout South America. However, its reproduction is poorly known. This species was studied from Aug/2001 to Feb/2003 in the municipalities of Rio Claro (22° 19′ S; 47° 42′ W) and Itirapina (22° 15′ S; 47° 49′ W), ca. 30 km apart, State of São Paulo, Brazil. Observations began at dusk and finished around 1100 pm. Occasionally individuals were monitored throughout the night. Data on calling sites, reproductive period, size of adults, clutch size, and oviposition sites were registered. Reproduction started at the end of the dry season (Aug-Sep), and extended throughout the rainy season. However, there were differences concerning the reproductive period between both localities related mainly to local rainfall. Males called from the edges of temporary or permanent ponds, began vocalization activity at dusk, and finished around 1100 or 1200 pm. During the peak of the reproductive period calling activity could extend up to 400 or 500 am. Mean snout-vent length (SVL) of females was 151.7 mm (N = 11, SD = 11.6, range 165 - 125), and mean SVL of males was 155.9 mm (N = 17, SD = 12.5, range 180 - 135). Males and females did not exhibit sexual size dimorphism in SVL (t = 0.9032; p = 19). Eggs embedded in foam nests were observed mainly in Oct- Dec at both sites. Mean number of eggs per clutch was 4099 (N = 5, SD = 3085.6, range 9470 - 1817); mean diameter of foam nests was 25.4 cm, and mean height was 11.4 cm. Both populations occurred at low densities. The species exhibited prolonged breeding period associated mainly to rainfall, as observed for other populations in Brazil.

23897: The Cantão State Park is located at the right margin of Araguaia River, close to the city of Caseara, State of Tocantins. The park area is approximately 89,000ha of floodplains covered mainly by primary forests and hundreds of lakes. The present investigation is part of a larger project developed in that area in 2000 by a team of researchers from INPA and it aims to determine the abundance of fish species, by means of catch per unit of effort (CPUE). The fishing equipment used was a set of 10 gillnets of different mesh sizes (24 to 140 mm), in 24 hours fisheries, in six lakes, in four different hydrological periods (high, lowing, low and rising water). All fishes were identified, counted and weighted and the results were expressed in terms of number of specimens and biomass by square meter per 24 hours. Out of the 233 species recorded, 136 were captured with gillnets and for this group, CPUE was of 1.83 individuals and 154.4g/m2/24h. The lowest CPUE value was found during the flood period (0.43 specimens and 66.82 g/m2/24h) whereas the highest was during the lowing period (2.57 and 270 g/m2/24h). The dominant species in number of specimens were Auchenipterichthys thoracatus, Moenhkausia dichroura, Bryconops sp. and Hemiodus unimaculatus. Considering weight, Pygocentrus nattereri, Osteoglossum bicirrhosum, Hydrolycus armatus, Rhaphiodon vulpinus and Ageneiosus brevifilis dominated in the catches. We conclude that Cantão State Park presents a rich and abundant fish fauna, with fishing yield above the average found for other places in Amazonia. This also indicates that Cantão is a healthy environment and as such it deserves the conservation efforts developed so far for the area.

23898: Bull sharks, Carcharhinus leucas , and nurse sharks, Ginglymostoma cirratum , are two shark species that are found in close association with humans. Divers near shallow reefs often encounter nurse sharks. Many times divers will interact with nurse sharks, resulting in bites. Bull sharks are known to be an aggressive species and often feed in the shallow beach environments where swimmers are attacked. Little is known about the composition of bacteria species associated with either shark species. Oral swabs were collected from populations of both species in the Gulf of Mexico and the Caribbean Sea to identify bacteria and determine possible health hazards that may be associated with infections from bites. In addition, cloacal swabs were collected to identify possible antibiotic-resistant species of bacteria that may be present in these sharks. No published literature is available on the possible implications of antibiotic resistance in sharks from the marine environment. Studies conducted on birds of prey in close proximity to humans show great potential for antibiotic resistance to natural and synthetic antibiotics. Results will be presented on data from Louisiana and Belize. The Louisiana populations represent sharks that are rarely in direct contact with swimmers, while the Belize populations are regularly in contact.

23899: An overview of studies involving elasmobranchs is given, including current trends for the future. Past studies mostly focused on systematics and commercial exploitation. Present studies are focusing on fisheries biology, movement patterns and greater efforts towards legislation and conservation of elasmobranchs as a sustainable resource. The immediate future will hold constant updates on fisheries biology models coupled with information on movement patterns via satellite tracking. Further studies of immunology and other biological fields will follow as well.

23901: The Atlantic sharpnose ( Rhizoprionodon terraenovae ), bonnethead ( Sphyrna tiburo ), blacknose ( Carcharhinus acronotus ), and finetooth ( Carcharhinus isodon ) sharks are small coastal species caught in directed fisheries and as bycatch in waters off the eastern U.S. coast. A new stock assessment of the small coastal shark (SCS) complex and individual species was conducted using new biological and fishery information that has become available in the last decade. CPUE series analyzed through Generalized Linear Mixed Models revealed fairly flat trends. Several stock assessment models were used to evaluate the status of small coastal sharks using Bayesian statistical techniques. A nonequilibrium Schaefer biomass dynamic model was used to describe the population dynamics of exploited SCS stocks using the SIR algorithm for numerical integration. A reparameterized, nonequilibrium Schaefer surplus production model using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method for numerical integration was also applied. This state-space model accounts for both process and observation errors in a unified framework. Finally, a lagged recruitment, survival and growth (LRSG) state-space model was used to model the dynamics of SCS stocks. Results of the base-case and alternative scenarios indicate that the current level of removals is sustainable for the SCS aggregate and the individual species analyzed.
